Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Why is the Trump administration trying to dismantle the ICC?
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The US has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. Washington’s sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court (ICC) came hours after one of its former judges, Navi Pillay, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. It has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. The US has denounced the court in the past, especially after it issued the arrest warrants for Israeli officials. Washington has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges, but the latest move seeks to cripple the operations of the court, according to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Why is the US so against the ICC? And will Europe defy Washington and defend the court? events.summary: Fresh off final game with Argentina, Messi leads Miami vs DC United in Major League Soccer in the United States. Lionel Messi said his farewell to ‌the Argentina national team earlier this week when he played his final match ⁠for the three-time world champions, ending a 21-year international career. Inter Miami won the Campeones Cup on September 16 in their first match under recently hired coach Kily Gonzalez, but ‌they drew with San Diego and lost 2-1 at Columbus last Sunday in two league matches since. Messi has been stellar once again this season, with 21 goals and 13 assists in league play as he chases his third consecutive MLS MVP award, but Miami will need more contributors as it has won only once in its last 10 league matches. “Leo is a person who every day conveys it ⁠and passes it on to his teammates, and he demands from ⁠all of us that you have to be at 100% in every way,” Gonzalez said on Friday. The 39-year-old’s final bow came in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed ⁠Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires on Tuesday. Messi left as the country’s most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international stage ‌into ‌a story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs.

events.title: Apple discloses deal to hire team and license tech from personalized podcast startup Huxe
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Apple revealed in a regulatory filing that it has reached an agreement to bring on team members and technology from personalized audio startup Huxe, in what’s commonly known as a reverse acqui-hire deal. As first reported in MacRumors , Apple disclosed to the European Commission that it has agreed to make employment offers to “certain employees of Huxe AI,” and to “receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights.” Reverse acqui-hires emerged in recent years as a way for larger companies to hire key team members and license technology from startups without acquiring the startups outright — presumably allowing them to build up AI talent and tech without drawing as much antitrust scrutiny. (Confusingly, these deals have both been referred to as “reverse acqui-hires” and as plain old “acqui-hires.” ) In the case of Huxe, the startup was founded by developers who’d previously worked on the AI-generated podcast features in NotebookLM (recently renamed Gemini Notebook ). But Huxe announced on May 21 that it was shutting down , with the team posting on the Huxe website that the company would be removing its app from the Apple and Google stores, halting service, and deleting user data. “The team is moving on to new things, and we won’t be continuing development of the product,” the company said. It also thanked its users, saying, “The fact that you used it, told friends about it, sent us your suggestions and your ideas, made it feel like we built it together.” On June 9, shortly after Huxe’s announcement, Apple notified the European Commission of its deal. The filing does not say who received employment offers or if they accepted. Nor does it disclose anything about Apple’s plans. Possibly related: Huxe’s shutdown announcement came just a day after Spotify unveiled AI-powered podcast generation features of its own , so Apple could be hoping to add similar functionality to its Podcasts app. Tech executives seem enamored with the idea that personalized audio can replace regular podcasts (and maybe even parent-child interaction ?), though it’s not clear how many normal listeners agree. events.title: Manchester United held by ten-man Tottenham as woes for both continue
events.summary: Ten-man Tottenham fight back from a goal behind to draw 1-1 at Manchester United in the Premier League. Dominic Solanke rescued a 1-1 draw for 10-man Tottenham to ramp up the pressure on Manchester United boss Michael Carrick on Saturday. Solanke’s stoppage-time header edged Spurs off the foot of the Premier League table after it seemed like they would pay a heavy price for not taking their chances in a dominant display at Old Trafford. list 1 of 3 A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona list 2 of 3 Ronaldo returns after Portugal quarrel to score in Al-Nassr win list 3 of 3 Africa Cup of Nations may stay as a biennial event, says CAF chief Motsepe Bryan Mbeumo put United in front against the run of play 17 minutes from time before Rodrigo Bentancur was shown a straight red card. But not for the first time this season, Carrick’s men failed to make a man advantage count. Manchester City won 1-0 at Old Trafford last month despite playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Solanke stooped to head in Sandro Tonali’s cross to leave United with just six points from their opening six league games. Tottenham had three weeks to fester on dropping to the bottom of the table during the international break after a disastrous start to their 300-million-pound ($397m) rebuild in the transfer window. Roberto De Zerbi’s men took until the closing stages of their fifth league game to even score a goal, and a much-improved performance was undone by a familiar lack of cutting edge up front. Before kickoff, the United supporters took aim at local rivals City, who have been found guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League financial rules. But the home fans soon had their own troubles to concentrate on as Spurs penned United inside their own half. Solanke should have opened the scoring when he fired too close to Senne Lammens before Mohammed Kudus blasted wide at the end of a flowing Tottenham move. Chances continued to come and go for the visitors after the break, much to the frustration of a visibly animated De Zerbi. Solanke spooned over, and Destiny Udogie curled wide before the game appeared to run away from Spurs. Carrick helped turn the tide with a triple substitution on the hour mark. Carlos Baleba added more dynamism to United’s midfield on his first appearance since a 70-million-pound ($92.6m) move from Brighton, while the introduction of Joshua Zirkzee allowed Matheus Cunha to drop into a deeper role. United had barely threatened Antonin Kinsky’s goal until Mbeumo was afforded too much room to spin onto Cunha’s pass and fire into the far corner. To compound Tottenham’s woes, Bentancur was then shown a straight red card for a headbutt on Luke Shaw after an angry confrontation between the pair. But United again failed make their man advantage count. Solanke finally ended Tottenham’s wait since May for an away goal when he outmuscled Lisandro Martinez to glance in Tonali’s cross. The point edges Spurs up to 18th, with only goals scored keeping them inside the relegation zone. United are just three points better off in 12th.

events.title: Ship captains and crews transiting the Strait of Hormuz make so much danger pay that they’re ‘almost being viewed as mercenaries’
events.summary: The high-risk, high-reward business of moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz has gotten riskier and more rewarding. Despite steady attacks from Iran, oil tankers and other commercial vessels have continued flowing through the narrow waterway. With protection from the U.S. military and help from pipelines bypassing the strait, Persian Gulf oil flows returned to prewar levels . But seeking to reassert its leverage over the global oil chokepoint, Iran has stepped up drone and missile strikes on ships recently, including those outside the immediate vicinity of Hormuz. While traffic has dipped in response, ships continue to cross, with many making shuttle runs in and out of the Gulf to unload oil cargoes via ship-to-ship transfers. Then other vessels deliver the barrels to customers. For those onboard the ships willing to tolerate the risks in the Gulf, a hefty payday awaits. Tanker captains can earn $100,000 a month for transiting the strait, plus a $50,000 bonus for each trip, sources told the Financial Times . That “danger money” is up from regular pay of about $15,000 a month, and is necessary for shipowners to keep their fleets crewed. Meanwhile, sailors typically make at little as $1,500 a month. But trips through Hormuz can bump up earnings by at least four to six times their normal rates, the report said. Other hot spots also offer hazard enhancements, albeit less than what’s available for Hormuz trips. According to the FT , captains and sailors get double pay in the southern Red Sea , where Houthis have been attacking Saudi ships, and in the Gulf of Oman, where many ship-to-ship transfers take place after Hormuz shuttle runs. Because many ships and their crews are dedicated to the shuttle runs, they are in constant peril—allowing them to stack up all the bonuses and danger money for each trip. A source told the FT that those brave enough to stomach the near-constant threat of attacks are “almost being viewed as mercenaries,” though some unwilling crew members are reportedly being pressured to stay onboard. Since the Iran war started on Feb. 28, at least 93 ships have been hit, and 24 sailors have been killed, according to the International Maritime Organization. In addition to the hazard pay for crews, shipowners are also paying for insurance, and the war risk can command 6%-10% of a ship’s value—translating to up to $20 million for a supertanker sailing through the Gulf. All the added costs have made shipping expensive too. Freight rates for cargoes crossing the Strait of Hormuz hit a record high of $1.3 million per day, up from last year’s daily rate of $20,000-$50,000. All the ships needed to get oil out of the Gulf have also contributed to a global tanker shortage that’s spiked freight rates around the world. Shipbroker Gibson  pointed out that hiring a tanker to travel from the U.S. to China costs about $80 million, more than the $74 million price tag for a standard SpaceX Falcon 9 launch. Brokerage SSY estimated that rates are now the highest since the advent of the supertanker in the 1960s, even after adjusting for inflation. Shipping costs have become so extreme that oil producers and even commodities traders are looking to own their own tankers to control the expenses. But if freight costs get too high, they could erase the margins that can be earned from oil and refined fuels. For instance, European refiner Repsol saw its margin drop from $36 per barrel in the third quarter to $15 in October, according to analysts at RBC. Further reduction in margins could eventually force refiners to reduce how much crude they process. The hazard premium could get worse in the Persian Gulf. Analysts have warned the Iranian regime, facing an existential threat to its rule, could re-escalate the war and take back its grip on the oil trade. Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, pointed out recently that Iran can still destroy regional oil infrastructure, such as drilling and refining capacity, and can escalate if President Donald Trump rejects diplomatic off-ramps. “Iran did not wage a scorched earth campaign—but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long,”  he posted on X  late last month. “That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
events.summary: US leader suggests Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war amid tensions with Kyiv over a diesel deal with Russia. United States President Donald Trump says Ukraine should replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a new leader, lashing out at him for Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said at the White House on Saturday, adding that “for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does.” list 1 of 3 Russia kills 20 in Ukraine as US hosts ‘productive’ talks to end war list 2 of 3 Putin tells Trump peace talks are unlikely, cites Ukraine drone attacks list 3 of 3 Why is US turning to Russia for diesel despite sanctions? Trump said that under Zelenskyy, Ukraine has “lost 30 percent of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over 2 million people killed. That’s a war that should have never have started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Following the remarks, Ukraine’s foreign minister defended Zelenskyy. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Andriy Sybiga said in a post on X. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.” Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices ahead of the US midterms, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure. He has also sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices. Trump suggested on Saturday that if he had been US president in 2022 “that war would have never started”. “There was no reason that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence,” he said. The remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, according to Ukrainian officials. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than four and a half years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed at least 60 people over the past four days. On Friday, Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine. He said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional three million tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he added. The move drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy. After Russia’s strikes on Saturday, he wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia”. Zelenskyy said the attacks show Moscow understands “any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities.” The president said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days. He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s used to intercept Shahed drones. Ukraine’s European allies have expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions. Trump’s announcement about the deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine. Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami on Friday to discuss a proposal to end the war.

The winger was Barca’s brightest spark in the first half, continuing his fine goalscoring form for England in the recent Nations League matches. Barca defender Eric Garcia forced a save from Getafe goalkeeper David Soria with a drive from distance as Flick’s side controlled the game. Getafe defender Zaid Romero gave the ball away in his own box for Barca’s second, passing it straight to Jesus, who stroked into the bottom corner. Soria denied Olmo before Yamal teed up Kounde for the third. The defender, making a record 194th appearance for Barca for a French player, overtaking Eric Abidal, was on hand to turn home from close range from teenage star Yamal’s cross. Barca, who also won their Champions League opener, have nine victories from nine matches across all competitions.

events.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
events.summary: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms F ootball, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game. What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “ spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales. Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride. The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this. How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air. The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made. But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then. The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis. That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess. At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly. Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

events.title: Shipping companies offering sailors 'crazy money' to transit Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Shipping companies offering captains $US100k a month to transit Strait of Hormuz Before the US-Israel attacks on Iran, well over 100 commercial ships passed through the strait each day. ( Reuters ) Oil tanker captains in the Persian Gulf are being paid up to $US100,000 (about $143,000) a month to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, industry insiders and maritime unions say, as Iran and the United States continue to impose separate blockades of the critical waterway. Gulf oil producers are increasingly desperate to get their oil out of the region and onto market after a recent step-up in attacks from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on tankers attempting to pass the dangerous choke-point. The new wave of assaults on vessels followed reports last month that crude shipments were edging back toward prewar levels, indicating Middle Eastern oil exports were recovering. Facebook ads seen by the ABC show some seafarers in Asia have been offered double or triple their pay as well as "danger money" bonuses worth tens of thousands to work in the Gulf. The vast sums of money are being used to persuade them to stay on vessels and continue running the strait despite the risk of attack. "Right now [the captains] are getting paid crazy," Indian marine engineer Harshal Singh told a podcast in late September. "A ship captain usually get 15 lakh Rupees per month (about $22,000). Right now in Strait of Hormuz they can make 1 crore rupees (about $143,000) in a month." The commercial tankers struck as they transited the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks were "highly, highly targeted", according to marine traffic watchers. Captains receive pay increases while they are in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Oman, and again during each Hormuz transit, according to Indian union representatives. But the journeys come with substantial risk, with at least 24 seafarers killed in 100 confirmed incidents since the war began, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. In this month alone, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has recorded nine incidents of attacks on tankers within the Strait of Hormuz. For many shipowners, the risks are being outweighed by revenues reaching levels rarely seen in the industry's recent history. "They are offering [seafarers] double, sometimes even five times the wages they will get during the transit of Hormuz," Manoj Yadav, the general secretary of the Mumbai-based Forward Seamen's Union of India, told the ABC. In India, where the vast majority of the world's seafarers are from, the salary bump is a huge draw. But unions have warned seafarers are at risk of being exploited and some have very little choice in performing a job that could cost them their lives. The strait's significance has been in the spotlight since Iran placed an effective chokehold on the shipping route, used for 20 per cent of the world's oil and gas trade, at the end of February. After months of gridlock, the US responded by implementing its own blockade on Iranian shipments through the critical energy artery. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war. ( Reuters ) Sailing into the Gulf, loading and coming out again now carries great risk. While the US intercepts vessels attempting to trade with Iran, the IRGC targets ships sailing in the strait and harasses them, including through drone overflights and surveillance, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center said last weekend. It means fewer operators are willing to make the voyage, and transit remains below typical prewar traffic levels, when more than 100 commercial vessels crossed the strait each day. "I think the issue is less [to do with] insurance and more availability of crews that are willing to make that hazardous transit because of a significant amount of attacks," former Australian naval officer Jennifer Parker told the ABC. An increasing number of ships have attempted to get around Iranian controls by taking the south corridor route, which hugs the Omani coast, rather than the north corridor route, which sails close to Iran. Ships navigating the strait also take "dark journeys" by travelling at night with their GPS signalling equipment switched off. Marine intelligence companies previously told the ABC some of these dark transits have occurred with the knowledge and permission of Iran via diplomatic-level negotiations. Others have not.

events.title: Archie the flying fox joined Richard Morecroft behind the news desk
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft's foster journey with grey-headed flying fox Archie Late veteran presenter Richard Morecroft is best known for his decades of news reading, but unbeknownst to viewers, he was sometimes joined at the desk by a furry companion. Morecroft, who died this week aged 70, was a familiar presence as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS. But if you were to peek under his shirt as he read particular news bulletins in late 1987, you would find another passion. Wrapped inside a handkerchief was a baby grey-headed flying fox. Morecroft adjusting Archie before presenting the NSW 7PM news bulletin. ( ABC News ) Archie was considered well-versed in current affairs. ( ABC News ) Morecroft originally thought it was a boy and named it Archie. "I think probably of its species, that little flying fox ... was probably the best educated in terms of knowledge of news and current affairs," he said in late December, 2001. "Thousands of people watching at home wouldn't have known that there was a small furry animal wrapped in a handkerchief stuffed inside my shirt." The presenter said the handkerchief was used to keep the pup warm. Morecroft fostered two-week-old Archie, who he believed belonged to the Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park colony, after completing a Wildlife Information and Rescue Service (WIRES) training course in the late 1980s. Archie and Morecroft recorded their journey together in a 30-minute Wildscreen episode with ABC TV's natural history unit, titled Raising Archie. "This is a young grey-headed flying fox which came from a colony not very far from Sydney," he explained during the program. "His mother died and so I'm the new foster parent for a few months. "What we're hoping is that eventually he will be able to rejoin the colony and get back into the wild." Morecroft encouraging Archie to fly. ( ABC News ) He said pups needed lots of attention. "They have to have nappies changed, their fur cleaned and be wrapped up as they would be in their mother's wings." At one point, Morecroft encouraged an older Archie to fly. The documentary also highlighted threats facing colonies, including overdevelopment and the impact of flying foxes raiding orchards. Morecroft also interviewed iconic naturalist, David Attenborough, with an older bat named Gollum. A letter Morecroft sent to his trainer in November 1987 reveals more about how he cared for Archie. "It's been a delight (and occasionally quite a challenge) to have the opportunity to raise a young flying fox," he wrote. "According to weight and forearm measurements (90 grams and 60 millimetres) a couple of days after receiving her, she must have been very young when orphaned. "However, she seems to be progressing well (now 107g and forearm 71mm) and is enjoying exercise sessions." Baby Archie, the grey-headed flying fox. ( ABC News ) He said Archie "took particular delight" in being groomed. "Warm, damp cotton buds are great for the armpits and the 'hip pits!'" the letter read. "And a soft baby's toothbrush grooming the fur produces either a relaxed ecstasy or a vigorous cooperative effort with tongue and one foot." John George, whose late wife Helen trained hundreds of people to care for native animals, including Morecroft, said the presenter was "totally committed". "She loved it, loved him and she could rely on him totally," he said. Morecroft was an active member of the wildlife rescue, as seen here with the founder Mikla Lewis (centre) at the 1991 Christmas party. ( Supplied: WIRES ) WIRES founder Mikla Lewis still remembers being surprised by Morecroft's call. "One day I picked up the phone and this voice on the other end said, 'Hello, I'm Richard Morecroft and I'd like to join'," she said. She said he was "really besotted" with Archie. WIRES bat unit coordinator Storm Stanford said bats these days did not stay with carers as long, and incubators were used for warmth to reduce disease risks. "Back when Richard was doing it, we didn't know about lyssavirus or, I think it just came in the year after or a few months after he was doing the caring," Ms Stanford said. Archie was fostered at two weeks old. ( ABC News ) She said the disease was spread by saliva through a cut or a bite, which could cause a fever, fatigue and seizures. There is a vaccine, but people are told not to handle bats, even while wearing gloves. Ms Stanford said caring for a pup could take at least four or five hours a day. Archie was eventually sent to a creche to socialise with other bats away from their carers, before being released back into the colony.

events.title: Photos: Thousands march across Europe to demand end to Israel’s war on Gaza

Demonstrations in London, Berlin, and Rome denounce ongoing Israeli attacks on Gaza ‘ceasefire’ anniversary. Several thousand pro-Palestinian protesters have marched through European capitals, demanding an end to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. In London, demonstrators moved past the British parliament carrying placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine”. “We are here today to mark three years of the ongoing genocide in Gaza,” Aimee Shalan, director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, told the AFP news agency, calling for “full sanctions on Israel”. A so-called ceasefire took effect a year ago, but Israel continues to strike Gaza on a near-daily basis. The attacks have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the truce began, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. London’s Metropolitan Police said they made “several arrests”, including a man and a woman holding placards supporting Palestine Action, a group banned under UK law. Officers had also warned they would use public order powers to compel anyone wearing face coverings to remove them, pledging “zero tolerance” for hate crimes. In Berlin, about 3,500 people joined a march organised by United for Palestine, police said, setting off from a square between the chancellery and parliament. Many condemned Germany’s arms exports and longstanding military support for Israel. Similar marches were held in Warsaw and Rome, where protesters denounced ongoing Israeli bombardment and their governments’ ties with Israel, echoing calls for an immediate and lasting ceasefire. Israel’s genocide has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,200 Palestinians since October 2023.

events.title: I moved my family from Australia to New York City 12 years ago. It's led to some very expensive regrets.
events.summary: Although I have some expensive regrets, I am ultimately glad I moved my family from Australia to New York City many years ago. Courtesy of Natasha Silva-Jelly I grew up in Australia and always dreamed of living in New York City , so I moved my family there. Living here comes with costs, like missing family in Australia and being unable to visit them often. We've spent a ton on rent, and I've moved around the city a lot, but there's no place I'd rather be. It was my lifelong dream to live in New York City . Wild, given that I was born in a small rural town in Australia, where I grew up riding dirt bikes, not reading fashion magazines. The Land Down Under was a big, beautiful place offering an idyllic, laid-back beach life, but I always felt a pull toward The Big Apple. That lust further ignited in the '90s as I watched the city depicted in shows like "Friends" and "Sex and the City." So in 2014, on the cusp of turning 40, I dragged my husband, our Bengal cat, and our two sons — then 2 and 9 — to New York. We told ourselves we'd come for a year, for an adventure. Twelve years later, I'm still here. It's certainly been one hell of a (ridiculously expensive) ride. The rent we've paid feels astronomical, and we've moved so many times Some parts of New York City, including where we chose to live in Lower Manhattan, can get especially expensive. Ultima_Gaina/Getty Images In New York City, rental costs are no joke. We traded our beautiful 1890s cottage — three-bedroom, two-bath, front porch, huge yard, tree-lined street, 10 minutes from Bondi Beach — for a two-bedroom loft apartment in Tribeca that cost us $8,000 a month. (This is not unusual for a two-bed in this neighborhood.) By comparison, the monthly mortgage on our cottage in Sydney was, after conversion, less than half of that price. Still, we knew we were choosing to live in a more expensive neighborhood in Lower Manhattan, and we did so because it felt like a great place to raise our kids. We loved the community, the quiet cobblestone streets, and the access to Hudson River Park. Our loft was essentially a large box, with windows only at the front. It was also a fifth-floor walk-up, and between the angry downstairs neighbors who complained constantly about the sound of kids moving around and the fact that I had to carry a toddler and a stroller up five brutal flights of stairs, we left in under a year. We moved around the corner to another loft, this one even more expensive, and lasted a little over a year until the building was condemned and we had to move — again. At one point, my husband and I had considered buying a property in NYC with our nest egg, but we didn't have a clue how to navigate the competitive real-estate market, and it seemed clear we'd only get a teeny apartment for our budget. The math didn't add up, and the risk of owning freaked us out. So we kept rolling the dice on renting. Between my husband and me separating, the kids outgrowing smaller apartments , and landlords unexpectedly hiking up the rent, I've moved about 10 times since coming to the US. My kids got a solid free education, but college costs felt tough to swallow I'm grateful my kids have been able to get a great public-school education in New York City. Courtesy of Natasha Silva-Jelly A financial reprieve in NYC is that public education is free, though school admissions can be complicated, with factors like zoning and lottery systems shaping where kids end up. Thankfully, both of my boys got into a highly regarded public school in Manhattan, and I was impressed with their education. I was also glad we (mostly) dodged expensive private schools — except when my youngest attended a language-immersion school for about $30,000 a year. He came out knowing basic Mandarin, which would have been worth the investment — only he's since forgotten all of it. Then comes the killer: college. After graduating from high school, my oldest was accepted into a prestigious university in the Midwest to study engineering. Sure, he could've attended a more affordable or in-state school, but a lot of "New York rats" (that's what my boys proudly call themselves) want to leave the city they grew up in — and their parents — to go to college somewhere else. Getting into a respected college also felt like a major flex, and we all felt the pressure for him to attend, no matter the cost. So, his dad and I haggled over merit and financial aid and took out student loans to cover his first year. Add kitting out his dorm room, him blowing up our Seamless account (despite having a paid meal plan), and the costs of us flying out to visit and flying him home … year one probably cost around $70,000. He didn't end up staying after his first year, which meant our student loans were due far sooner than we planned. The silver lining of not completing his degree is that, unlike many college graduates in the US , he's not saddled with four years' worth of debt. Going home feels like an expensive, uphill battle — and it's tough being far from family Our ideal time to travel to Australia would be in the winter, but it's expensive and comes with challenges. DenisTangneyJr/Getty Images Our rent, as established, doesn't leave much in the budget for vacations — or for airfare back to Australia to see family and friends. As Aussies, our ideal time to go home is around Christmas, when it's summer there, and many people are off work and school. However, that privilege can set us back upward of $4,000 in round-trip airfare alone for the four of us. On top of that, each way, we'd have to take two flights, totaling over 22 hours in the air. In my opinion, we need three weeks for a proper trip Down Under , especially as I have to visit my loved ones in two cities. Considering our sons' public schools only granted about a week off around that time of year, it rarely seemed worth the money or jet lag. This also explains why we typically only make it home every other year. Some costs are even harder to reconcile with when living on a separate continent and in a different time zone from so many loved ones. From afar, I'm watching my mum age from 10,000 miles away (she just turned 80), and how my sister must carry the load of caring for our father as he faces health issues. There are so many milestone birthdays, weddings, funerals, and family events I've missed and can never get back. Still, I'd choose moving to New York City every time I don't regret making the move to New York City over a decade ago. Courtesy of Natasha Silva-Jelly To be clear, a lot of these costs were tied to choices we made as we sought to give our family a certain kind of life in NYC . Despite the emotional and financial pain, do I regret moving? Not for a New York minute. This city has an incredible, lively vibe. We've forged deep friendships, created new traditions, and lapped up the electrifying culture on tap. events.summary: Operations suspended at King Khalid International Airport after another attack this week, Civil Aviation Authority says. The latest attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital has injured several people, according to the country’s Civil Aviation Authority. Operations at the airport in Riyadh were temporarily suspended after the attack on Saturday afternoon, said the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). Its statement added that officials were assessing the damage and determining the exact number of injuries. list 1 of 3 Saudi-led coalition says it’s carrying out operation in Yemen list 2 of 3 Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’? list 3 of 3 UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’, urges dialogue On Thursday, at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in Houthi attacks at the airport, according to GACA. Those attacks were launched by Yemen’s Houthi group, which is at war with Riyadh and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in Aden. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen on Saturday, said the Houthis have yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack. But the Iran-backed group has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target. Earlier on Saturday, King Khalid airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic. The airport did not specify the cause of the disruptions in its initial advisory. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also instructed Saudi citizens travelling to the kingdom to contact local embassies if their travel itineraries have been disrupted following the attack. Following reports of the latest attack, President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether the United States planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the ⁠⁠⁠⁠recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said. At the same time, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in the kingdom. The US mission said it was “aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh” and “strongly recommends” all US citizens avoid the airport and surrounding areas. The British and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”. Japan’s embassy “strongly” condemned Houthi attacks on airports and other Saudi civilian facilities. Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights because the airport had closed due to a “security situation”. On Thursday, the Houthi military spokesperson said that the Yemeni armed group had launched a ballistic missile towards the airport in Riyadh, claiming that the missile successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic. Days earlier, alleged Houthi attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports killed three civilians and injured 36 others.

events.title: Christa Pike is discharged from a hospital and back in prison after becoming the first person to survive lethal-injection drugs during an execution
events.summary: Christa Pike, who survived  Tennessee’s attempt to execute her  by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, her attorneys said Saturday. Pike, 50, was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her attorneys said in a written statement. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” the statement said. Pike had been hospitalized since  surviving two doses  of  pentobarbital  as the state attempted to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. At one point she was on a ventilator and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. However, they said Pike woke up and began talking and walking with assistance. The Death Penalty Information Center says Pike is the first person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the execution. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed.” The failed execution brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of what went wrong. The state’s  prison chief resigned  in the wake of the failed execution As the process got underway Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Union says cruise ship crews still open to exploitation under legal loophole
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cruise ship crews still vulnerable to exploitation as government announces updated protections A decades-old exemption to Australian labour law for cruise ships has been extended with some new protections for workers. ( ABC News: Jasper Wells ) A legal exemption for cruise ships from Australian labour law has been altered to allow some new protections for crew. Critics say the legal loophole that left them vulnerable shouldn't have existed in the first place and allows for worker exploitation. The exemption was due to expire at the end of the year but has been extended to 2028. The union that represents cruise ship workers has warned that the exploitation of staff will become "embedded" in the industry after the federal government extended a decades-old exemption that allowed cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour law. The government has announced new protections for cruise workers following an ABC News investigation that revealed allegations of shocking conditions among the crew on some Carnival Cruise vessels. It includes the ability to collectively bargain and make complaints to the maritime safety regulator. Punishing conditions face Carnival crew Passengers boarding a Carnival cruise ship are promised a world of endless food, relaxation and oceanic luxury. But for the crew, life is vastly different. But the government has decided to continue the practice of allowing cruise ships an exemption to labour laws, extending the long-standing exemption until 2028. The ABC revealed in August that workers were accusing the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations. Transport Minister Catherine King called the allegations "horrifying". Catherine King said the new conditions on the exemption would help draw tourists as well as protect workers. ( ABC News ) In response to the investigation Australia's anti-slavery commissioner said: "I think some change in this area is long overdue." Exemption should never have existed: union Maritime Union of Australia national secretary Jake Field said the exemption should never have existed in the first place and did so at the expense of Australian jobs. Introduced in 1998, the exemption lets cruise ships avoid Australian labour law and instead follow the looser international Maritime Labour Convention. The new obligations are the first time cruise operators have had conditions attached to their exemption. Originally expiring at the end of this year, it was extended until 2028 with the new conditions that ship operators cannot restrict crews rights to collective bargaining, and complaints about working conditions must to be reported to the maritime regulator, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority. Under the new conditions, cruise operators can no longer restrict crews' rights to collective bargaining. The ABC has seen letters from Carnival that warned crew against the presence of Maritime Union of Australia representatives at ports and reminded staff that they were under no obligation to stop. Carnival corporation operates over 90 ships globally, with around 100,000 crew on their ships at any one time. ( ABC New: Pete Garnish ) Transport Minister Catherine King said in a statement that the changes would protect workers while supporting Australia's maritime industry. Carnival and Royal Caribbean Cruises did not comment when asked if they would begin bargaining with crews. Carnival said it was considering the details of the announcement. Carnival operates three ships full-time in Australia: Adventure, Encounter and Splendor. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Regulator to have more oversight of complaints The changes also mean that all crew complaints regarding the Maritime Labor Convention must be reported to the Australian regulator. It is intended to give the government a better understanding of the types of complaints being made about conditions and how they are managed. The government has said it will be the last time the exemption is renewed and it is considering a review of the laws, the findings of which are not yet public. Carnival operates three ships full-time from Australia, with roughly 1,000 crew on each, mostly flown in from South-East Asian and African countries. In a previous statement to the ABC, Carnival rejected the allegations made by crew and said the maritime authority had carried out "surprise inspections of our three ships in recent weeks and cleared Carnival on each occasion". It said that the company followed international standards.

events.title: Anthropic's Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case
events.summary: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said NEW YORK -- An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said. It's the latest example of AI models acting in unintended ways and manipulating government and other websites during tests. In a report Friday , Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission. The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said. Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site. Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police. There are rising concerns about AI companies’ unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation. In September, another AI company, OpenAI, disclosed six reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models. events.title: Trump says he’s evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi Arabia’s fight against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen after fresh attacks on Riyadh
events.summary: The airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, was attacked again Saturday and evacuated, two regional officials said, just  days after three Saudi citizens , including a pilot, were killed as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the  Iran war. President Donald Trump told reporters he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the  Iran-backed Houthi rebels  in neighboring Yemen who have claimed this week’s attacks on King Khalid International Airport as well as other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.” In the latest attack, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights at the Riyadh airport and many people were wounded, one of the regional officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Ambulances were seen rushing there. The surge in attacks has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition  launched a major military offensive  against the Houthis. There was no immediate Houthi statement Saturday. A resident said he heard explosions in Riyadh Saudi civil aviation authorities said operations at the airport had been suspended and the number of wounded and damage were being assessed. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport. The attacks on airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, has rattled markets and the region. Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces in an attempt to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. The rebels’ gains gave them better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that’s a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships. Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign ended that. Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials  told the AP  last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran. Officials said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive. The Saudi and Omani foreign ministers spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region, the kingdom said Saturday. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.” Flight disruptions are growing This week, the Houthis warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations. At least 225 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines have been among the airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for the next few days. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.” The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said. In Thursday’s attack, the Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution
events.summary: Pope Leo XIV describes capital punishment as an ‘attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person’ in post on X. Pope Leo XIV has declared that the death penalty is “inadmissible” while his home country, the United States, announces plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. Marking World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, the pope reiterated the Catholic Church’s teaching on capital punishment, writing on X that it was “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person”. list 1 of 2 Christa Pike case underscores prevalence of botched executions in US list 2 of 2 ‘Barbaric’: US lawmakers condemn plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution “The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” his post said. “Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” added the leader of the Catholic Church. The American Pope’s comments come days after US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said on Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan on December 3 will be livestreamed. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in 2009. Pope Leo did not specifically refer to the planned execution, or last month’s botched execution attempt on Christa Pike , who survived two doses of the lethal injection in Tennessee. But his post came hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, told Vatican News that the plan to livestream Hasan’s execution was “unacceptable”. It was Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, in 2018 who first amended official Catholic teaching to declare capital punishment “inadmissible” in all circumstances. Previously, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the official compendium of church teaching, said the church did not exclude recourse to capital punishment “if this is the only possible way of effectively defending human lives against the unjust aggressor.” The planned livestream of Hasan’s execution has sparked outrage across the US political divide. Republican representative Austin Scott said he supported executing Hassan but that “livestreaming executions is what Jihadists do. America is better than that.” Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Hasan should “face justice”, but that public executions are “the kind of thing that Iran and the Taliban do. Is this who we want to be associated with?” On Thursday, a Pentagon official confirmed the plans, but on Friday, Vice President JD Vance, who is a practising Catholic, expressed doubt on whether the livestream would be going ahead, telling reporters that if it is, “I’m not going to be watching it.”

events.title: I moved back to my boring hometown. As a parent, boring looks pretty good.
events.summary: The author wanted to leave her hometown as a child. Courtesy of the author I grew up thinking my small hometown was boring and couldn't wait to leave. Housing costs eventually brought my partner and me back when we wanted to buy. Now I appreciate the family support and community I couldn't see as a teenager. I didn't think parking spaces would have a particularly big impact on my life, but ultimately, it was the thought of not having to parallel park on the street every day that made me realize I was going to move back to the town I grew up in. My partner and I were trying to buy our first home together and hoped to stay in Oxford, the city where we had lived for the past five years. I was speaking to a real estate agent about what we were looking for, and he raised his eyebrows slightly when I told him our budget. He told me that if I wanted an off-street parking space within our budget, we needed to consider smaller towns outside the city. There was one town which we knew very well, as I'd grown up living there, 25 minutes away. My parents lived there, and we went back often, so my hometown was the obvious choice for our move. At first, I resisted the idea of moving back home Initially, I was resistant because I felt moving back was a cop-out. I'd remembered growing up feeling bored and like I couldn't wait to move somewhere else, but when the agent showed us what we could get for our budget — a house, with parking and a garden, rather than a tiny flat with no outside space - the maths and the logistics started making sense. We were planning to start a family in the not-too-distant future, and I wanted to put down roots so the prospect of being close to my parents and a place I knew was appealing to me. We decided to go for it, and 12 years later, I'm now raising my own kids in the same town where I grew up. People know me from when I was little I've learned that raising kids in your hometown is a unique experience. Lots of people know you from when you were young, and it can sometimes feel like you have gone back in time. The author moved back to her hometown 12 years ago. Courtesy of the author It's weird dropping my kids off for clubs at my old school, and even weirder when I see people who I went to school with dropping off their own kids on the school run. I still feel like we're the kids, not the parents. And sometimes I cringe knowing that people know my past mistakes or what I was like as an awkward teenager. When my kids were small, I thought I might have made a mistake. I worried it was very unadventurous, and I didn't have as much access to culture, jobs, and city life. My town is quite small and quiet, and I miss living in a city , the architecture, services, and atmosphere. For a while, I considered moving to the coast or back to the city. But as we've all gotten older — my kids are now 7 and 9 — I have realized how lucky I am. Being close to my parents has made a huge difference As my kids have grown up, being close to my parents and seeing them regularly has made a big difference in my life. My son is autistic, and it's hard to find childcare — but parents are able to help us out a lot. Proximity means we can all help each other with caregiving, and it has made my life much easier. I'm now grateful that both my kids and I get to spend time with my parents so easily, and glad of the family support network I have around me. Living where you grew up has other benefits, too. I'm still close with some of my old friends who have stayed local, too, and I love seeing them. I also have lots of hometown knowledge and know where the best places to eat, play, and visit are. I have learned to love where I live and have put down my own roots here as an adult rather than a child. I have made new friends and feel a part of the community in the part of town where I now live. There are downsides, like a lack of culture, but it's not hard to hop on the bus or train, and I am happy to travel for events and trips in exchange for the benefits. I've realized there's no perfect living arrangement, but it's a constant weighing up of the pros and cons of where you are physically with where you are in life. For me right now, the downsides are well worth the benefits of hometown living - and the fact that I rarely have to parallel park turned out to be just a cherry on the top. events.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to Tennessee prison
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Pike survived two doses of lethal-injection drugs on September 30, renewing scrutiny of capital punishment. Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital and returned to a Tennessee women’s prison after surviving the US state’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said on Saturday. The 50-year-old is back in the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she had been incarcerated for 30 years. She had been in hospital since September 30 when officials administered two doses of pentobarbital in an attempt to execute her. list 1 of 3 Christa Pike is awake after surviving execution: What happens now? list 2 of 3 Christa Pike was nearly taken off life support before waking, lawyers say list 3 of 3 Christa Pike almost taken off life support before she woke up Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Her lawyers said she was continuing to receive medical care in prison and that they would monitor her recovery. They also expressed gratitude to the first responders and medical team who treated her. The failed execution has drawn attention to the US death penalty as a separate controversy unfolds over the military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan. The former army psychiatrist was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. His execution is scheduled for December 3. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement on Thursday of the livestream drew criticism , even from some supporters of capital punishment. Vice President JD Vance questioned on Friday whether it would happen and said he would not watch. In a social media post, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina called the proposal “beyond disgusting”. Archbishop Paul S Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, also condemned the plan, calling it “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death”. In Tennessee, however, Pike’s failed execution has not prompted Republican legislators to reconsider capital punishment. Instead, some have discussed alternative methods, including the electric chair and firing squads. Support for the death penalty in the US has declined from its peak in the 1990s. Ten states have abolished capital punishment since Pike was sentenced in 1996, but executions continue nationwide. Thirty people have been executed in the US this year, with eight more scheduled, mostly in Texas and Florida. A Pew Research Center poll in July found that about two-thirds of US adults considered the death penalty morally justified for people convicted of murder. But roughly six in 10 said it did not deter crime, while about seven in 10 said there was some risk of an innocent person being executed.

events.title: After Anthropic’s Claude AI submits a false tip on a Philadelphia unsolved homicide case, police say ‘cases involve real victims, grieving families’
events.summary: An Anthropic  artificial intelligence  model submitted a false tip to a Philadelphia police website about an unsolved homicide case, authorities and Anthropic said. It’s the latest example of AI models  acting in unintended ways  and manipulating government and other websites during tests.  In a report Friday , Anthropic also disclosed a separate incident when its AI model submitted forms to an undisclosed government website instead of stopping before submission. The incident in Philadelphia occurred on July 18 when the AI model Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages, Anthropic said. Claude filled out a form on police site PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com indicating it might have information regarding an unsolved murder listed on the site. Philadelphia Police said in a statement they were unaware of the incident until Anthropic notified them on Wednesday. Then they found the submission in the website’s tip records and confirmed it was marked spam and never forwarded to police. There are rising concerns about AI companies’  unchecked AI agents meddling with everything from U.S. government websites to healthcare data. Critics have been calling for more regulation. In September, another AI company, OpenAI,  disclosed six reports  of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in artificial-intelligence models. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the Philadelphia Police Department said in a statement. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.” Anthropic said in its report that most of the reported behaviors are forms of what it calls “persistence” — “in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping.” The company said it was modifying its training to “reduce the likelihood of further misbehavior.” Anthropic said it briefed the White House on cases that involved U.S. government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, and notified each agency involved. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Petra Power looks to modernize energy for data centers and defense vehicles
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. As AI gobbles up an ever larger amount of energy, the hunt is on for efficient and cost-effective power sources. One of the companies leading the charge is Petra Power . Petra, which was founded in 2017, sells solid oxide fuel cells — ceramic devices that convert fuel, like natural gas, into electric power without burning it. The company markets them as a more efficient and environmentally friendly way to operate data centers and large vehicles. Petra’s founder, Aaron Goodman, told TechCrunch that his company’s product has significantly lower fuel costs and emissions than traditional power sources, and that they have much less of a physical footprint, too, because they’re more compact and lightweight. The efficiency, and the cost savings that come with it, is what makes the fuel cells attractive. “Combustion takes fuel and creates explosions,” Goodman said, describing how traditional power generation works. “Those explosions create heat. That heat creates motion. The motion powers an electromotive force, which eventually creates electricity. It’s a lot of steps, and they all have so much loss in them that you end up with a really inefficient system.” Petra’s fuel cells skip most of these steps. “What fuel cells do is they take the electrons directly off of the fuel, so they strip the fuel of its electrons, which creates electricity,” he explained. “It’s one step, no loss, and subsequently, in theory, at least, they’re much, much more efficient.” As a result, companies that run off fuel cells stand to save a significant amount on fuel costs, Goodman said. Although it may offer an innovative product, the customer base is still emerging for Petra. Goodman said that his company is targeting two different types of customers: data centers and the Defense Department. Goodman doesn’t want to reveal specific agreements just yet, but said Petra is currently working with neoclouds and other infrastructure providers that were a few steps down from the hyperscaler crowd. The target for first deployment with these customers is 2028, with full-scale production for the company hopefully set for 2029, Goodman said. “Hyperscalers are an ICP [ideal customer profile] for us, and we talk a lot to them, but we don’t have anything firm with them yet,” said Goodman. “We’re still kind of working in that direction. Obviously, they’re the largest consumers of power. They’re the ones that we can make the biggest impact with, so that’s where we’d like to go.” The other customer — the government — is also still taking shape. The idea is that Petra’s fuel cells will be able to provide auxiliary power for land vehicles, meaning electricity for onboard equipment when the main engine is off. But Petra’s product has not actually deployed on a live vehicle yet, Goodman clarified. Instead, the fuel cells are in the testing phase, during which the government is deciding whether to move forward, he said. Petra is a small team — some 15 people — but the company is growing, Goodman said. Petra has so far received nearly $9 million in contracts from the Defense Department, and the hope is to scale that work significantly in the coming years, he said. Petra Power was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200 , a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. events.title: Eritrea urges UN to intervene in standoff with Ethiopia
events.summary: The neighbouring countries blame one another for starting war amid heightened tensions and fears of a wider conflict. Eritrea has asked the United Nations to take “deterrent measures” after what it called Ethiopia’s “declaration of war” in the conflict over the Tigray region. Eritrea’s request comes a day after Addis Ababa, in a letter to the Security Council, accused Asmara of launching an “all-out invasion”, saying Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometres (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s Tigray. list 1 of 4 Ethiopia and Eritrea accuse one another of launching war list 2 of 4 Will Ethiopia’s neighbours intervene as Tigray war escalates? list 3 of 4 Witnesses spot Eritrean troops inside northern Ethiopia as tensions flare list 4 of 4 Ethiopian PM Abiy demands Red Sea access as tensions with neighbours rise In a separate letter to the council on Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh said the claims of an Eritrean incursion were part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression and urged the UN to intervene, invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows measures from sanctions to military action. The neighbouring countries have accused each other of starting a war over Tigray, where Ethiopia says Eritrea is backing rebels. An alliance of seven armed groups launched attacks against federal Ethiopian forces in the northern region last month, as they attempt to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. Eritrean forces have since reportedly intruded into Ethiopian territory, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). The Ethiopian army pushed TPLF rebels back this week and seized the region’s capital, Mekelle. It also said it launched drone strikes against Eritrean troops in the region. “Eritrea requests the UN Security Council to forcefully condemn Ethiopia’s deplorable declaration of war against Eritrea … and take the requisite deterrent measures,” Eritrea’s Saleh said in the letter on Saturday. He said Ethiopia’s action would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”. Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos on Friday accused Eritrea of “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. Timothewos invoked Ethiopia’s right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, but he did not specify what measures the country was taking. Faisal Roble, a Horn of Africa specialist, believes both sides are “preparing for the last phase of an open conflict”. “There is really no doubt that both of them are inching towards an open conflict,” he told Al Jazeera from the Kenyan capital, Nairobi. “Whatever they write to the United Nations, it is just posturing and making sure that they have some sort of international support on their side,” the analyst added. In his letter, Saleh called Ethiopia’s actions “deceitful attempts to rationalise its brazen acts of war”, claiming that they were “hollow in substance”. Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Friday of pursuing aggression against Eritrea through its demands for sovereign access to the Red Sea. Writing on X, he did not explicitly confirm or deny the reported troop crossings. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, and they fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years. Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly insisted that it has a right to direct sea access, which Eritrea interprets as a threat to invade and seize its port at Assab. TPLF fighters battled Ethiopian government forces, then backed by Eritrea, in a devastating 2020-2022 war.
