events.title: ‘Fantasy economics’ hit reality: Boomer vs. Gen Z fight roils France as pension costs drive debt crisis and education cuts that fuel student riots
events.summary: Bond market turmoil and the simultaneous mass student protests at French schools are not a coincidence and point to the generational tradeoffs made in government spending, according to Nobel laureate Paul Krugman. In a Substack post on Thursday, the economics professor at the City University of New York’s Graduate Center acknowledged that the high debt and deficits driving up French bond yields lately are not unique to the eurozone’s second largest economy. In fact, the U.S. is guilty of the same fiscal sins, especially as aging demographics push entitlement spending up faster than revenue comes in. “But France does stand out, even among fiscally troubled nations, in one main way: its persistent inability to get realistic about retirement,” Krugman added. That’s as France’s official French retirement age, when workers can collect full benefits, was just 62 in 2023, while the average actual age of retirement was lower than anywhere else in Western Europe at only 60.4 years. Meanwhile, French students are rioting in the streets to protest missing teachers, run-down classrooms, and buildings that aren’t equipped for rising temperatures. Protestors blame years of underinvestment in public education. Krugman drew a straight line from France’s retirement largesse to the student unrest, highlighting the generational tensions over how to allocate public resources to baby boomers versus the country’s youth. “Thus the fiscal pressure caused largely by France’s very generous government pension plan has led to cutbacks in other spending, notably on education,” he wrote. “France is effectively handing over large subsidies to older French at the expense of everyone else. Mass national student demonstrations should come as no surprise.” Of course, U.S. debt is also on an unsustainable trajectory as spending on seniors jumps amid more baby boomer retirements. But even some Republicans have expressed openness to tax hikes to keep Social Security’s trust fund solvent. For his part, French President Emmanuel Macron attempted to raise the retirement age to 64, but intense political pushback has stalled those efforts. And the front-runner in France’s presidential election next year, far-right leader Marine Le Pen, has vowed to roll back the official retirement age to 62 and even previously suggested dropping it to as low as 60. “This would be extremely expensive and is symptomatic of a general unwillingness on the part of France’s rising right to face reality,” Krugman said. “Again, this is hardly unique to France — think of all the false promises and claims Donald Trump has made. But for now, at least, financial markets believe that fantasy economics is an even bigger problem for France than for the rest of us.” Indeed, markets are pricing in growing odds of a French debt default . Earlier this month, French 10-year bond yields jumped to the highest since 2002, and the premium over equivalent German yields widened to the most since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011. Those metrics later eased, but France’s fundamentals remain troubling, with anemic GDP growth, a budget deficit estimated at about 5.4% of GDP, and rising debt-service costs as yields jump. France’s debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to climb to 122% next year from 119% this year, and the government’s latest plan failed to halt the surge in bond yields as investors doubted its credibility. Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry, global strategists at Macquarie, also drew a connection between the French debt crisis and the student protests . In a note Wednesday, they warned that the longer the protest go on, the more likely it is that the government will cave and approve more spending, which would make the debt situation worse. That would drive up yields on French bonds, making borrowing to fund that spending even more expensive—and thus worsen the problem that the rioters are complaining about. “France is veering toward a full-blown civil crisis because of its political polarization, which heretofore had been manifested mainly in the political realm itself, and at the ballot box only,” they wrote. “And rather than being isolated events, we think a direct and self-reinforcing causal connection can be drawn between the rise in France’s debt yields and the street riots of the past few days.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Christa Pike left the hospital and returned to Tennessee prison after failed lethal injection
events.summary: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was released from the hospital and is back in prison more than a week after she survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection , her attorneys said Saturday. The big picture: The failed execution was unprecedented. Pike, 50, got two doses of the deadly drug pentobarbital on Sept. 30 and was still breathing. The state called an ambulance and Pike got life-saving care at a local hospital. Pike's attorneys said they believed she was "brain dead" and on life support. It shocked them and her doctors when she woke up and began talking earlier this week . What they're saying: Pike's attorneys said she had returned to Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had been housed for decades. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," the attorneys said in a statement. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery." Catch up quick: Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review to determine how Pike was able to survive the attempted lethal injection. Another execution set for December was called off while that investigation plays out. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

events.title: Hurricane Isaias leaves two dead and 800,000 without power in US Southeast
events.summary: Storm damage stretches across Florida and Alabama as officials warn of continued flooding and possible tornadoes. Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, has killed two people and left hundreds of thousands of customers without power across the southeastern United States. The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane before weakening as it moved inland through Alabama overnight. list 1 of 3 Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry? list 2 of 3 Hurricane Polo brings fears of heavy rain and landslides in Mexico list 3 of 3 Hurricane Polo lashes Mexico as Nolo strengthens near Hawaii One person died in Birmingham, Alabama, when a tree fell on a house overnight, according to local emergency officials. A second person was killed in Escambia County, Florida, after a tree fell during the storm, according to local authorities. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said on Saturday that state officials had not confirmed any storm-related fatalities, including the report from Escambia County. Isaias hit land with sustained winds of 169km/h (105mph), bringing powerful gusts and heavy rain to the Florida Panhandle. By Saturday morning, the storm had weakened to a post-tropical cyclone with wind speeds of about 55km/h (35mph). More than 900,000 electricity customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday morning. That number has since gone down to under 800,000, according to PowerOutage.us. Fallen trees and downed power lines caused widespread disruption, while flooding forced road closures in parts of southern Alabama, including Houston County. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said on Saturday morning that her team was concerned about “strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes”. Local officials in Pensacola, Florida reported strong winds that damaged an airport and tore the roof off a hotel. Trees and power lines also came down across the city, leaving some residents without electricity and roads blocked. Despite the storm’s weakening, officials warned that dangerous conditions could persist. Heavy rainfall threatened flash flooding across parts of the Southeast. “The flooding story is not over,” DeSantis said on Saturday, warning that saturated ground and continued rainfall could cause dangerous flooding a day or two after the storm passed. He said state search and rescue resources would remain available in case rapidly rising waters required emergency rescues. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to be alert for contractors seeking to exploit storm victims as homeowners begin repairing damaged properties.

events.title: A family of 4 lives in an RV full time. It's helping them pay off debt while traveling.
events.summary: Haylea Rossi and her family live in an RV full time. The Roamin Rossis The Rossi family has been living in an RV full time for six years. Their lifestyle allows them to travel and spend more time together as a family. They hope to keep living the RV lifestyle until they pay off debt and feel more financially secure. The view from Haylea Rossi's bedroom is constantly changing. Sometimes, she can see snowy mountains. A week later, she could see waves crashing on the shore. No, Rossi doesn't have a green screen that rotates outside her home . She and her family live in an RV full time, traveling the country year-round. The mom of two told Business Insider that she loves RV life for lots of reasons, but especially because of the financial freedom it gives her family. The Rossi family was at a crossroads in 2020. The Roamin Rossis In 2020, Rossi, 31, didn't get to see her husband, Ryan Rossi, 34, much. Rossi was at home with their two children, Liam and Olivia, who are now 12 and 10, while her husband finished up his military service. "He deployed almost every single year," Rossi, who is a content creator and social media creator for brands, told Business Insider of her husband's time in the military. "He was constantly away." When her husband's service was finally done, the Rossis wanted to make up for lost time. When her husband got a remote job as an independent insurance adjuster, which required him to travel to Colorado for six months of training, Rossi was excited that her family could be together. However, they struggled to find a housing option they could afford as they relocated, particularly because they were trying to pay off debt at the same time. They decided to try RV life. The Roamin Rossis The Rossis took the expensive housing in Colorado as a sign to do something different: buy an RV . Rossi said an RV was more affordable for her family than buying or renting a house, and the six-month span seemed like a good way to test out the lifestyle, which was completely new to them. "We went into it knowing if it wasn't a good fit, we weren't going to stay in it," she said, adding that she had some trepidation about RV life. "Once I did some research before we actually did it, I was like, 'There's a whole group of people who do this, and they actually travel, and they experience life,'" she said. With all that in mind, they decided to give it a go, buying an RV and heading to Colorado. "We lived there up in the mountains for six months, and then said, 'This is kind of the best thing ever. Let's travel,'" Rossi said. They've been on the road ever since. The Rossis have had two RVs in their six years of traveling. The Roamin Rossis Their first RV was a 2020 Forest River Sabre. They renovated the interior for a more custom, tiny-home feel, as many RVers do. That RV got totaled, which led the Rossis to buy a newer Forest River Sabre 36DBB in January 2026. It's slightly larger and has separate bedrooms for their kids, unlike their first RV. The Rossis haven't customized their current RV, as the newer design is a good fit for their family. The new vehicle cost $70,000. When you enter the RV, you're greeted by the main living space. The Roamin Rossis The vehicle's main room houses a kitchen and a living area. The kitchen has a stove, oven, microwave, and refrigerator, but it doesn't have a dishwasher. There's also ample built-in storage, including a hidden pantry that sits behind their TV and fireplace. A large island sits in the center of the room, which Rossi said is a big upgrade for their family. "It's really spacious compared to a normal little dinette table," she said. The Rossi kids do most of their schoolwork at the kitchen island. The Roamin Rossis Rossi homeschools her children on the road, doing many of their lessons from the island and taking them to see the places they're learning about in their travels. They also took one seat out of their couch, so Rossi's husband has a dedicated desk in the living space and does not have to use the same surface as the kids. Liam Rossi's bedroom is visible from the living area, as it sits in the loft above the space. They also have a projector screen that pulls out from above the TV, so the family can have movie nights. The right side of the RV serves as the primary suite. The Roamin Rossis If you walk to the right when you enter the RV, the primary bathroom and bedroom sit a level above the living area, almost like a private suite. One wall of the bedroom is made entirely of closets, giving the Rossis built-in storage. Their washer and dryer also sit in one of the closets. The Rossis' daughter has the second private bedroom. The Roamin Rossis Although Olivia Rossi's bed takes up much of the space , the bedroom is actually packed with storage for the whole family. There's a closet for her clothes, a shelf for her and her brother's shoes, and space under her bed for storage. The mattress also lifts completely to reveal a hidden storage compartment where the family keeps items such as winter clothes, extra toys, and holiday decor. "You have to live pretty minimally if you live in an RV. You have to be strategic," Rossi said. "It's definitely a challenge at times to cut everything, but we make it work." There's also a second bathroom attached to the bedroom, which Olivia and her brother use. The Rossis do most of their travel in the fall and spring. The Roamin Rossis Ryan Rossi's work can sometimes dictate where the family travels, as he gets sent to different locations after storms. Most of the time, though, they can travel where they want when he's working remotely. Rossi said her family usually stays in a new place for about two weeks, giving them time to explore. They do most of their traveling in the fall and spring, spending summers in Kansas City with family and winters in Florida . Many RV families spend time in Florida during the colder months, so they have a community of friends to spend time with in the winter. Rossi loves the freedom of life on the road. The Roamin Rossis Rossi said that the quality time she gets with her family because of RV life is the biggest benefit of her lifestyle. "We had such a big section of our life where we did life away from each other," Rossi said, adding that being able to actually experience everything with their kids is a gift for her and her husband. She also thinks the experience has changed her family's perspective on material goods for the better. "When we had a house , my kids had so many toys, and they played with maybe a quarter of those toys," she said. "They would much rather be outside riding their bikes or doing something out there." Living in the RV isn't always easy, though. The Roamin Rossis Rossi loves that the RV makes it easy to spend time outdoors, but it can be challenging on days when that isn't an option. events.title: With or without Hamas
events.summary: Hamas’s fate will not profoundly shape Gaza’s future. As we begin the fourth year of a war that has brought the near-total destruction of Gaza, calls for Hamas to surrender administrative authority and evacuate the Strip are intensifying. For Gaza to have any viable future, it is argued, the group’s political and military wings must be dismantled. While Hamas’s fate is a critical question, charting a meaningful path towards recovery is impossible without addressing the realities that gave rise to it in the first place. What is happening today in Gaza is directly related to the origins of the Palestinian-Israeli question, which has little to do with any particular armed group. Hamas did not exist in 1948, when hundreds of Palestinian villages, including Naj and Huj, were depopulated and destroyed during the Nakba – the Palestinian catastrophe that accompanied the creation of the State of Israel – to make way for the establishment of Sderot, Or HaNer and numerous other Israeli cities and villages built upon their ruins. The group had not yet been established in 1967, when the Arab-Israeli War took place and Israel initiated its military occupation of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, while simultaneously seizing and unilaterally annexing East Jerusalem—actions that actively set the stage for the broader Israeli settlement project. In the following decades, the occupation profoundly affected Palestinian society. That, combined with growing religious influence—as the number of local mosques tripled from 200 to 600 between 1967 and 1987 — and a vacuum left behind by a fading secular nationalist leadership, prepared the ground for the rise of faith-based nationalist factions. The outbreak of the First Intifada in 1987 was a political turning point that directly triggered the creation of Hamas. The group was established by a group of Palestinian men, including three prominent figures. Ibrahim al-Yazouri, was born in Bait Daras, near today’s Ashdod, and was just eight years old when soldiers of the Haganah killed members of his family and expelled the survivors to Khan Younis, south of Gaza City. Another founder, Abdulaziz al-Rantisi, was born in Yibna—a village near Jaffa whose ruins now sit beneath the Israeli city of Yavne. He was only a year old when Israeli forces expelled his family to Khan Younis. Lastly, Ahmed Yassin, was born in al-Jura, a village near Ashkelon that was razed to the ground by the Israeli military. He was 12 years old, when he and his family had to flee their home and settle in al-Shati refugee camp on the Gaza coast. Highlighting this history should not be misunderstood as an attempt to downplay Hamas’s responsibilities. However, the group’s actions cannot be separated from the historical context and the role the State of Israel has played throughout this process. Unlike the self-proclaimed ISIL (ISIS) and other groups that have emerged in recent years—which lack deep roots in local societies and rely on obsolete ideologies—Palestinian factions are deeply intertwined with local society and national identity. While Hamas’s trajectory is marked by several disastrous decisions—most notably its fatal decision to launch the assault on Israel on October 7, 2023—the group remains, above all, a symptom of a century of suffering, oppression and a relentless struggle for self-determination. Any proposed solution – with or without Hamas – to the war in Gaza that fails to address these underlying realities is bound to fail. It must be emphasised here that the widespread tendency in the West to frame the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination as a “reward for Hamas” is deeply flawed. It stems from a systemic prejudice that must not be normalised. The right was enshrined in international law and supported by an overwhelming majority of nations long before Hamas’s attack. It is also a mistake to equate Hamas’s actions with the will of the Palestinian people. Today, nearly 50 percent of the population of the Gaza Strip is under the age of 18; when Hamas won the elections in 2006, more than half of Gaza’s current residents had not even been born. Furthermore, in an Arab Barometer survey conducted in the West Bank and Gaza between late September and early October 2023, only 29 percent of Gaza respondents said they trusted the Hamas-led government. The majority blamed poverty on internal factors; 31 percent directly pointed to the Hamas authorities as being responsible for the situation. Crucially, a majority (54 percent) supported a two-state solution to the conflict; 73 percent favoured a peaceful resolution. Just 20 percent favoured military action. The presence of Hamas in Gaza cannot justify the Strip’s wholesale destruction and the crimes committed against civilians that have resulted in Israeli officials facing accusations of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

events.title: We tried McDonald's Snack Wraps in the US and UK. We can see why the British are up in arms about the 'downgraded' item.
events.summary: After sparking disappointment from fans in the UK, we compared both versions of McDonald's snack wraps in the US and UK. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider & Erin McDowell/Business Insider McDonald's just relaunched its fan-favorite Snack Wrap in the UK. Fans were left disappointed by the "downgraded" menu item. We tried the US and UK versions of McDonald's Snack Wraps to see how they compare. The Snack Wrap has officially landed overseas. McDonald's brought the fan-favorite item back to UK menus on October 6, marking its first appearance there since it was discontinued in 2016. Much like in the US , British fans spent years calling for its return — and McDonald's finally answered. However, shortly after the launch,  The Sun  reported that a few British McDonald's customers were disappointed by the "downgraded" menu item, lamenting the removal of cheese from the wraps and calling it "a bit plain" on social media. We decided to put each version to the test. Our London-based reporter, Roya Shahidi, thought the UK's version of the Snack Wrap, while light and crispy, was disappointing overall and needed cheese. On the other hand, our US-based reporter Erin McDowell was impressed by the flavorful sauces and crispy chicken tenders included in each of her wraps. Here's how McDonald's Snack Wraps in the US and the UK compare in terms of taste and value. UK-based reporter Roya went to a McDonald's in Islington, London. McDonald's in Islington, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider There were no ads inside the McDonald's about the Snack Wrap's return. McDonald's in the UK has only one version of the Snack Wrap. McDonald's Snack Wrap on the menu in London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider Unlike in the US, where you can choose between a spicy or ranch version of the wrap, the UK only has one option. The UK version contains 282 calories and costs £1.99, equivalent to about $2.62. When ordering in the app, you can upgrade the Snack Wrap to a medium meal deal for £5.59 ($7.38), which includes a drink and fries. The UK Snack Wrap was neatly packaged. The Snack Wrap in the UK. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider Roya took the Snack Wrap to the office to eat. The UK Snack Wrap comes with a chicken tender, black pepper mayo, and shredded lettuce. The UK Snack Wrap comes with a chicken, black pepper mayo, and lettuce. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider Roya found it disappointing that there was no shredded cheese inside, unlike in the US, especially since the previous UK iteration did contain cheese. At this McDonald's, adding a cheese slice would cost 50 pence — equivalent to about 66 cents. There was a generous amount of mayo and shredded lettuce in the wrap. However, while she is a fan of the UK McDonald's Chicken Selects, Roya felt the portion was too small for the price. The chicken breast was tender and crispy, but the wrap overall was quite bland. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider Roya thought the mayo serving was generous, though as someone who prefers other sauces, she would have liked the option for something else. The black pepper mayo had a mild kick, and the lettuce added a nice crunch, but overall, it was missing something extra, like cheese. The UK-based reporter thought the ingredient distribution wasn't great, with one side containing no lettuce. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider As its name suggests, the Snack Wrap makes a good snack because it's light; however, it's not filling enough as a meal in its own right. Business Insider reached out to McDonald's for comment, but did not immediately hear back. Snack Wraps have been back on menus in the US since July 2025. Erin McDowell/Business Insider McDonald's brought back its Snack Wraps nationwide last summer, marking one of the year's most anticipated fast-food launches. The $2.99 wraps come in ranch and spicy-pepper varieties, with chicken tenders, lettuce, and shredded cheese. The wraps began disappearing from menus in 2016 and were officially discontinued in 2020. A petition calling for their return later drew more than 18,000 signatures. The US Snack Wraps contain 390 calories for the ranch version and 380 for the spicy version, and cost $2.99 each. When ordering in the app, you can upgrade the Snack Wrap to a medium meal deal for $11.09, which includes a drink and fries. In the US, they come in two varieties — spicy and ranch. Erin McDowell/Business Insider This is arguably the biggest difference compared to the new UK version, along with the addition of shredded cheese. Our US-based reporter Erin tried both wraps and was impressed by the amount of sauce in each. Erin McDowell/Business Insider Both wraps are made with McDonald's new chicken tenders, which launched in the US in May 2025. The spicy Snack Wrap packed more heat than Erin expected. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The lettuce tasted fresh, and Erin was impressed by how substantial the wraps were. Though billed as snack-sized, one was filling enough for a quick lunch. The spicy sauce had a noticeable kick without being overwhelming — enough heat to earn its name. She also enjoyed the ranch version of the Snack Wrap. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The ranch version tasted lighter but still packed plenty of flavor. Its creamy sauce balanced the fresh lettuce and crispy chicken tender, while the shredded cheese added a mild savory note and a little extra texture to each bite. The tortilla wrap itself also seemed lighter and less doughy in the US. We can see why McDonald's fans across the pond are disappointed by this new release. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider & Erin McDowell/Business Insider While both reporters were excited to try the Snack Wraps, we felt a little let down by the UK version. The key differences between the US and UK versions of the snack wrap are the absence of cheese in the UK version and fewer flavor options, which ended up greatly affecting our final takeaways. While Erin would — and has — order these snack wraps again after their first launch, Roya wasn't so sure, given the bland flavor profile, less-than-satisfactory presentation, and mediocre distribution of ingredients. When it comes to Snack Wraps, McDonald's fans might have to head to the US to get the tastiest version possible. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump’s Medicaid cuts strip health coverage from some legal immigrants—including refugees and victims of human trafficking
events.summary: New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of  broader federal changes  to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage. The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest  Trump administration policy  to target foreigners. The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025  tax cut and policy law , with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate. Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to a strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a  broader immigration crackdown . “This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda. Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted. Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.” D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately. Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes. The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018. Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care. “Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said. Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive. Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved. Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S. Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border. “You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment. The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others. Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel. “I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said. Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the  administration deferred  over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states. As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF. In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF. As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office. Without coverage, people will turn to emergency rooms for care. When people delay seeing a doctor, conditions can worsen and become even more expensive to treat. “At the end of the day, it does raise the cost for the states because once you get these people in for something that could have been prevented, they could not go to the doctor because they were uninsured; they most likely will end up at a hospital in an emergency room,” said Carmen Feliciano, the vice president of policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights organization. UnidosUS partners with community organizations to help provide medical care, but Feliciano said they already are overwhelmed and would not be able to support the number of people who are going to lose medical coverage in the coming months. “We are not going to have the capacity to serve all the people who need it,” Feliciano said. events.title: JPMorgan makes bullish call in fixed income space, suggests it's a once in a generation opportunity
events.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management is making a bullish call on an underinvested market group: high-quality fixed income. Priya Misra, a portfolio manager at the firm, sees a once in a generation opportunity for investors. "You can actually take credit risk in the highest quality companies and still get [a] 6.5% [yield], Misra told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "So, you actually don't have to go down in credit [quality]." She suggested the strategy is particularly well suited for investors concerned about having too much exposure to artificial intelligence stocks. "There's a huge AI exposure," Misra said. "What fixed income gives you is this diversified set of returns. It's not just an AI trade or a tech trade. You have the Treasury trade. You have credit outside of AI." Misra co-manages the JPMorgan Core Plus Bond Fund ETF (JCPB) . The fund has almost $16 billion in assets under management, with just over three-quarters of its holdings in BBB-rated debt and above, according to the firm's website as of Aug. 31. "We've actually been increasing some of the double-B [and] single-B exposure because there has been a widening in high yield spread," she said. "We like some investment grade. And now, we've started in the last few days to increase some duration as well, thinking we may be nearing the end of that rate move." The JPMorgan Core Plus Bond Fund ETF is down more than 5% so far this year as of Friday's close, according to FactSet. "You want to be looking bond by bond and sort of sector by sector to see where the macro and you have to do the bottom up as well to make sure that companies are not over levered," noted Misra, who's concerned about how higher rates could hurt the housing market. BondBloxx co-founder Joanna Gallegos is also advising investors to take advantage of "historically attractive" yields across debt markets. "You want to really consider getting some corporate debt into your portfolio," Gallegos said in the same interview. "It's really in the investor's best interest to start looking at the income that's back in fixed income. It can offset the volatility in your portfolio." Part of her bull case: Base rates are high, and they're stable. "The fundamentals of these corporations are so strong, and the economy continues to grow," added Gallegos. "We really think that's being lost in the narrative around Treasury rates." Her firm BondBloxx is known for fixed-income exchange-traded funds in sectors including Treasury, corporate, private credit and emerging markets. One of its funds includes the BondBloxx Private Credit CLO ETF (PCMM) . As of Friday's close, it's down 0.6% so far this year, according to FactSet.

events.title: Russia’s deal to supply the U.S. with diesel is unlikely to ease pain at the pump, experts say. ‘It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic’
events.summary: A new pact that calls for Russia to boost the U.S. supply of diesel over the next few months is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say. President Donald Trump announced Friday that  he had struck a deal  with Russian President Vladimir Putin to immediately supply the U.S. more than 300,000 tons of diesel. That would be followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November, then 4 million more tons at some point after that. The deal marks a stark reversal of policy by the U.S., which from the start of Russia’s war with Ukraine had banned imports of Russian oil, and comes at a time when the U.S. economy and consumers are being squeezed by a global rise in oil prices due to the  eight-month-long U.S. war with Iran . The price of diesel has  shattered records  in recent weeks, ratcheting up inflation for a broad swath of consumer goods. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. hit a record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22, according to motor club AAA. It averaged nearly $6.28 a gallon on Friday, up from almost $3.68 this time last year. Diesel prices have hit records in Europe, too. Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That’s because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on  online orders and  packages in the mail . Shoppers may feel more and more sticker shock, particularly in the grocery aisle. Perishable foods, like meat and produce, face one of the most immediate strains of expensive diesel because they need to be hauled in and restocked frequently — or may be harvested using farm equipment powered by the fuel. That’s turned up the heat on Trump and the Republican Party to address  surging prices  ahead of  the Nov. 3 midterm elections . The president’s approval ratings on the economy have hit a new low, according to  an AP-NORC poll  released last week, as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods. A limited impact, at best Energy policy experts on Friday expressed doubts that a boost in diesel supply from Russia will have a significant impact on oil prices, whether in the U.S. or globally. “It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” said Michael Lynch, distinguished fellow at Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics. “If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now,” Lynch said. And while the White House may be counting on this move to give some relief at the pump for U.S. truckers, ranchers and farmers who have been hit hard by rising diesel prices, that’s not a given. “The best you could hope for is a tiny dip in prices locally in places like the New York-New Jersey area, Philadelphia maybe,” Lynch said. “It just means that the oil is just going to be shuffled around and it’s not really going to change the price globally or across the U.S.” If Russia, which in July moved to ban diesel exports due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries, now believes it is able to resume exports of diesel, then that will help stabilize global diesel prices, said Daniel Sternoff, senior fellow at the Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy. However, prices are likely to remain elevated overall because a lot of refining capacity in the Middle East isn’t available to the world market due to the disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz from the ongoing U.S.-Iran war. “Refined products like diesel are still barely half of prewar levels,” Sternoff said. “So, even if there were to be some follow-through from the Russians to put a little extra diesel into the world markets, it might take the edge off of prices, but it will not substantially lower them.” While the deal between Trump and Putin probably won’t have much of an impact on prices for diesel consumers in the U.S., it will benefit Russia, said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. That’s because Russia is trying to offload its summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months, Seigle noted. “I don’t think it’ll be enough to materially lower prices in the United States or Europe, but it does certainly let Moscow off the hook in terms of revenue squeeze,” he said. events.title: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports and lower tariffs for some European exports to China
events.summary: The top trade envoys for  China  and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said. Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains. The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.” The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year. China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures. He said that China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them. The head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Sigrid de Vries, said that the deal appears to avert further instability in the EU and “can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties.” Sefcovic said he will brief EU leaders meeting in Brussels next week and seek their approval. “They would have to see that this is convincing enough to take the other steps,” he said. “We are in a situation that they (China) could put under the threat whole sectors in the European industry, literally thousands of jobs and the public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side.” Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value. The two sides will meet next by video in January and then in person in March. Growing tensions China has been pushing for the EU to stop blocking Chinese imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington’s behest. Earlier, Sefcovic had said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an  October deadline  for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions  have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The  EU has moved  to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted  measures to  protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. China had a global trade surplus exceeding $1 trillion last year Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China’s global trade surplus hit  $1.2 trillion in 2025  and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics. And on Wednesday, Germany blocked the sale of a major logistics firm in the port of Hamburg to the state-owned Chinese shipping behemoth Cosco over security concerns. “As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Despite starting the Iran war, Trump still thinks he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize and complains the winner is someone ‘who nobody has ever heard of’
events.summary: President  Donald Trump  veered far from midterm election politics during a rally in upstate New York on Friday, aiming a bitter diatribe at the Norwegian Nobel Committee for giving the Peace Prize he has long sought to South African jurist  Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a former U.N. human rights chief, for her work on justice and accountability for war crimes and genocide. Trump unspooled a lengthy argument explaining why the award was “an indelible stain on the country of Norway,” saying he “should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t.” Trump claimed, as he often does, to have ended eight wars, though some of the conflicts the president claims to have resolved were merely tensions, and his role in easing them has been disputed. Meanwhile, the war with Iran that he and Israel started — which Trump predicted would last mere weeks — remains unsettled and is a weight on his party as it faces a dour electorate ahead of midterm elections. An  Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research  poll conducted last month and published Oct. 1 found 71% of U.S. adults disapproved of Trump’s handling of Iran, with 28% approving. The conflict has pushed gas prices higher, and polls show voters blame Trump for the high cost of living. Trump bitterly described Pillay as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations who nobody has ever heard of,” adding: “The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization. And we will not forget, Norway, ” Nobel diatribe eclipses political mission It was a lengthy deviation from an event aimed at promoting Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee in the race for New York governor. While Trump criticized Democratic incumbent Gov. Kathy Hochul, who is running for her second full term, he spent as much time excoriating New York Attorney General Letitia James, a prominent Trump adversary who brought civil charges against Trump and his business. As a result of James’ charges, a court found Trump liable for fraud. An appeals court subsequently threw out the massive financial penalty but upheld the fraud finding. On Friday, from the stage at the Oncenter in Syracuse, New York, Trump called James “a dog.” Trump has been on a series of political stops, trying to stoke loyalty among his base as Republicans work to fight off possible setbacks in their effort to hold congressional majorities on Nov. 3. Friday’s mission was to lift up Republican Blakeman in the Democratic-leaning state. In Trump fashion, Blakeman, Nassau County’s executive, has suggested Democrats might steal the election, played up fears about immigrant criminals and posted  AI-generated videos  depicting the state as dangerous and unaffordable. And while he invited Blakeman onstage, Trump spent large swaths of time pushing back against a national narrative that voters in the United States do not have faith in his handling of the economy. Trump tried convincing voters that the economy is humming Trump spent much of the first half of the rally — just 25 days before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans can keep control of Congress — trying to talk past Americans’ gloomy feelings about the economy. “The poverty rate has just reached its lowest level, the best number,” he said. “Lowest level in American history.” “The job numbers are the best. The stock market has soared,” Trump said. And while gas has fallen a few cents per gallon in the last week, it remains about 15 cents higher per gallon than a month ago, according to AAA. Trump briefly veered from his economic cheerleading to call on oil retailers directly to “start dropping their prices now.” The latest AP-NORC poll, also found only 26% of U.S. adults approved of Trump’s handling of the economy — a new low — down from 32% in July. Notably, only 17% approved of his handling of the cost of living. Trump has largely steered clear of political battlegrounds in his travels so far,  focusing on red states and friendly crowds  at a moment when Republicans worry that  his unpopularity  could drag down the party. The most closely watched U.S. House race in New York state is several hours away from Syracuse, where  Republican Rep. Mike Lawler  is trying to fend off a challenge from Democratic candidate Cait Conley. Blakeman has emphasized his independence from Trump On the campaign trail, Blakeman argues he’s winning over Democrats and independents, painting himself as the moderate candidate in his race against Hochul. He dismisses the idea that his closeness with the president could hurt his chances in blue New York. In an interview, Blakeman denied he was aligned with the president on everything. “I am somebody who takes every issue and makes a decision based on good advice from smart people and common sense,” he said. “I’ve proved my independence over and over and over again. I make my own decisions. I call my own shots,” he said. Hochul has emphasized Blakeman’s ties to Trump — mirroring much of the Democrats’ national strategy for the midterm elections — hoping the president’s dismal approval ratings help sink her Republican foe at the ballot box. In a sarcastic press release, Hochul’s campaign described Trump’s visit as “an extremely boring puppet show” and said Hochul, like Trump, is asking voters to pretend the president is on the ballot. “Why is Trump in Upstate New York?” the campaign asked. “Because Bruce Blakeman, for some reason, begged him to do so.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
events.summary: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met in Alaska last year Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies. Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that. It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine. Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts. Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror". "We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote. He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 21 hours ago Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people Published 5 hours ago Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small". He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US". "Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms." The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment. The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine. The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't." She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday. Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace. "We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace." Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war. That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation. Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror" The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market. Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large." An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world." Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.

events.title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
events.summary: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from PERM, the Labor Department program that lets employers sponsor foreign workers for green cards. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing laid-off American workers with foreign hires. Data shows two-thirds of Microsoft's H-1B approvals went to people already working at the company. Amazon and Meta, the nation's two largest H-1B work visa sponsors, were not suspended. As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas. The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers. Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended. The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad. All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45. The biggest sponsor wasn't suspended Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals. The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

events.title: I'm a Massachusetts native. Skip Salem and check out this less-crowded neighboring city for Halloween fun.
events.summary: I think Beverly, Massachusetts, is better than Salem in the fall. Sarah Sweeney/Endicott College I'm from Massachusetts, and I love visiting Salem, but it can be too busy in the fall. Instead, I think Beverly, Massachusetts, is an amazing, less-crowded alternative. Not only is the Halloween decor incredible, but the place also has great food and historic charm. Anyone from Massachusetts knows that during Halloween, Salem is packed tighter than a Candy Crush board. I've visited Salem many times, but I like to avoid the area from September through the beginning of November because of the surge in tourism. Each year, the city welcomes roughly 1,000,000 visitors every October, with 96,000 people going on Halloween alone. During the fall, crowds flood the streets on ghost tours, take selfies in front of the statue of Elizabeth Montgomery from "Bewitched," line up at the Salem Witch Museum, and try to snag a ticket to the Haunted Witch Village at the Salem Wax Museum. It's always exciting to welcome new guests who are eager to learn about the city's twisted history. But during October, Salem's narrow streets and scarce parking make its charm hard to enjoy. However, a recent three-day staycation in Beverly, Massachusetts —just three miles away from Salem's city center — gave my family and me the best of both worlds: easy access to Witch City, plus a quieter place to eat, explore, and sleep. Until this year, I'd thought of it as mostly Salem's sleepier sister, but my time there made me realize I'd been overlooking it as a must-visit destination in its own right. Beverly has Halloween spirit without Salem's October crowds Halloween on the Hill features thousands of hand-carved jack-o'-lanterns, twinkling lights, and decorations. Mary Dettloff/The Trustees of Reservations Downtown Beverly has the independent restaurants, family-owned boutiques, and historic architecture that I love about Salem, minus the holiday crowds. I loved checking out the trails at Long Hill estate, which houses 114 acres of land and gardens. For most of October, the grounds' pathways feature thousands of hand-carved glowing jack-o'-lanterns, twinkling lights, decorations, and treats like cider as part of the Halloween on the Hill event. I've attended the event twice and can't recommend it enough. Our hotel was beautiful — and cheaper than many places in Salem My family and I stayed at the recently renovated Wylie Inn in Beverly, which sits on Endicott College's leafy seaside campus and has direct beach access. Not only is the hotel stunning, but most rates for a late-October night are cheaper compared to places I've stayed in Salem. Plus, parking at the Wylie Inn is free, so you don't have to worry about competing for a spot at a public garage. The food and sweet treats were incredible The crispy chicken sandwiches from Flip the Bird were so tasty. Sarah Sweeney/Endicott College During our time in Beverly, we dined at Flip the Bird, a fast-casual restaurant that had the most delicious, crispy chicken sandwiches and frothy frappes. The desserts in Beverly also blew me away. On our last day, we hit up Prides Crossing Confections. This family-owned candy shop — housed inside a former train station — featured Halloween treats and tasty chocolate lollipops. Like Salem, Beverly is rich in historic charm and cultural activities The Cabot House was the first brick residence built in Beverly. Abby Battis/Historic Beverly Sure, Salem is full of incredible tales and features many cultural attractions, but the same is true for Beverly. While visiting, we checked out Cabot House, an 18th-century Georgian-style mansion. Stepping inside this home, which was the first brick mansion built in the city, I instantly felt like I had traveled back in time to Beverly's founding. Along with Cabot House, there are plenty of other activities to plan a getaway around — instead of just limiting yourself to Halloween-themed activities in Salem. For example, the Montserrat College of Art offers five free galleries in Beverly, and the nonprofit Cabot Performing Arts Center hosts comedy and music acts. Hiking through Witches' Woods was incredible One of my favorite moments during the staycation was hiking at the Beverly Commons Conservation Area. This 409-acre preserve was once a major thoroughfare during colonial times, and during the witchcraft hysteria of 1692, the forest became known as Witches' Woods after families sought refuge there. Now, centuries later, as I walked beneath peaceful canopies of trees, I couldn't believe that Salem's busy streets were only a few miles away. If you want to brave the Salem crowds, it's a short drive or train ride away Even though Salem is very crowded in October, it's only a short train ride away from Beverly. Amanda Shammas Beverly is incredible, but if you're still itching to check out the scene in Salem, luckily, it's conveniently located nearby. Beverly has multiple rail stations, with direct trains to Salem that take about five minutes. Plus, during October, the Massachusetts Bay Transit Authority offers extra train cars, more departure times, and discounted fares. But if you have a car, Salem is only about a 15-minute drive from Beverly, though holiday traffic can make the trip much longer. I'm a fan of Salem's free parking lot at Fort Avenue, which is about a 20-minute walk to the center of the action. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How de-extincting dire wolves and woolly mammoths may extend human life
events.summary: To join the CNBC Technology Executive Council, go to cnbccouncils.com/tec Colossal Biosciences is on a mission to revive extinct species. The company has created three genetically engineered dire wolf pups and is working on the woolly mammoth. The science of de-extinction has implications for the environment, medicine and research on evolution. Colossal Biosciences' efforts to bring back extinct animals like the woolly mammoth and dire wolves have drawn comparisons to Jurassic Park. CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told CNBC's Julia Boorstin at the CNBC AI Forum last week that he understands those comparisons. "I think anyone that saw Jurassic Park in the 90s and didn't say it was cool, like I don't think they're probably very fun at parties," Lamm joked. "But yes, I saw the movies. I love them. They entertained us. They scared us." However, Lamm said, "I constantly have to remind people on X that, you know, they were movies," he said. "I don't think Jurassic Park had any conservation or general human benefit models to it, so we've tried to take a slightly different perspective." Since viable dinosaur DNA is no longer available, bringing back dinosaurs is, in fact, impossible. But what is underway at Colossal, besides the dire wolf and woolly mammoth projects, is work to genetically engineer the dodo bird, the Tasmanian tiger, and a giant bird called a moa, among others. "It's highly likely in the next coming year or two, people will continue to see us deliver extinct species back to Earth, and we could even have more dire wolves, too," Lamm told Boorstin. The process of creating the wolf pups involved taking genetic material from a skull and a tooth that were tens of hundreds of years old. Using AI models, Colossal used the ancient DNA to reconstruct the dire wolf genome and map it to its closest living relative, the gray wolf. The team then created embryos by editing the cells of modern gray wolves. Three pups, named Romulus, Remus, and Khaleesi, have been born to domestic dogs used as surrogate mothers. Skeptics, Boorstin pointed out, say that they didn't really de-extinct a dire wolf, rather, they created a genetically modified gray wolf. Lamm called this a "semantic argument" that "misses the forest for the trees." "Gray wolves are just genetically modified dire wolves. They were just done by nature or God or however you want to classify it," he said. Colossal is undertaking a similar process in their woolly mammoth project – that involves genetically modifying an Asian elephant. Lamm told Time in August that the company is aiming to have a woolly mammoth birth in the 2030s. "We call it a woolly mammoth," he said. "Because if it looks like a duck, it quacks like a duck, it serves ecological functions of a duck, it's a duck, in our perspective." Lamm became interested in this work after a 2019 meeting with renowned Harvard geneticist George Church, who Lamm called "arguably the father of synthetic biology." Church, who initiated the Personal Genome Project, had been dreaming about bringing back the woolly mammoth for decades, he told CNBC in 2021. However, the vision to revive animals like the woolly mammoth goes far beyond creating a real-life Jurassic Park with previously extinct creatures. "[Church] had this vision that we could leverage CRISPR and all these tools and technologies to bring back extinct species, use some of those technologies for human healthcare, and then build this programmable life model that we could apply to so many different use cases on Earth," Lamm said. Those use cases include those aforementioned conservation-focused benefits that de-extinction promises. For example, the engineered woolly mammoths could help fight climate change by stomping down snow cover in high-altitude arctic regions, which keeps soil frozen, and knocking down trees, thereby converting heat-absorbing forests into grasslands. But the processes around de-extinction are also opening new doors in genome engineering and developmental biology, Lamm said. That could have implications on "everything from microbes to plastic in the oceans to gene therapies and targeted delivery for humans to eradicating genetic diseases," he said. Lamm theorized that these efforts around DNA synthesis could even lead to developing crops or trees that grow faster. "We're pushing the bounds of DNA synthesis to synthesize the largest cargos of DNA," he said. "That will be massively transformative for how we think about programmable life." A company spun off from Colossal, called Astromech, is pushing into what Lamm called "convergent evolution," studying what causes species that are similar in nearly every way to have different immunities or other health issues, such as why elephants get cancer at a fraction of the rate humans do. That research could be leveraged to solve human healthcare challengers or pandemic responses, Lamm said. Astromech was valued at $2 billion in March, according to D Magazine .

events.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account.

events.title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
events.summary: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference. The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October. Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote. “The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028. “These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.” In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election. Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023. He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits. Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.
