events.title: Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported. The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin. Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday. Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation. Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by phone after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan. Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end. The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump. Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call. Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said. The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday. Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports. A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard. The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast. An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged." Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies. Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

events.title: UAW tries to reassert political power in Michigan despite internal divisions
events.summary: Membership is divided over which party best represents working-class interests. SHELBY TOWNSHIP, Mich. -- Walter Usakowski was mowing his lawn in a northern suburb of Detroit when three canvassers from the United Auto Workers approached. “I don’t even need to talk to you,” Usakowski said. As a retired member, he was already supporting the union’s slate of Democratic candidates in the Nov. 3 midterms. But he is not sure how many of the other “guys in the shop” will vote for Democrats. He worked at Ford Motor Co.’s Sterling Axle Plant for more than 45 years, and he knows many members who backed Republican President Donald Trump . The election-year canvassing was one part of the UAW’s efforts to reassert its political power in Michigan, a premier political battleground. Although the union generally backs Democrats, its membership is more divided over which party best represents working-class interests. It also is reckoning with past corruption scandals , a drop in membership and a lack of transparency that has eroded trust within its ranks. “It’s not going to be an overnight thing,” said JJ Jewell, who is part of the UAW’s Community Action Program executive committee. “Even if this election goes fantastically, that’s not mission accomplished. That means we’re 1% of the way done.” Jewell and others made the rounds on a recent sunny Saturday in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. Many of the union members they met in a neighborhood of well-kept suburban houses were retirees, and while most said the cost of living was their top concern , they did not agree on whether Democrats or Republicans would better address it . One resident, who said she blamed billionaires for the country’s problems, planned to vote for Democrats. Another street over, a couple said they both supported Trump and declined to take a flyer of the UAW-endorsed candidates. In a microcosm of broader political rifts , union voters remain politically divided. Union voters have traditionally been seen as a Democratic-leaning constituency, but Trump made direct appeals to them with his anti-elite rhetoric and promises to overhaul international trade agreements that sapped factory jobs. In 2024, voters who were union members or were in a household with a union member split between Trump and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris , with more than half voting for the then-vice president and 44% for Trump. Betty Anderson, a UAW member, thinks the organization is on the right track, but she is not confident about bridging internal political divisions. She said she is angry with members who voted for Trump, whom she sees as selling out the working class. “I don’t think those people are ever going to be on our side,” Anderson said. “They think they have an opportunity to be in an elite class.” Since 2017, more than 10 UAW officials have pleaded guilty in a corruption investigation that found millions of dollars of union dues were stolen. Members also faulted leaders for closed-door contract negotiations that they said destroyed trust in the UAW. Shawn Fain was elected UAW president in 2023 on a platform of transparency, and victories in labor disputes with Detroit's three major automakers bolstered member support. Leaders hope this will translate into votes for its candidates. “I think the UAW members now are starting to fall a little more in line,” said Usakowski, the retired axle plant worker. On Friday, Fain said he won reelection to lead the union for four more years. The results have not yet been certified. Hurricane Isaias updates: 3 dead as Isaias downgraded to post-tropical cyclone Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Mark DePaoli, director for one of the UAW’s southeast Michigan regions, said the union hosted forums with candidates where any member could ask questions. The UAW endorsed progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate primary even though rival Haley Stevens , a four-term congresswoman, worked as chief of staff on an auto bailout task force during the Great Recession, a position she frequently cited while campaigning. “I don’t think anybody expected us to endorse him,” DePaoli said. In its announcement, the union referenced El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare and criticism of corporate money in politics. El-Sayed wore a UAW pin during the first Senate debate with his Republican opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers . “The UAW’s backing of Abdul was critical in winning a historic primary despite being outspent by tens of millions of dollars, and will be just as critical in winning" next month, El-Sayed spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement.

events.title: Pokémon card values are soaring. What collectors should know before buying or selling
events.summary: What is driving interest? Pokémon and other trading-card games are drawing strong collector demand, while sources say high sports-card prices are pushing some buyers toward non-sports cards. What determines value? Authenticity, condition, graded population, liquidity and verified transaction history can sharply affect what a card sells for. What is the biggest risk? Counterfeits are rising, especially in Pokémon submissions, making authentication and careful price research critical before buying. In 2022, a rare Topps 1952 Mickey Mantle baseball card — one of sports-card collectors' holiest grails — sold for $12.6 million. Wow, you say, that's a lot of dough for a thin piece of cardboard, slab of bubblegum not included. Well, what do you say about a 1998 Pikachu Illustrator Pokémon card going for $16.5 million earlier this year? If you're pro wrestler and social media influencer Logan Paul, seller of the item, you say, Not a bad return on the $5.3 million (plus a trade) I paid for it in 2021. Those are extreme examples, but a vivid illustration of how TCGs — shorthand for competitive trading card games, led by Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh! — are encroaching on an over-saturated sports-card market as an enticing investment opportunity. Throw in vintage and modern-day non-sports trading cards, depicting historical events and fictional characters ranging from the Civil War to Luke Skywalker, and it's a whole new ballgame. The record $16.5 million Pokémon card sale is drawing fresh attention to a collectibles market where grading, scarcity and authentication can determine whether a card is worth dollars or hundreds of thousands. "It is one of our fastest-growing categories that we've seen and one of the largest contributors to [our] growth over the last number of quarters," said Adam Ireland, vice president and general manager of collectibles at online marketplace eBay , which also provides authentication and price guides for TCGs and non-sports cards. "From an investment point of view, you start with Pokémon," he said. "It was the most searchable term within the eBay collectibles environment through the first half of the year." Heritage Auctions, which deals in art, jewelry, coins and many other collectibles, launched a dedicated TCG department six years ago. "Now it's a $50-million category," said executive vice president Joe Maddalena. "That's just TCGs. I'm not talking about Star Wars and any of that stuff," he said, though he added that non-sports stuff contributed around $10 million to Heritage's overall sales in 2025, which topped $2.1 billion. While buyers can find myriad non-sports cards for less than $10 — almost like investing in penny stocks in hopes of eventually striking gold — Maddalena and Ireland cited some eye-popping sales on their respective platforms. A first-edition Pokémon Charizard card worth $20,000 pre-Covid is now valued by Heritage at $500,000. A Tyler the Great Warrior Yu-Gi-Oh! card shattered records when it was auctioned on eBay for $311,211, while Magic's Black Lotus card has gone for $500,000 on the site. Heritage sold a 1977 Luke Skywalker card for $687,500 in May. Whereas collectability, value and investability of sports cards can rise and fall on the real-world performance of athletes, both trading-card genres share common factors. For instance, rookie cards of superstar athletes are highly coveted; the non-sports counterpart is referred to as first appearance. Especially critical are the authenticity, physical condition, total graded population, liquidity and pricing of specific cards, criteria determined by professional grading services such as PSA and CGC Cards. How cards are graded for monetary value PSA (Professional Sports Authenticator), founded in 1991, is the most recognizable grading service. Its process begins when a trained grader examines a card to verify its originality or genuineness, then assesses the quality and condition of the card using PSA's grading scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most pristine, aka gem mint. There generally are very limited populations of PSA 10s of highly sought-after cards, thus their astronomical values. PSA has been grading non-sports cards since its inception, "but with more people viewing it as a potential asset class or thing they want to potentially invest in or speculate in, you're seeing more demand for grading services in the last seven years," said PSA president Ryan Hoge. Indeed, PSA graded more than 19 million cards in 2025, up from two million in 2020. The company had already graded more than eight million cards as of last May, with output from January through April up 39% year-over-year. Much of that uptick, Hoge said, is attributable to TCGs. "Collectively, TCGs [account for] 50% of our current business, more than all the sports cards combined.

events.title: Ex Goldman Sachs CEO got into Harvard University at 16 from public housing—and says higher education is the best way to break into the middle class
events.summary: Some business CEOs have put the college degree on blast , questioning if higher education is really setting students up for success in the workforce. But the former CEO of Goldman Sachs , Lloyd Blankfein , is pushing back against that narrative.  Blankfein has witnessed the power of a strong college education firsthand. The billionaire finance leader was born into public housing in Brooklyn, sharing a bedroom in his small New York City apartment with his grandmother or sister until he went off to college. At the time, his high school was on the brink of shutting down, Blankfein told CBS earlier this year—but the then-teenager battened down the hatches, studied hard, became class valedictorian , and got into Harvard University at just 16 years old. It was the launchpad to his illustrious career in finance, including a 12-year reign at Goldman Sachs . Fast forward five decades, and Blankfein still believes schooling is the great wealth equalizer, even as AI threatens to swipe white-collar roles at a dizzying pace. “I think education is the real accelerator for most people into the middle and upper classes,” Blankfein told CBS . Blankfein says college helps make workers a ‘complete person’ Higher education has long been lauded as the best path to success, but some leaders are encouraging budding workers to skip college altogether.  Palantir and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel —a Stanford University alumnus—has been particularly outspoken, even offering young entrepreneurs $200,000 grants to ditch the “corrupt institution” of higher education and “build new things” with his Thiel Fellowship . Blankfein hit back at the tech mogul’s rhetoric, advising the next generation of movers and shakers to set themselves up for success by going to college. “I strongly disagree with the technology investor Peter Thiel,” Blankfein wrote in an excerpt from his upcoming memoir, Streetwise , shared with Vanity Fair earlier this year. “To succeed in a career, you have to know the technical minutiae of your field, of course. But you also need to be a complete person—the kind of person other people want to engage with.” The ex-Goldman Sachs leader, an alumnus of both Harvard University and Harvard Law School, says the elite college nurtured his confidence, writing skills, love of history, and engagement with current events. It was no cake walk—Blankfein wrote that he “survived” the experience more than he enjoyed it. But it was still “the best place to have gone.”  Blankfein might have missed out on that essential growth, integral to his career success, if he’d passed up on the college experience altogether. “Your undergraduate years are your best opportunity to make yourself uncomfortable in a way that can help make you more curious and interesting,” he continued in his book.  Other CEOs agree: college builds essential skills, including the liberal arts While some leaders with elite college degrees are bashing higher education, others like Blankfein are crediting their education to their current success.  Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi says his alma mater, Brown University, prepared him to take the corner office with a diverse skillset at the ready. Engineering taught the ride-hailing leader “how to solve complex problems,” while liberal arts “just captured my heart.” “One of my secrets is—really, I do give Brown credit for this—this balanced education that I kind of stumbled on,” Khosrowshahi said during a panel at the Ivy League college last year.  “Learning all of the…really important basics of engineering, but then marrying that with liberal arts, that really taught me to communicate in a compelling way, which is an absolute necessity when you’re in a leadership position.” And despite whisperings that the traditional college pathway is on the outs as AI takes over workforces, some leaders are optimistic. Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi told Fortune last year that “education will be completely revolutionized” for the better thanks to tech innovations, creating new jobs never seen before.  And Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei is adamant the college humanities track won’t be tossed aside in a tech-driven work landscape. In fact, the discipline will continue to be critical to innovation at even the largest AI businesses.  “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” Amodei said in an interview with ABC News earlier this year. “The ability to have critical thinking skills and learn how to interact with other people will be more important in the future, rather than less.” A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 10, 2026. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: I work hard to stay close to my friends. A researcher says it’s good for my well-being—and these 3 habits can help
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships What we lose when kids can't connect, IRL Psychology and Relationships Social isolation can inhibit success: ‘You need to make time for people' Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Raising Successful Kids Stop telling kids they can do anything—what parents can say instead to raise successful kids, says psychologist Psychology and Relationships Worried about interrupting someone’s scrolling? Here’s what experts think Not to brag, but without realizing it, I've become a model friend — someone my loved ones admire for how well I maintain my relationships . At least, so they tell me. Last month, my closest friend asked me for pointers on how to stay connected to her community while balancing work, well-being and everything else in her life. It's no easy feat. Loneliness levels in the U.S. are high, and instead of turning to each other, many people reach for their tech devices , found an American Psychiatric Association poll published on May 12. Eight percent of Americans report having zero close friends, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center survey of about 5,000 U.S. adults. Some businesses now offer to facilitate the friendship process, offering summer camps for adults or guidance from friendship coaches that can sometimes cost thousands of dollars. And when you do form friendships, you could grow apart for a number of reasons, says Jessica D. Ayers , an assistant professor of psychological science at Boise State University: classic ones like moving to a different state for a new job or being in different stages of life, or newer ones like trying to keep up with each other on social media and forgetting to keep in touch outside of your smartphones. Especially if your friends have busy lives or don't often reach out to make plans, putting in the work to stay in touch may seem like a fundamentally selfless gesture. In fact, making the effort to maintain friendships can benefit you too, says Ayers, who researches the science of friendship and how to maintain connections. Staying in touch with friends can improve well-being , lower levels of depression and loneliness , decrease anxiety, and even "increase our chances of survival after things like major surgery ," she says. The benefit is mutual for both parties, Ayers says, especially in "long-lasting and sustained relationships." And a high degree of social fitness contributes to a longer, healthier and more fulfilled life , according to an ongoing 88-year-old Harvard University happiness study. Put simply, your friendships can help you succeed. Staying in touch can require a lot of hard work, at least on paper. I didn't fully realize this until I considered just how many strategies I have for keeping in contact with my community. I set up multiple one-on-one hangouts per month with a rotating cast of friends, clear time in my calendar to be present for my loved ones' birthday celebrations and stay up-to-date in five-plus group chats with friends and family. In a sense, I was trained to do this: I have five siblings, and growing up in our household, showing up for each other was a non-negotiable. But there's more to it. Whenever a friend crosses my mind, I reach out to them , just to see how they're doing or ask when we can hang out in the near future. I host small get-togethers — one of my favorites was an October 2025 party themed around the movie "Coraline." I travel to visit my friends who live in different states at least once a year, or plan vacations together with them. Ayers says she approves of my practices. Even the simple act of sending a friend a quick note because you briefly thought about them is "a brilliant practice," she says, adding: "It is the best thing you can do." The first step: 'Just reach out' to your friends To keep your friendships healthy and strong, Ayers recommends three things: "Just reach out to them," she says. It doesn't have to be super frequent, but let your friends know you value them: "When they come to your mind, send them a text, 'Hey, thinking of you.'" Prioritize relationships built on intrinsic qualities over external ones, Ayers recommends. Friendships based on shared values like loyalty and honesty are often much more meaningful than connections built on more superficial qualities, she says. Bring something to the table in each friendship, and expend a reasonable amount of time, resources and energy to show up for your friends — even if, sometimes, you'd rather stay home. In other words, be the friend you'd want others to be to you. "Remembering that you are a valued person in this relationship is important," says Ayers. Ayers and her best friend live in different states — Idaho and California, respectively — she says. They send each other voice memos throughout the week, ranging from quick check-ins to 15-minute breakdowns of an important update, she says.

events.title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’
events.summary: Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up. Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England . But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story. Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset. The businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt. As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs. And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge. Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup. The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50. Bekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room. He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head. Hugh Thomas, a food writer from Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.” Some, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs. Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomed a cage of endangered red squirrels . But there, too, lay a problem. The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds. Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.” While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds. People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas. Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.

events.title: How Supreme Court justices are leaning in major 401(k) case over private funds and underperformance
events.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court heard a case this week in which a former Intel employee alleged company retirement-plan fiduciaries breached their duty by investing in hedge funds and private equity, pointing in part to the funds' underperformance. Lower courts already rejected the claims, ruling underperformance alone is not enough without showing a "meaningful benchmark" for courts to assess performance. Several justices appeared receptive to Intel's position during oral arguments. A ruling for Intel could make some retirement plan sponsors more comfortable adding alternative investments to 401(k) plans, though the largest employers may still move slowly. The Supreme Court heard a major case this week concerning an Intel retirement plan which could result in a decision that influences employers' appetite for private investments in 401(k)s. Many plan sponsors are in limbo, awaiting the Supreme Court decision and finalized Labor Department rules covering alternative investments before changing their 401(k) menu, even as the asset management industry is gearing up with new products. "I think companies want to know what's going to happen with the proposal and what's going to happen with the Supreme Court case before they go rushing in to change their investment strategies," said Elizabeth Hopkins, principal at Hopkins ERISA Law and a former senior trial attorney with the Labor Department, who filed an amicus brief in the Supreme Court case on behalf of former high-ranking DOL officials. Here's what employers and employees need to know about forces influencing the market for private investments in 401(k) plans. What Justices Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch and Kagan said Employers have been whipsawed for the past several years by changing government policies on alternative investments in 401(k) plans and a high-profile lawsuit filed in 2019 by a former Intel employee. That case, Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee, which the Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Tuesday, Oct. 6, concerns private investments in a defined contribution plan like a 401(k) and the circumstances under which these investments are appropriate. The case is not challenging whether alternative assets like hedge funds and private equity can be used in a 401(k) plan alongside stocks and bonds. Rather, the question before the court is whether a retirement plan underperformance claim requires alleging a "meaningful benchmark." The heart of the dispute is how to handle claims by employees that plan sponsors have invested their retirement funds imprudently. Employees contend that the relatively low returns on Intel's plans reflect a breach of fiduciary duty. The lower courts disagreed. Their reasoning: claims of underperformance alone are not enough without showing a "meaningful benchmark" for courts to assess performance. During the arguments, Supreme Court justices seemed skeptical that plan sponsors' investment choices should provide easy fodder for litigious individuals. Justices frequently turned to a fruit metaphor, with Justice Clarence Thomas summing up his take on the Ninth Circuit's decision as: "you can't compare apples and oranges…if you have a fund…that is designed to produce high returns but riskier returns…you can't compare that to a fund that is to protect against losses." Several other justices, including from among the liberal side of the court, seemed to agree with his line of reasoning, Ronald Mann, co-director of the Charles Evans Gerber Transactional Studies Center at Columbia Law School, noted in an analysis on SCOTUSblog . Justice Elena Kagan, for instance, commented, "the thing that you need … is another apple." Justice Samuel Alito challenged the employees' attorney, Matthew Wessler, to clarify whether his position was that one could "state a claim by comparing apples and oranges but supplement that with the suggestion that the strategy was flawed." Justice Amy Coney Barrett opted for the same metaphor as well. Meanwhile, Justice Neil Gorsuch asked Wessler to "agree with the general principle that when we're limited to underperformance claims … a meaningful benchmark of some kind is required, apples, not oranges." Wessler did not respond to a request for comment for this article. The underlying problem for the court seemed to be the lack of a benchmark. Notably, justices explicitly asked Aimee Brown, assistant to the Solicitor General, how much guidance the court should provide in this case. Brown's view was that the court should suggest "some parameters" for what a "meaningful benchmark" needs to be. "Prudence is about process and not about performance," she told the justices. Legal experts say SCOTUS seems likely to side with Intel Attorneys who attended the arguments in person, listened to the recording or read the transcript took the justices' questions as a sign they were leaning toward siding with Intel and affirming the 9th Circuit.

events.title: We met on a 7th-grade field trip. Twenty years later, I secretly recreated it and we rekindled our romance.
events.summary: The author and her husband met in 7th grade. Courtesy fo the author My husband and I met on our seventh-grade field trip to a local amusement park. Twenty years later, I planned a surprise trip back to the park. It was the best we've felt since having a baby last year. According to my childhood diary, I met my husband on our seventh-grade field trip to Canobie Lake Park — a local theme park , an hour north of Boston. From the Ferris wheel overlooking the freshwater lake to the 90-year-old wooden coaster called the Yankee Cannonball, it would be hard to find a more idyllic spot for a middle school meet-cute in New England. The author and her husband went to school together. Courtesy of the author We weren't childhood sweethearts . We didn't start dating until our late 20s, but despite the sweeping romance we had reconnecting and getting married, we fell into a postpartum blur after having a baby. As we adjusted to our new lives, romance kept falling down the priority list until it practically flatlined. But with the 18-month mark around the corner, I was ready for a comeback, and my husband absolutely did not see it coming. Postpartum romance takes a village Luckily, my parents offered to watch our daughter on many weekend afternoons, to give us time off. Yet left alone, we defaulted too easily to catching up on work and home improvement projects . We needed friends to shake us out of Mom-and-Dad mode. I'd been hoping to orchestrate a surprise trip to Canobie Lake Park all summer, ever since I realized we'd passed the 20th anniversary of our meeting there. So, when two of our bandmates mentioned they were free to hang out one Saturday, I immediately called them in secret, and we hatched a plan. The author planned a surprise for her husband so they could reconnect as a couple. Courtesy of the author It all kicked off when our friends offered to take my husband and me to a fun spot with live music for the day — a winery conveniently located near Canobie Lake. With the decoy destination in the GPS, the four of us piled into one car and set off, bathing suits hidden in the trunk. At the last second, we veered off course, pulling into the park as if it were a complete coincidence. I wish I had a video of his face when we arrived. The only other time I've seen him so surprised and delighted was when I showed him the positive pregnancy test. Everything about the theme park surpassed our expectations Tickets were $48 per person. Parking was free. There was no line at the gate. We showed up at 4 p.m., sunlight glittering off the lake bordering the park. There were families with strollers all around, but it wasn't too crowded. I didn't hear a single tantrum being thrown for the entire five hours we were there. We did exactly what 13-year-olds do after being let loose in an amusement park without supervision. We rode roller coasters all night long. Played summer camp games while we waited in line. Made silly faces in the photo booth. Got soaked from head to toe on a log flume called the Boston Tea Party. Shared a basket of chicken fingers as a snack, and then forgot to have dinner. Rode the gondola and watched the sun set over the lake. Made fun of the totally-not-scary haunted house. Started a screaming competition with a bunch of pre-teen girls on the opposite side of the swinging Pirate Ship. It was the kind of perfect date that only happens in a PG-13 movie The highlight was when we stumbled upon The Hit Collective, a boy band trio from Las Vegas, kicking off a summer residency at the park. They serenaded the crowd with songs from One Direction and K-Pop Demon Hunters, and even pulled kids up onstage to take Polaroid selfies with them while they performed. In keeping with the childhood nostalgia , we used my disposable camera to take a group photo with them after, like they were the Jonas Brothers themselves. Many things about the park felt the same, but I had so much more fun as a thirty-four-year-old than I did at thirteen. I wasn't scared of roller coasters anymore, for one. After giving birth, going upside down for a few seconds isn't quite so intimidating. I actually enjoyed being jokingly peer-pressured into the rides I used to be scared of. And I had no qualms saying no to the rides I know I hate (instead of going on the drop tower just to impress my crush). We didn't just feel like kids; we were reminded of how much fun we could have as a couple. We fell in love again, holding hands, as we decided which ride to take next together. What began as a romantic gesture to celebrate the start of our friendship turned into a time machine adventure we'll remember for the rest of our lives. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The big unknown behind Democrats' polling leads
events.summary: Poll after poll spells trouble for GOP candidates — in purple states and deep-red ones alike — but while Democrats see a blue wave coming, some Republicans see a polling mirage. Why it matters: Pollsters worry they're flying partly blind. Even a modest polling error could mean the difference between Republicans retaining control of Congress and President Trump facing Democratic majorities in both chambers. The big picture: Polling Trump voters has long been notoriously difficult. The polls underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Midterm polling has been more accurate, though some still underestimated Republican support in 2022, notes Scott Keeter, senior survey adviser at Pew Research Center. Catch up quick: With less than a month until the midterms, the polls paint a bleak picture for Republicans. The House: Democrats lead Republicans 49.8%-41.9% in the RealClearPolling generic congressional ballot average. Cook Political Report projects Democrats will gain nine to 19 seats, enough to win a narrow majority. The Senate: Cook now sees a potential Democratic net gain of two to six seats. Democrats need four to take control, and Cook just moved the Kansas Senate race into its toss-up column. Trump: The president's approval rating stands at 37.6% in Cook's polling tracker . A recent Economist/YouGov poll found 35% approving and 60% disapproving of his performance. State of play: Research suggests Republicans have become somewhat less likely than Democrats to participate in telephone surveys, and response rates overall have plummeted since the late 1990s, per Pew . "We definitely have more people answering surveys who voted for [former Vice President Kamala] Harris than who voted for President Trump," says Brent Buchanan, a Republican pollster and founder of Cygnal. "But if you're a good pollster, you still get the other people." Pollsters can compensate by giving greater weight to Trump voters or adjusting samples to better reflect the Republican electorate, which skews male, white and working class. Advanced statistical modeling tools can also take a poor sample and make it look like the true electorate, though results may be inaccurate for subgroups like young people or Hispanic voters, Pew's Keeter says. But that has risks: "The adjustment assumes that the Republicans who respond to a poll are similar to the Republicans who don't respond to the poll," Rice University political science assistant professor Matthew Tyler tells Axios. Tyler said weighting GOP respondents more heavily can backfire if those willing to answer polls are also more willing to vote Democratic than the Republicans who never respond. That could inflate the apparent size of a Democratic wave. Between the lines: Predicting who will actually vote can dramatically change the results. YouGov chief scientist Douglas Rivers found Democratic leads ranging from six to 16 points depending on how likely voters were identified in a September survey — and called the 16-point margin "almost certainly an overstatement." The bottom line: Even with the questions about the accuracy of recent polls, most pollsters believe Democrats have the edge heading into Election Day. " I think it's telling that we're hanging our hopes on, 'The polls are wrong,'" Buchanan says. "That's not very strong."

events.title: The Iran war is exposing dangerous gaps in the US military system built to save wounded troops
events.summary: Military medical officials said that as US forces entered the war with Iran, they lacked the same level of medical support they saw during the Global War on Terror. US Central Command Public Affairs The American doctors weren't in the room, or even in the country, when they were informed that the man's crushed limb could be saved. The US service member had been deployed aboard a ship in the Middle East, but an equipment accident in March had left him with severe injuries that exceeded the ship's medical capabilities. He had to go ashore for care, but there wasn't a US-run medical facility available nearby. At a host-nation hospital in the region, local doctors monitored and treated him while reassuring their US counterparts from afar that he was in stable condition. However, when he arrived at the American military hospital in Landstuhl, Germany, a week later, doctors saw a limb that had turned almost black and a life in danger. The incident, described publicly to an audience of military medical professionals by US Army Col. Jennifer Gurney during a panel on trauma case studies, speaks to a problem American forces have confronted amid the conflict with Iran. The system built for treating wounded troops during the post-9/11 Global War on Terror has struggled in this new fight. Gurney, who recently rotated out after serving as director of the Pentagon's Joint Trauma System , shared details of the incident at an August conference that Business Insider attended. Her remarks were not an isolated warning. Other military leaders who spoke at the event, along with half a dozen military medical officials interviewed separately, described a casualty-care system grappling with a battlefield far different from Iraq and Afghanistan . Officials who spoke with Business Insider said that at the beginning of the Iran war, medical capabilities close to the fighting were constrained by persistent drone and missile threats . They said that medical facilities on or near military centers have only recently received improved protection. Additionally, large, US-run hospitals in the region are absent, officials said, and reliance on host-nation hospitals, combined with limits on American oversight and fragmented records, has complicated efforts to track both patients and lessons from the war. The US once operated large Role 3 hospitals, such as this one in Afghanistan in 2011, during the Global War on Terror. Donna Miles/Department of Defense A spokesperson for Central Command , which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, told Business Insider that the combatant command maintains "an extensive casualty care system" with liaison officers and "active embed teams" in the host-nation medical facilities. They added that the command surgeon's office "follows every case all the way back home." CENTCOM said the system performed effectively overall and that 95% of wounded service members — most of whom had concussion-related injuries — were able to return to duty within hours or days. Do you have a story to tell about combat casualty care during the Iran war? Business Insider wants to hear from service members, medical personnel, family members, and others with firsthand experience or insight into how the military is treating, moving, and tracking the wounded. You can contact reporter Kelsey Baker on Signal at KelseyBaker75.75. A Pentagon Inspector General report to Congress released in mid-September documented some of the operational challenges surrounding casualty care during the conflict, echoing what officials told Business Insider. The independent investigation found a reliance on foreign medical centers due to the "resource and force protection challenges" of establishing large, fixed facilities. The report also said that US Army medical evacuation helicopters were forced to relocate in response to Iranian strikes, leaving US troops heavily dependent on ground vehicles and local ambulances in emergencies. "We refined a trauma system for 20 years that we cannot lift and shift to this current environment," a senior medical official with combat experience told Business Insider. They recalled a deep sense of helplessness upon realizing that "we really didn't have a functional battlefield trauma system" when the war began. A trauma system built for past wars The US military spent two decades building an unmatched medical system for saving the lives of wounded service members. During the Global War on Terror, it operated a tightly connected chain designed to move severely wounded troops rapidly from the battlefield to advanced levels of care. During the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, US and coalition forces maintained "Role 3" hospitals near major combat hot spots in those countries that provided advanced surgical care options beyond damage control — such as orthopedic, neurosurgical, and facial surgery — and postoperative care. When the war with Iran began, that infrastructure was no longer in place. With the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and a vastly diminished footprint in Iraq, Role 3 hospitals were gone. "Our service members should not pay the price because we can't organize and implement our battlefield trauma system," Gurney said at the August conference. A Defense Health Agency spokesperson told Business Insider that the discussion by Gurney and other military medical leaders "should not be interpreted as a characterization of current medical posture, partnerships, or personnel presence across the region." "The panel's purpose was to identify lessons that can inform the continued development of the globally integrated Combatant Command Trauma System, rather than to assess or characterize current operations," the spokesperson said. Three medical officials told Business Insider that when the US launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran at the end of February, US medical teams near enough to the fighting to treat American troops wounded by drones and missiles lacked adequately protected facilities, limiting them. And the military's nearest major hospital was in Germany, thousands of miles away. Those gaps became evident one day into the war. Six American service members were killed in Kuwait in March by an Iranian strike. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images On March 1, an Iranian drone struck US forces at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait, killing six US service members. Some injured troops drove themselves to a hospital, and later waited in safe houses for evacuation, survivors told The Washington Post . "There was absolutely no evacuation plan," an Army colonel wounded in the blast told The War Horse , an online publication covering the military. One soldier who survived the attack told Business Insider that troops scrambled beforehand to find medical supplies. A rehearsal that should have had troops physically walk through each step of a mass-casualty event was glossed over, they said. events.title: I started an Airbnb business with my friends with 4 cabins. Now we manage more than 500 properties.
events.summary: Samuel Sévigny and his friends started a short-term rental property management company and scaled from 10 properties to over 500 in four years. Chaletô Samuel Sévigny cofounded Chaletô, a Quebec-based rental management firm, with friends in 2022. They've grown the company in four years and now manage over 500 properties. Sévigny said that some things run more smoothly at scale — others don't. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Samuel Sévigny, 32, the cofounder and marketing director at Chaletô, a short-term rental property management company based in Quebec, Canada. Sévigny started Chaletô in 2022 with four of his friends and has scaled to over 500 cabins and condos. The following has been edited for length and clarity. It started as six friends fresh out of college. We all had other jobs. It was in 2016, and we wanted to invest in real estate, diversify, and get started in life. One of our co-founders had condos in downtown Quebec City already, so he pitched us the idea of investing all together and building our own cabin , and to manage it ourselves. So that's what we did. We launched our first cabin together in 2019, then our second in 2020, right in the middle of COVID. Fast-forward to 2022, and we had four different units that we owned and managed, and we wanted to delegate the process of managing them. We couldn't find anyone who was professional enough for our standards, so it was just like most origin stories: it starts with a problem that we're trying to solve. In the meantime, our neighbor started pressuring us, asking if we could manage his property because he could see that we were rented pretty much the whole year. We said no at first, but he kept asking. At some point, we decided to say yes. It started with our neighbor, then it was the neighbor's neighbor, and then the whole street. Then we had 10 properties under management in 2022. Sévigny and the rest of the Chaletô founders. Chaletô The six of us had to sit down and say, "Hey, what are we going to do with this? It's getting serious." Either we'll make this a serious, legitimate business , or we stop, because there's no in-between. So in 2022, we decided to incorporate Chaletô . We grew from 10 to 500-plus units in four years. We decided to make it a real thing and to go all-in. When we scaled our business, our gains scaled, too The biggest difference between an individual host and a property management company is really the optimization at scale. When you're a professional host, you're dealing with your own cleaner, your tech stack is under one roof, and you've got one or two listings. You're paying the higher-bracket price for all the tools you're using. You probably decide to cut different tools because you maybe don't have the resources, or the time, or the training to be able to use them well. I'm thinking about dynamic pricing tools. I'm thinking about AI automation for operations. I'm thinking about a bunch of things like that, because that's not your day job. I was working in advertising in Montreal and doing Airbnb hosting on the side. I was managing the guest messaging on nights and weekends, so I really lived the individual host dilemma of having a full-time job and then dealing with guests Friday and Saturday when you're off from your day job. I lived through that for several years, so I really, really understand how it feels. One of the Chaletô properties. Chaletô When you make this a full-time gig and it becomes a full-time business, then you make gains at scale. You get a little bit more leverage with relationships within the industry. For example, you can negotiate cleaners' contracts a little bit easier. That comes with professional management, and that's the main benefit of having it at scale. Also, you can attract talent for specific things in your business that you couldn't if you were alone. If you're managing only one or two properties, there's no need to have a full-time dedicated revenue management person, someone who's trained for this, sophisticated, and educated about that. But when you manage 50 or 100 properties, it becomes interesting because you can optimize each function of your hosting business. Our business works best when we're not distracted by the latest trends When you scale, it's easy to get distracted. You see it in every industry possible: real estate, service, and tech. It's like when something starts clicking, and it works, and everything seems to be working for you, then the easiest shortcut for entrepreneurs, I think, is jumping on all the opportunities. It would be easy for us to say, "We're going to keep investing in real estate because we're giving the service to support it," but it's a different beast. Investing is totally different than servicing the owners. Now you're distracted between two different businesses: you're scaling one, and then you're trying to scale the other. Another Chaletô cabin. Chaletô Another problem we face is the speed at which AI is moving, not only for our industry but for everyone. At what stage does it become mature enough to be implemented within our business, and where do you focus? Because it seems like there is a new tool and there's a new shiny object being created by the next engineer every other week. One of our challenges is always, do you keep hiring people and training them and keep it very hospitality based, or do you optimize with AI , and is it mature enough to support that optimization, or is it just a super shiny object and a gamble? So far, I'll say I don't think we have 100% the right answer to that. We prefer to hire and grow our team for now and really double down on service when everyone's running towards AI . We also prefer to hire actual people from Quebec. They speak French first, English second, and they can support any type of customer service issue because they live here, they understand the market, they understand the region, and the experiences around it. We use tech to support our business, but every couple of months, it feels like you have to re-challenge yourself. Is this still the right tech? Are you overpaying for it? Because AI is going at a speed that is so fast. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement that the Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences. Why it matters: The Trump administration has made a show of flexing American power, sometimes with grisly footage. Now, it's preparing to make the government's ultimate punishment available for all to see. The big picture: Americans are increasingly encountering shocking images on their phones, often without warning. Graphic footage of Charlie Kirk's assassination spread widely across social media, searing in the brains of social media users — often young ones. Since Oct. 7, 2023, footage from the Hamas attacks and Israel's military campaign in Gaza has circulated online. Some videos have spread from Telegram to social platforms like X , where clips are easy to find. Footage of the August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte train went viral across X, stirring debate about crime and public safety. Trump later said he had watched the video and wished he hadn't. A livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts interviewed by Reuters. Public executions are increasingly rare worldwide. In recent years, most have taken place in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. Friction point: Tech companies are now facing the question of whether they would allow the Pentagon to livestream the execution on their platforms. Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009 at the Fort Hood Army base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3. TikTok and Kick said that livestreaming the event would violate their policies, The Verge reported. YouTube, Meta, X and Twitch did not respond to The Verge's requests for comment. Yes, but: Elon Musk has positioned X, in particular, as a bulwark against internet censorship in the name of free speech. Hegseth's plan is putting the limits of that free-speech philosophy to a new test. The platform defended its decision to keep graphic content of the Kirk shooting on the platform, saying: "We will continue to stand against violence and censorship, ensuring this platform amplifies truth and open dialogue for everyone." After a bishop was stabbed during a livestreamed church service in Australia in 2024, X defied government demands to remove footage of the attack worldwide. Zoom out: Hegseth's announcement raises the prospect of reversing America's nearly century-long retreat from public executions. He justified making the execution public, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky, which drew 20,000 spectators, is widely considered America's last public execution. A modern-day livestreamed execution could reach billions. The intrigue: Vice President JD Vance questioned Friday whether the execution would actually be livestreamed and said he wouldn't watch if it were. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) posted : "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. …Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." President Trump told reporters he had approved the decision to livestream the execution. The bottom line: America spent nearly a century moving away from public executions. Now, with real-world violence just a click away, the U.S. government is preparing to show one to the world.

events.title: We rode 12 rides at Disney World without paying for Lightning Lanes. The secret was leaving our kids at home.
events.summary: The author and her friend went to three parks at Disney World. Courtesy of the author I went to Disney World with a friend instead of bringing our children. We visited Hollywood Studios, Magic Kingdom, and Epcot in a single day. It was surprisingly empty. Without kids slowing us down, we rode 12 rides and explored at our own pace. My friend and I felt like we were overdue for a trip without our kids . Between the two of us, we have seven children, ranging in age from 6 to 10, including three pairs of twins. We knew we wanted it to be a warm-weather destination to extend the feeling of summer, as the leaves are already turning red in Maine, where we both live. The author grew up going to Disney World. Courtesy of the author The one destination we kept coming back to was Florida. And because we are both huge Disney fans , I threw the crazy idea of going to the parks without our kids. Getting to feel like a kid again alongside my friend was one of the most uplifting experiences in my years as a mom. We got Park Hopper tickets Because we still wanted to lounge by the pool and drink frozen drinks, we figured we'd dedicate one day and one day only to Disney World. So we got Park Hopper tickets that allowed us to move between parks. The way we used them was absolutely key, and was very different from the trips I've taken with my kids. Whenever I've gotten Park Hopper tickets at the parks with my kids, I've felt like I wasted my money because they just wanted to do one park at a time, or we would take forever with meals, snacks, potty breaks, and all the things little kids require. The author and her friend got park hopper tickets at Disney World. Courtesy of the author With just the two of us, we were able to do three parks: Hollywood Studios , Magic Kingdom, and Epcot. Our initial plan was just to do two and skip Magic Kingdom, but we did so much of Hollywood Studios by 1 p.m. that we decided to add one more stop. We rode 12 rides Sure, our approach was not to do absolutely everything in every single park. We were just going with the flow, especially considering that we didn't splurge on Lightning Lanes since we didn't have a firm plan and didn't want time slots to deter our adventure. On the Sunday we were there, Lightning Lanes ranged from $24 to $27, depending on the park. We started our day at Hollywood Studios because we are both big Star Wars fans and hadn't done that area yet. We were able to get on rides super quickly without waiting in line. After we made our way to Toy Story, I finally rode the highly coveted Slinky Dog Dash, which had by far our longest wait at 45 minutes. The author and her friend got to ride everything they wanted. Courtesy of the author Both my friend and I grew up going to the parks , and we knew we had to ride the Tower of Terror because it's just a classic. I hadn't done that ride in 15 years (my kids are not enthused about thrill rides), and it was even better than I remembered. When we entered Magic Kingdom, our first reaction was how empty it was — especially for a weekend day. I looked at the map, and wait times were surprisingly low. I think that going during a day when Mickey's Not So Scary Halloween Party was happening played in our favor. Those attending the ticketed event can enter after 4 p.m., so while we didn't have the park to ourselves, our longest line was at Tiana's Bayou, at 30 minutes. The author didn't have terrible wait times at Disney World. Courtesy of the author To end the night, we moved on to Epcot to experience the International Food and Wine festival, another thing we had never been able to do because kids have little patience to walk from booth to booth to try new things. At one point, while we were eating, it started drizzling, so we made our way into the Frozen Ever After ride to wait it out, because after all, October is hurricane season in Florida, and some weather is to be expected. We tried 6 different foods We actually didn't know the food festival was happening, but we knew we wanted to end the night at Epcot because we wanted a full meal there, since we had only been snacking at the other parks. As soon as we entered the festival section, we grabbed a frozen mango margarita (we had earned it) and started our dinner with samosas and chicken tikka masala at the India stand, then followed up with a spiked mango lassi. We then moved to Greece, where we had a spanakopita that was out of this world. The author's favorite food was the Mexican paleta. Courtesy of the author After that, we went to Brazil, where we had a moqueca de camarão and a frozen caipirinha — the latter had nothing on the margarita and mango lassi we had just finished. We finished the food portion of our tour around the world with some escargot in France. But the last thing we had was a Mexican paleta, which was, hands down, my favorite thing of the entire day. We then walked around the park, rode rides with no lines, danced to live bands, and kept reminding ourselves that we wouldn't have been able to do all of this if our kids had been there with us. After over 27,000 steps and hours of laughter, we headed out of the most magical place on earth and collapsed in our beds. For one day, I wasn't anyone's mom. I was just a girl at Disney with her best friend, and I didn't realize how much I'd missed myself. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Buffett's 'trips down YouTube rabbit hole' revealed
events.summary: Berkshire Hathaway Portfolio Tracker (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.) Buffett's 'nightly trips down the YouTube rabbit hole' revealed Warren Buffett watches CNBC in the morning, but nearly every evening he "can't get enough" of watching YouTube clips while sitting on a recliner in front of an "enormous" television in his Omaha home. A Wall Street Journal article this week quotes friends as saying he's "hardly ever" looking at anything related to investing or finance, although he is a "fan of Berkshire Hathaway's own content" and "proud of how it performs on the video platform." Instead, it's things like "Glenn Close clips ... commercials from the 1950s ... Paul Anka videos ... speeches by complete unknowns ... show tunes, railroads, the big-band era, Nebraska and early Frank Sinatra performances from the 1930s." He will also go down some "random rabbit holes." For example, Buffett might "come into his office, gushing about a moving amateur rendition of 'My Way.'" Sharon Osberg, the three-time world bridge champion who has taught Buffett and Bill Gates the finer points of the game , is also Buffett's "frequent viewing companion," says the WSJ. She reports "Warren's range is broad. It can be the silliest things," like a "really good documentary on Roy Cohn" or "the Uzbekistan version of America's got talent ." Osberg says Buffett has also been watching clips featuring his late friend and business partner, Charlie Munger, including a 2017 appearance at the University of Michigan. "You feel the bond between the two of them as he watches Charlie. It's really quite something." The WSJ knocks down the idea Buffett's YouTube habit had anything to do with Berkshire's big investment in Alphabet , the platform's corporate parent. "He just really likes watching the clips, friends say." The article notes that while Buffett, now 96 years old, is notoriously slow to adopt new technologies, in this instance his move to YouTube is in line with an ongoing shift from streaming to video clips that has made the platform the most-watched video provider on TVs in the U.S. Berkshire Hathaway added another $192.6 million to its bet on homebuilder Lennar late last week. In an SEC filing Monday, Berkshire reports buying 2.4 million shares of Lennar Class A at an average price of $79.65 and 15 thousand shares of Lennar Class B at an average price of $78.33 on Thursday, October 1 and Friday, October 2. Since Berkshire's stake topped 10% in mid-September, it's been required by an SEC rule to disclose additional purchases within two business days. There's been no filing so far this week, so it appears there wasn't any new buying through at least Tuesday. In total, Berkshire has added $595.3 million of Lennar shares on 11 trading days since September 17. At today's closing prices, its disclosed 12.2% stake of 29 million shares is valued at $2.2 billion . At the end of last year, it owned just 7.2 million shares, then worth $742 million. Over that period, LEN has dropped more than 25% as rising interest rates have made homes less affordable. events.title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review. Experts are alarmed
events.summary: Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review. The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb). But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage . The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing. The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “ promises kept ” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken , injure or kill people. But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception. Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science. “The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues. “I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added. The FDA did not respond to a request for comment. The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”. Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts. Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”. Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity. Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical. “They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.” How TOR led to children eating rocket fuel chemicals The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats. Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample.

events.title: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
events.summary: Dollar General, BJ's Wholesale Club, Lululemon and Under Armour have said in earnings calls that they have already cut or plan to cut assortments. Analysts said that after trimming product lines, brands may focus on raising prices to get back to healthy growth. Box retailers can offer thousands of individual brands, so product cuts can help streamline assortments and stabilize their businesses. Trimming assortments comes with challenges, as retailers risk losing customers and have to answer to investors as their revenue base shrinks in the short term. Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets. As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs. In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%. Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make. When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems. "If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly." Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns. Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue. "Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price." Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power. Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years. "Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer." Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand. Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level. "It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel. He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026. Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June. For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices. Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business. "When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel. BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.
