events.title: Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI
events.summary: Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” opens this weekend as a broader run of films takes on tech leaders and artificial intelligence. The slate includes portrayals or documentaries involving Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes and Sam Altman. The new releases land as polling shows high public concern about AI risks and growing unease about data centers. This weekend marks the kickoff of a slew of films centered on some of the biggest figures in technology and artificial intelligence , as public concern about the industry grows. Sony Pictures' " The Social Reckoning " is expected to open to around $7 million domestically this weekend. The scripted film is a follow-up to Aaron Sorkin's "The Social Network" from 2010, which went on to win three Academy Awards. While Sorkin's first "Social" film focused on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg 's founding of the company, "The Social Reckoning" follows the 2021 leak by Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, who exposed internal documents from the tech giant. "It brought back really warm memories for me," Haugen told CNBC recently about the film. "And so I felt it captured the spirit of that time period." The box office this weekend will also see a limited release of Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour Elon Musk documentary, called "Musk." Early showings have drawn critical acclaim, but it's also been criticized by Musk himself on X, saying the film has zero integrity. "You Can See Everything," the documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim via A24 Films, releases on Oct. 16. Christmas brings "Artificial" from Neon to theaters. The scripted film depicts OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and his brief firing from the role in 2023. "It looks like an awful movie, but I appreciate people's creativity, and I really do support that," Altman recently told CNBC. "I get why people have anxiety. And also if they need to, like, project that anxiety onto someone or have a little bit of relief and poke fun at me, it doesn't bother me." Netflix is also joining in. The streamer's latest installment of its "Instadocs" series will premiere on Monday, highlighting the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and autonomously hacked into the company's infrastructure. These films come at a critical time as the public has grown increasingly concerned about the dangers of AI and wary of the data centers that power the technology. A recent Quinnipiac poll showed that 73% of Americans are concerned about AI's threat to human survival, while a Pew Research survey showed that 54% think data centers are bad for the environment. The question now is whether these films will push that public perception even further toward the brink. David Kirby, Cal Poly's director of Science, Technology & Society, said the public attention on these films is only adding fuel to the fire. "Movies are incredibly persuasive media," he said. "Stories are incredibly persuasive. We've known this for centuries." "I think the people at the top, they're worried about it partially because they don't like to look bad. They don't like people questioning that they know what they're doing or that they're not the people who are going to be saving humanity," he added. Hollywood has a history of releasing films that researchers and observers have linked to changes in public opinion. The 2004 blockbuster "The Day After Tomorrow" was recognized for drawing attention to climate change, while the 2013 documentary "Blackfish" was credited with changing perceptions of SeaWorld and marine mammal captivity. Kirby credited films like "Deep Impact" and "Armageddon" from 1998 as forcing governments to spend more money and attention on the topic of asteroids hitting the Earth. "Was the science right in it? Not really. It's controversial, but in terms of raising awareness … that's what you want," Kirby said. "You need to break into that public attention. You need people to start paying attention to you. Movies, that's a perfect way to do that." events.title: Squeezy olive oil bottles, Meghan’s pot filler tap and the rise of ‘cheffy’ kit in home kitchens
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . Social media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buying T he Duchess of Sussex is no ordinary home cook, but when Meghan appeared on Instagram this week at a hob presided over by a special pot filler tap , it spoke to a shift in the everyday kitchen – the rise of “cheffy” kit. While the pot filler is now most often found in luxury residential kitchens, it was reportedly invented in the early 20th century as a functional fixture for commercial kitchens. It joins a wealth of other restaurant equipment to have infiltrated our homes, from squeezy olive oil bottles to stainless steel mixing bowl sets. At Sous Chef, a UK-based independent speciality food brand, sales of chef presses are up 26%, while sales of chef’s trays are booming, according to Holly Thomson, the company’s food editor. For Ella Risbridger, author of The Kitchen Book: Good Food for Every Day : “It’s an amazing thing, the blurring of lines between restaurant and home kitchens.” A byproduct of the increasing visibility we have of professional chefs at work, whether via open kitchens in restaurants or “chefluencers” on social media, the utilitarianism and gadgets of restaurant kitchens are increasingly aspirational. This week, in a home tour with Architectural Digest, Julianne Moore showed off her Ikea industrial shelves. “People now can see what is happening in professional kitchens,” says Risbridger, “and likely, if they are watching The Bear or a lot of cheffy Instagrams, the algorithm knows that and knows what you might, might, want to buy for yourself.” From the white T-shirt to the Japanese Hasegawa chopping board , people want to channel Carmy and Syd as they make dinner midweek. Thomson suspects it might have something to do with the economic climate – people are thinking: “‘I’m not going to spend 90 quid on a meal, but I might invest in these products that are going to help me take eating at home a bit more seriously.’” According to James Lawless, a spokesperson at David Mellor, this shift links back to the pandemic, which “reignited interest in home cooking”. “Professional chefs’ equipment may have specialist functions, but it isn’t special,” says Lawless. “They are first and foremost tools to perform a particular function.” For Thomson, they are “an extra piece of kit that adds a bit of ease, finesse, or streamlines the process”. Coming from a professional kitchen, where “you don’t have anything that takes up space that isn’t fully useful, used every day and has multiple purposes,” they’d have to be. Of course, one person’s useful can be another’s waste of space. In the case of the pot filler tap, in an ordinary small kitchen that might be unnecessary, but, according to Helen Parker, the creative director of deVOL Kitchens, it “has become the must-have addition to a larger kitchen”. Sometimes, you don’t know what you don’t know. As Thomson says of the squeezy olive oil bottle, which, at a few quid, is proof that this isn’t all about expensive equipment: “Precision squirting is just so useful, and once you’ve done it once, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is so much better than glugging oil out of a bottle.’” For Risbridger, “the trick is that it’s nice to buy something fancy for a hobby – it’s often a shortcut to taking yourself more seriously … you can now access a reasonably cheap version of something professionals use, and that makes you feel more like a professional. Which increases confidence. Which makes the thing you make better, whether or not you could have achieved it without the gadget.”

events.title: Starter homes are getting harder to find. These 20 cities are bucking the trend.
events.summary: Starter homes are becoming harder to come by in all but a few major metros. dpproductions/Getty Images The market for starter homes is decreasing, but some cities still have plenty available. A report from Realtor.com shows that fewer than a quarter of large metro areas are starter-home-dominant. The number of starter homes is falling nationally, but it's increasing in some cities. As mortgage rates continue to reach new heights , options for first-time buyers are dwindling. Even starter homes — affordable properties that entice first-time homebuyers get their foot in the door — are jumping in price. The inventory of starter homes has recently decreased across the country. Data from Realtor.com shows that the national starter home share dropped from 38.1% to 36.2% from August 2019 to 2026, but the price during that timeframe increased 30.8%, from about $260,000 to $340,000. Realtor defines starter homes as homes listed at or below 80% of the median list price in that metro. A recent report from Realtor analyzing 8,300 ZIP codes in the largest 100 metros found that only 18.3% of those ZIP codes were starter-home dominant. "Affordability is only part of the story. What matters as much is whether affordable homes are actually for sale in the places where buyers want and need to live," Realtor senior economist Hannah Jones said. "For first-time buyers, the search is increasingly shaped by the geography of opportunity, not simply a metro's headline price. Keeping homeownership within reach will require more entry-level homes at attainable price points." It could be a while before the housing market gets back to "normal," but there are still areas that have more starter homes than others. events.title: I moved from Massachusetts to Nashville for a partner. Though we broke up, I've made my own life here.
events.summary: The author moved to Nashville for a relationship that didn't last— but she doesn't regret it. Courtesy of Phoebe Farrell-Sherman After college, I moved from Massachusetts to Nashville with my partner. My friends and family urged me not to move for someone else, but I went anyway. Though we broke up, I found a job and made friends, and I don't regret the move. Like many freshly minted adults, when I graduated from college , I wasn't sure exactly what to do next. I had dreams and goals; as a writer, I wanted to pursue an MFA, but the timing didn't feel right. My future was obscure to me — except for one thing. ' Whatever I did, I wanted to do it with my girlfriend of a year. And I did know for certain what my girlfriend wanted to do next: to get her master's at a university closer to her family in Kentucky than our New England undergraduate school. She was admitted to Vanderbilt in Nashville, and suddenly, moving there seemed like my most likely destination. My friends and family advised against the move Without exception, my friends and family urged me not to make a major life decision based on a relationship that might not last. They thought I would feel alienated in Nashville, and not without reason, since I grew up in Seattle and was living in Massachusetts, and had never spent any meaningful amount of time anywhere that fell between the West Coast and the Northeast. I found ways to rationalize my decision to follow my girlfriend — getting recommendations on what Nashville might have to offer writers, securing an entry-level position at a book review magazine — but secretly, I felt ridiculous whenever I said I had my own reasons for moving. My reason was that I wanted to be with her. The move was fraught from the start, both practically and emotionally. We fought while packing. On the harrowing drive down, my girlfriend's car was so full that she couldn't see her blind spot, and I had to lean out the window to check for oncoming traffic every time she changed lanes. At first, I questioned whether I had made the right decision Once in Nashville, I picked up a second job to afford my half of our rent, working late into the night scooping ice cream after days at the magazine's office. On the weekends, we went to tailgates with my girlfriend's graduate school cohort or drove to visit her family. I didn't know anyone in the city, and I didn't have a car of my own. I was entirely dependent on her, and it was suffocating. Exhausted and terrified that the advice I'd ignored had been absolutely right, I sought out something, anything that might lead to making a friend. I started showing up alone to writing events, forcing myself to chat with strangers . And I decided to join a choir, though I had no idea how I would get to and from the rehearsals. At the first meeting, I asked if anyone might be interested in carpooling, trying not to seem as desperate as I felt. I had no idea that the two people who offered to give me rides would become part of my life for many years to come. The author (right), her partner (center), and her best friend, whom she met after moving to Nashville. Courtesy of Phoebe Farrell-Sherman I made friends, and they have been there for me It was those two friends who cheered me on when my temporary position at the magazine became permanent, which allowed me to quit my second job. They came to support me when a new friend I'd met at an open mic night invited me to lead a writing workshop. They celebrated me when I was promoted to an editor at the magazine. And they were the ones to comfort me when my relationship finally fell apart. So, yes, the relationship didn't last. But, as I reflected afterward, though I was sad things hadn't worked out the way I wanted them to, I was surprised to realize that I couldn't regret the path I'd chosen. We can never know what the future holds, and however we try to justify our choices, they're rarely perfectly rational. But perhaps the more reasonable thing to expect of ourselves is not that we choose perfectly, but that we work to make whatever we choose worthwhile. I moved to Nashville for love, but once I was in Nashville, I found an incredible job, a creative community, and two lifelong friends (one of whom is now my romantic partner). If I could do it all over again, I wouldn't change a thing. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Radio 4 , · 10 Oct 2026 , · 24 mins State Pension Age and Louise Botting Tribute The State Pension age went up again this week as part of its gradual shift from 66 years old to 67. The law says it will rise again to 68 by 2046, but that may change. A State Pension Age Review, the third to be held, is considering whether the rules around state pension age are appropriate in the light of the latest life expectancy data and will recommend how state pension age should be determined in the future. We'll speak to Dr Suzy Morrissey, who was appointed by the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions last year to prepare an independent report into the future of the State Pension age. Louise Botting, the former presenter of Money Box, has died at the age of 87 after a short illness. We'll pay tribute. Average mortgage rates hit a three year high this week affecting millions of homes owners looking to remortgage and people hoping to buy their first home. What's the best advice? And, the Bank of England has picked the animals to appear on the next series of bank notes. The hedgehog, barn owl, puffin and bumblebee were chosen after a public vote - with almost half a million people responding to a consultation. events.title: Here are the staggering numbers behind the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group's 321-day deployment
events.summary: The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned home this week. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Aaron J. Rolle USS Abraham Lincoln has returned from a challenging combat deployment. Its air wing flew thousands of combat missions, dropping over a million pounds of ordnance. The Navy says the deployment is shaping future carrier operations. The US Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned home this week after a long and difficult combat deployment. The numbers shared by the sea service for that deployment are staggering. The warship left its homeport in San Diego in November 2025 and was deployed for 321 days, which included 286 consecutive days at sea without a port call. The lengthy deployment, extended by Operation Epic Fury that kicked off the Iran war, set a modern-day record . As hostilities began at the end of February, the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group played a central role in the fight. The carrier strike group's embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 — a naval aviation force consisting of nine squadrons of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighters, and EA-18G Growler electronic attack aircraft, among other assets— flew nearly 4,000 combat flights during the 40-day operation. During the monthslong deployment, it flew 14,037 aircraft sorties and accumulated 31,460 forward-deployed flight hours. An estimated 20.5 million gallons of aviation fuel enabled the air wing's operations, the Navy said. During Operation Epic Fury, the carrier air wing's mix of fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft launched 1,499 precision munitions, dropping over 1.37 million pounds of ordnance on priority targets such as missile sites, defense production facilities, military infrastructure, and Iranian naval capabilities. Air assets also shielded the strike group from enemy action. The Navy said that the air wing, with its combination of stealth fighter jets and workhorse aircraft, effectively penetrated contested airspace and demonstrated the "Air Wing of the Future" concept in a real-world combat scenario. Among the air assets deployed with Carrier Air Wing 9 were F-35C Lightning II Joint Strike Fighters, fifth-generation stealth jets. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 3rd Class Angel Campbell Following the April ceasefire and the conclusion of Epic Fury, Carrier Strike Group 3 supported the Navy's blockade. When Iran began targeting commercial shipping, the group participated in strikes on Iranian coastal defenses and missile sites. It supported a second blockade before finally heading home. Over the course of its deployment, the Lincoln sailed over 93,000 nautical miles, supported by 72 at-sea replenishments. For its actions during the deployment, the strike group received the Presidential Unit Citation, one of the military's highest unit awards. The difficult deployment took its toll on the broader strike group, which also included three guided-missile destroyers. Multiple reports indicated that logistical strain caused by the war exacerbated the situation. Business Insider obtained written responses submitted to Congress by Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao late last month that revealed eight suicide attempts by sailors assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Cao said that multiple sailors attempted to jump overboard. There were no suicides, though. Cao wrote that "the men and women of Carrier Strike Group THREE have demonstrated exceptional resolve under demanding conditions," emphasizing that "operational decisions to extend deployments are never made lightly." He said the Navy is committed to preserving crew morale, health, and safety, and overall fleet readiness. Navy leadership has said that it is taking lessons from the deployment . The service has said that it is loading carriers up with more supplies to ensure self-sufficiency if logistics and support come under stress, adding quality of life improvements, and working to keep sailors and Marines better connected with loved ones. events.title: S&P lifts UK GDP growth view on resilient consumer spending and services sector
events.summary: S&P Global Ratings has upgraded its growth outlook for the UK, citing “reasonably resilient” consumer spending and services that have helped shield the economy from the conflict in the Middle East. Real gross domestic product in Europe's second-biggest economy is now expected to climb by 1.3 per cent, from a previous lowered prediction of 1.1 per cent , the New York-based agency said on Friday. S&P analysts noted that hospitality and professional services underpinned economic growth in the second quarter. GDP growth is seen to average 1.4 per cent from 2027 to 2029, expecting the economy to improve if the situation in the Middle East is “contained”. The agency also maintained the UK's long and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at AA, two notches below the top prime grade. An investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises. “The stable outlook reflects our view that the UK economy has remained, and will remain, resilient in the face of the energy shock emanating from the Middle East conflict, with growth remaining reasonably robust,” analysts at S&P wrote. “This is balanced against risks from the UK's constrained fiscal position, elevated public debt levels, and high government spending, including on debt servicing.” S&P also noted the UK's policy direction under Andy Burnham, the UK's sixth prime minister in the past decade. The start of his tenure in July was marked by questions about how he would handle the economy, including how to ensure fiscal discipline. Mr Burnham's government has “focused on devolution, industrial renewal, social care and closer ties with the EU, with simultaneous pledges to respect fiscal prudence”, S&P said. UK inflation was pegged at 3.1 per cent in August, the highest in five months, according to the Office of National Statistics, and well above the Bank of England's 2 per cent threshold. S&P said this has risen on domestic price pressures and energy and transport costs, underpinned by higher hydrocarbon costs. The agency expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 0.25 basis points at its November meeting after maintaining them last month, “then hold that level until the second half of 2027 because the current policy rate level of 3.75 per cent and soft labour market conditions suggest the UK may require less additional policy tightening than the eurozone”. Egypt's growth accelerates Meanwhile, S&P said Egypt's economy accelerated at its fastest pace in three years, but cautioned the North African nation remains vulnerable to shocks stemming from the conflicts in the Middle East. Real GDP in the Arab world's most populous nation jumped by 5.1 per cent in fiscal 2026, buoyed by non-oil sectors including manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, information and communication technology, and tourism, it said in a separate report. That compares to a 4.7 per cent reading in its previous estimate . Household consumption emerged as a primary factor, boosted by record remittances, easing inflation and stable labour market conditions, it added. S&P, however, projects this growth to ease to 4.5 per cent in the fiscal year 2027, as shipping disruptions related to the war are expected to further pressure trade, logistics and import prices. Consumption and investment activities are also predicted to soften amid persistent uncertainty and rising inflation. Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, according to Capmas data. S&P expects inflation to average 12.9 per cent in fiscal 2027. This might result in a policy reversal from the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates. S&P also kept its B sovereign credit rating on Egypt, which is six levels below investment grade, with a stable outlook. “Nevertheless, we expect the continued implementation of the reform agenda, including the commitment to exchange rate liberalisation, to enhance structural economic competitiveness over the medium term,” the S&P analysts said.

events.title: I used to feel embarrassed about graduating from a trade school. But now my career is safe from AI.
events.summary: Sade Slack says her job is safe from AI. Courtesy of Sade Slack Sade Slack chose trade school over a four-year college and became a surgical technician. She now has no student loan debt, but sometimes feels embarrassed for not attending college. She feels secure from AI because her job depends on reading people and reacting in real time. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sade Slack, a 38-year-old surgical technician based in California. It has been edited for length and clarity. I entered high school with a heavy load of AP and honors classes . My middle school grades had put me on an accelerated track, and I pushed myself hard to keep up. By 10th grade, I was burned out . I came home from school and slept for hours just to recover. I obsessed over making A's. Then the pressure started affecting how I handled tests. I got so anxious that I began avoiding them. Halfway through the semester, I dropped all my classes. That changed how I thought about success. I stopped worrying so much about what looked impressive on paper and started asking myself what kind of life I actually wanted. That's when I decided a trade school was the better option for me. My family was disappointed when I said I didn't want to attend a four-year college My high school had a second path: Seniors who weren't going to university could meet representatives from trade schools, community colleges, and companies that hire straight out of high school. Suddenly, I could see options I hadn't considered before. I got excited about my future again. Trade school was also much easier to get into. No SAT. No waiting to hear from a first- or second-choice university. They reviewed my transcript and application and accepted me into an 18-month surgical technology program. Tuition was about $23,000. My parents didn't understand why I would borrow that much money for trade school, and they refused to cosign my student loans, so I took out the loan myself. Once classes started, the choice made even more sense Anatomy, physiology, and sociology were built on subjects I had already studied in high school, but now I could actually use what I was learning. We trained with our hands. I wasn't memorizing information just to pass an exam. I was learning skills I would eventually use in an operating room with real patients. That matters even more to me now when students can ask AI to explain almost anything in seconds. AI can be a great learning tool, but in my job, eventually, you have to know the material yourself. There is no shortcut when a patient is on the table. While I was in school, I worked at Best Buy for $7.25 an hour to cover my living expenses. I landed my first job before my friends graduated from college Family issues had me moving between two states after graduation, so it took almost two years to land my first job . I still remember that first paycheck: about $1,100. I thought I was rich. I took my friends out for dinner and drinks. They were still in their second year of college. I had already finished school and started earning money. Even my parents eventually admitted they were glad I hadn't listened to them. I'm now working my dream job Today, I'm 38. I have no student loan debt . I have health insurance, a 401(k), and a pension through a major Southern California hospital system. Some of my friends are still paying off their college loans. My workdays can be brutal. A typical shift is 12 hours, and I might work six surgeries in one day. Some days, the breaks barely feel like breaks. But I love the work. As a surgical technician , I prepare instruments, equipment, and supplies. I also make sure the surgeon has what they need throughout a procedure. A big part of the job is anticipating what happens next. I watch faces. I listen for changes in tone. I notice when the energy in the operating room shifts. Sometimes I know what a surgeon needs before they have time to say it. That's one reason I'm not convinced AI is coming for my job anytime soon. AI will probably take over more administrative tasks . It may become more involved in the operating room, too. But surgery involves more than completing a checklist. You have to read the room. You have to recognize when a routine moment suddenly becomes serious. You have to respond before someone explains what they need. That human instinct still matters. For years, I was embarrassed when colleagues asked where I went to school I work alongside doctors with elite degrees. Some have had children my age attending Ivy League universities. Saying "trade school" made me feel like I had somehow fallen short. Not anymore — especially now with the rise of AI. A four-year degree can be a great investment. So can trade school. The important thing is knowing what you're buying. The work still challenges me. I'm still learning. Eighteen years later, that still makes the decision worth it. events.title: Tourism expansion v turtle nests: the dispute dividing communities in one Tobago resort
events.summary: Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat V isitors to Rocky Point in south-west Tobago are drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest. But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best. As elsewhere in the Caribbean, the need for economic growth has led to growing interest in tourism development. Rene Seepersadsingh, the first vice-president of the Tobago Hotel and Tourism Association , says: “Tobago is very focused on attracting private partnership investment because our tourism product is now in that evolution stage, where we’re looking to upgrade the offering that we have. “There are great opportunities for participation and development within the sector,” he adds. With that goal in mind, the 12 hectares (30 acres) of Rocky Point became the subject of a request for expressions of interest in 2021 from the government agency Eteck , which manages and develops economic zones. Eteck invited proposals from qualified firms to design and manage a premier hotel and property development on the site. Superior Hotels, a locally owned company, ultimately won. It received a 99-year lease to develop a $500m (£378m), 200-room property on the site, which also includes plans for a number of privately owned villas. Since then, the project has sparked a struggle that has been going on for the past four years, led by environmentalists, Tobagonians and others who believe the development will ruin Rocky Point. Duane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation – one of several entities that submitted an expression of interest to Eteck – is now advocating for increased accountability. A former hotel manager, he is an avid surfer at Back Bay and owns tourism-related businesses in Tobago. “Our focus is to make sure that whatever is done on that site is done in an environmentally sound way, in a way that preserves it for Tobago and for future generations,” he says. He says he and his associates replied to the expression of interest with a proposal for a small eco-resort featuring nature trails, turtle watching and a wax museum showcasing Amerindian artefacts discovered at Rocky Point. He also highlighted the remains of Fort Monck, a distinctive fort with well-preserved masonry. Kenny says the winning project’s initial design raised concerns about it seemingly ignoring many archaeological and ecological features at Rocky Point, and that the subsequent amendments still do not adequately address many of the issues raised. “The amount of concrete development on this site, at least in the current model, makes us worry that the impact on the environment will be significant,” he says, adding that in his view a 200-room hotel has little chance of success in Tobago, where most large hotels struggle to achieve sustainable occupancy levels. Michelle Cazabon-Mannette, an environmental biologist and director at the NGO SpeSeas , says more than 100 people submitted written objections to the Environmental Management Authority (EMA) as part of the environmental impact assessment, which the project needs to obtain a certificate of environmental clearance (CEC). She says that after widespread objections at town hall meetings and in written submissions, the project holder made only minor design adjustments. After the adjustments, the EMA granted Superior Hotels a CEC , with about 20 pages of mitigation measures attached that the project must follow. Kirkland Brathwaite, principal at Katalyst Solutions, an environmental and project management firm, says a CEC often includes several environmental impact mitigation measures, adding that a quality assurance project plan is mandatory to ensure proper monitoring. Cazabon-Mannette says the mitigation measures listed in the CEC are insufficient, though she acknowledges that “the project designs provided – on which the CEC is based – were conceptual and (Superior Hotels) made it clear these were not final designs”. Whatever form the final designs take, Cazabon-Mannette and Kenny say a 200-room hotel and numerous villas will probably mean removing many of the trees on Rocky Point. “A major concern is having an appropriate scale of development that would minimise the footprint in terms of the coastal vegetation that would need to be cleared,” Cazabon-Mannette says.

events.title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales
events.summary: In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales. Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely. When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere. Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople. Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16. “I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape. In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer. When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”. As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival , held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan. Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim. The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week. The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs. “The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.” Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way. Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge. Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders. Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company. One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies. “We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.

events.title: ‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staff
events.summary: Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale U nion officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints. “People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth. TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”. Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs. “People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.” “Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.” Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturers recommend sitting while operating the machines. Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations. Following the policy change, TSA workers were also required to sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union. “They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones. He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US. Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents. US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy. “A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.” AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees, launched a letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”. Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.” The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facing possible pay freezes and significant increases to their health insurance premium costs. Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judge ruling in January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction. TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year. The Trump administration has also been expanding privatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airport abandoned its plan to join the program.

events.title: Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them
events.summary: AI labs are spending tens of billions of dollars per year for Nvidia chips that run their models. The demand has led to the blossoming of an industry that hyperscalers once had to themselves, including lucrative one-off arrangements and asset-light strategies. Over 300 neoclouds now rent GPUs to businesses, according to a review from researcher SemiAnalysis, up 55% in under 11 months. Nvidia GPUs are the most sought-after processors in AI, and they're in such demand that the chipmaker's stock climbed to yet another record this week, lifting its market cap close to $6 trillion. Customers can now shop around for access to the chips at the giant clouds from Amazon, Microsoft and Google, as well as at so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave. They can also go to various online marketplaces or even buy the costly hardware directly. For Nvidia, it all adds up to unrelenting growth, as management anticipates $108 billion in revenue for the October quarter, which would mark an 89% year-over-year jump. But the paradox of choice can be a headache for companies needing computing power yesterday. While cloud infrastructure providers have ranked at the top of Nvidia's customer list for several years, the business is diversifying. Five clients accounted for at least 10% of Nvidia's accounts receivable in July quarter, up from three in January, according to a filing . Industry research firm SemiAnalysis counted 323 Nvidia GPU providers as of September, up from 209 less than 11 months earlier. "You're going to see a whole new crop of really, really exciting neoclouds with hundreds of billions of dollars backlog together," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at a Goldman Sachs tech conference in San Francisco last month. Here's a rundown of the various options for accessing GPUs, and why each might make sense: Many big companies spend tens of millions of dollars per year on a smorgasbord of cloud services from Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Since the 2022 launch of ChatGPT, companies have increasingly turned to the hyperscalers for GPUs so they can run generative AI workloads. The top cloud providers come with a reputation advantage. If a software company relies on Amazon and Microsoft for GPUs and other capabilities, it won't need to panic about prospective customers questioning its suppliers. "When you're talking to enterprises, your subprocessor had better be Azure," said Bindu Reddy, CEO of AI assistant startup Abacus, referring to Microsoft's cloud infrastructure. In the past year, leading AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI have committed to spending over $500 billion between Amazon and Microsoft, which controlled 59% of the cloud infrastructure market in 2025, according to industry researcher Gartner. "Hyperscalers are in a good position to show trust to the enterprises because of their 10-plus years of full-stack capabilities," said Gartner analyst Hardeep Singh. But hyperscalers don't always have as many GPUs as enterprises require, he said. Andy Jassy, Amazon's CEO, told analysts in July that the retailer and cloud pioneer won't be able to serve all the demand it foresees this year. "I believe this dynamic will also be true in 2027," he said. If the hyperscalers were adequate, neoclouds wouldn't be proliferating. Modal, a startup operating virtual sandboxes where AI agents work independent of main IT environments, went from running on the hyperscalers to signing up with the major neoclouds, and now it uses 25 of them, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson. "You can get a few hundred GPUs or maybe a thousand, but at our scale, we needed way more GPUs," he said. The hyperscalers themselves are also chasing the neoclouds. Google and Microsoft have started tapping CoreWeave, even as they all compete with one another. "Some of the hyperscalers have approached us about taking care of customers they're worried about because they don't have the ability to service those customers when they need it," said Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer of Nebius, a Netherlands-based neocloud with operations in the U.S. Video generation startup Reactor uses GPUs through Nebius and hyperscalers, said CEO Alberto Taiuti. The location of data centers matters, he said, because Reactor wants user-created videos to show up right away. Nebius delivers the specific GPUs Reactor needs, solid customer service and sufficient hardware and software, at a good price, Taiuti said. The most visible neoclouds can require some upfront payment, and chips might not come online for months, because providers raise funding based on contracts and set up the data center equipment, Bernhardsson said. It would be difficult for CoreWeave to turn over 10,000 GPUs to a new customer with one day's notice, said Chen Goldberg, an executive vice president. CoreWeave's near-term capacity remains essentially sold out, CEO Mike Intrator said on the company's August earnings call. If companies want GPUs immediately, they might have to go beyond the name brands.

events.title: Trump rages over Nobel Peace Prize loss
events.summary: President Trump lashed out late Friday night after he once again did not win the Nobel Peace Prize he has openly coveted . Why it matters: The award is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about frequently and believes he deserves. This year's prize went instead to a former judge of a court Trump has sanctioned and called "rogue" and "evil." Navi Pillay, the winner, reacted to the award by saying world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war," according to the AP . What he's saying: " I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel. I don't know what the woman has done," Trump said in a Truth Social post of nearly 600 words that went up just before midnight on Friday. "I settled 8 Wars, with letters being sent from every President and Prime Minister from the countries that I helped to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I'm about to settle, or win, two more, Iran and, Russia/Ukraine," Trump wrote. "They're both happening at breakneck speed but, forget them, it's the 8 that I've already settled, any one of which, in particular, Pakistan and India, would be far more than necessary to win the Nobel Prize. In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1." Between the lines: Pillay, this year's winner, is a former judge of the International Criminal Court and also the former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Nobel officials said she received the honor "for her efforts to promote peace and international law." Originally from South Africa, Pillay, 85, also served as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Zoom in: Trump took aim at that UN association as well. "In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help. The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said. The intrigue: Trump also blasted Norway, as he's previously done over Nobel snubs, though the country doesn't award the prize. "This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten. The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!" The bottom line: The president didn't hold back making his case for why he should have won — and why his loss was a personal snub.

events.title: I avoided shopping on Amazon for 449 days. Having a baby brought me back to it, but I'm shopping smarter now.
events.summary: The author found herself shopping on Amazon again after she had her third child. Courtesy of Kate Bratskeir I challenged myself to stop shopping on Amazon a few years ago. I went without it for 449 days, and became more thoughtful about my purchases. With my third child, I started shopping on Amazon again. But I still try to avoid it when possible. I bought 72 things from Amazon in 2024. The range of items runs the gamut: A replacement basket for the air fryer, dozens of children's books, an XL cone for my dog's post-surgery care, kids' birthday presents, skincare products I gave up on, pacifiers for my newborn twins before I remembered stashing some extras in the diaper bag, and lots of forgettable items in between. I was feeling uncomfortable about my consumption, my carbon footprint, and how second-nature buying on Amazon had become for me. I relied on the site to instantly cross off items on my to-do list. The lack of friction before purchasing became an issue It felt like the site's " 1-Click checkout " feature evolved into its own kind of mechanism in my brain chemistry: I was ordering things without doing any of the logical thinking that usually happens with in-store shopping, and I knew that was all by design. Making a purchase no longer had friction: Free shipping, a stored credit card and address, infinite stock, and a tantalizing algorithm all make shopping anywhere else feel like a chore. When it comes to Amazon, buying begets more buying, and I was getting sick of my high level of participation in that kind of ceaseless consumer culture and of funding a company with values that don't align with my own. I decided to stop shopping on Amazon So I challenged myself to see how long I could go without the platform, and after a month , the experiment became easier. The rush of not buying was addictive. I'd found adding back in some of the friction to online shopping — whether by deciding the thing wasn't worth the shipping fees or feeling too lazy to walk across my apartment to get my credit card — put the power back in my hands. I started to want for less, and my brain got the space it needed to recalibrate, adding logic back into my purchasing decisions . I'd ask, did I really need it? Could I borrow it? Did we have an alternative at home? With friction, these questions finally had the space to resurface. And I'd started to feel smug, living out my personal values every day by resisting the corporate machine. And then I had another baby. Having my third kid brought me back to Amazon, but I think more about purchases now Throughout my pregnancy, I was nervous about how I would manage the newborn stage without that infamous one-day delivery. At that point, my twin toddlers had outgrown the baby phase , where every month feels like a new experiment in which you'll try anything to survive. Three-year-olds can do without. But when you're exhausted and hormonal, and the baby won't sleep anywhere but under your chin, getting your hands on the swaddle that your mom friend swears by feels positively dire. So, after a 449-day run, I surrendered back to Amazon. If you're wondering what did me in, the answer is: Bottle nipples. Did you know that some nipples have different-sized holes — or "liquid flow speeds" — to control how fast or slow a baby can suck milk out of their bottles? It's a very specific and boring piece of information that isn't reflected on the shelves of CVS. My dear infant would only drink out of a size 2, we quickly learned, and so I chose my child over my morals and added the nips to my cart. And while I was online anyway, I also bought dishwasher detergent, additional bottles, and some extra burp cloths. Thrilling stuff. I felt like a failure. I'm hoping that once my tiny baby becomes a little bit bigger, I'll be able to end my reliance on Amazon once and for all. But even now, back on the platform, I've been able to practice some of the insight I picked up during my Amazon abstinence. For example, if there's something I need, I'll check with neighbors and friends before scouring the site. I recently scored a jar of pureed prunes from a friend whose baby has moved on to solids. I also choose secondhand first, whenever possible. Aside from hygienic products, everything my baby needs already exists in the world. A resale store near me, Once Upon a Child, sells 10 onesies for $10; when my child outgrows them, I can resell them to the store and use the earnings toward the next size. One of the great joys of my motherhood journey has been helping other parents avoid buying things I can give them. It is mutually beneficial, as they don't have to buy an overpriced motorized baby swing, and I can reclaim some floor space in my apartment. Plus, it's a lovely feeling to witness your best friend's baby in the dress your daughter was wearing just a few years before. The onslaught of baby products that will enter your social feeds the instant your egg gets fertilized is overwhelming. Marketing can often convince you that you need a certain item to be a good parent. Of course, this isn't true. Before adding anything to my cart, I try to remember to take a beat: Do I really need the thing, and do I really need it right now? I've found that hardly anything is urgent, and with 1-day shipping times, if something does end up seeming essential, I'll be able to get it. Relying less on Amazon isn't just for me; it's something I'm trying to model for my kids. In a world where you can access just about any material good with the click of a button, I want to show them the difference between needs and wants, the importance of patience and delayed gratification, and the satisfying pursuit of making do with what you already have. These are life skills I have not perfected, and likely never will. But I owe it to the kids — and myself — to at least give it a try. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Telegraph owner poised to make newsroom job cuts in investment promise U-turn
events.summary: Exclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundancies The new owner of the Telegraph is preparing to make significant job cuts to its newsroom, just months after stating it would invest in the title to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”. Axel Springer, the German media company overseen by its billionaire chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to be examining proposals that would make between 50 and 100 journalists redundant. A source familiar with the plans said a forthcoming consultation was likely to propose cutting a “significant proportion” of editorial staff, possibly before Christmas. They said such proposals called into question Axel Springer’s promise to “back an investment programme in [the Telegraph Media Group] to grow and expand the business”. A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group declined to comment. No redundancies have been announced to staff so far. It would mark the first big intervention by Axel Springer since its £575m purchase of the Telegraph earlier this year. The sale ended three tortuous years for the Telegraph and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition. The proposed cuts have confused some Telegraph figures, who are struggling to understand how it aligns with Döpfner’s pledge to “bring that uncertainty to an end”. At a recent Axel Springer leadership summit held in London, Döpfner is also said to have stated that the company could not cut its way to growth. Axel Springer, which also owns Politico and the German titles Bild and Die Welt, recently brought in consultants to examine the financial health of the Telegraph titles, which include the Daily Telegraph, the Sunday Telegraph and its online news operation. Döpfner has made no secret of his desire to boost the Telegraph’s US operation , with senior editors already deployed to the US to develop those plans. However, consultants are understood to have drawn up potential cuts to the existing news operation at the 171-year-old titles. Sources said consultants had also recommended that the Telegraph set up side projects to support its journalism, such as price comparison sites and healthcare. Some insiders were said to be baffled by some of the suggestions. A source familiar with the proposals said they would anger Telegraph staff, who had hoped Axel Springer’s ownership would mark the arrival of “sunny uplands” after three years of being “starved of any form of investment, pay rises or management changes that could move us on”. “The path to growth is not to cut jobs,” they said. “They’re still going to need to hire people in the States if they’re going to make any sort of push there, but staff haven’t been told where that money is going to come from.” The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed that it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m. However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.

events.title: Russian attacks kill at least 12 in Ukraine after Trump-Putin diesel deal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Russian attacks kill at least 12 in Ukraine after Trump strikes diesel deal with Putin Rescuers evacuate a wounded resident from an apartment building damaged in a Russian air strike. ( Reuters: Stringer ) At least 12 people have died after Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says. The strikes came a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, in stark contrast to sanctions he signed last month. Mr Zelenskyy said Mr Trump's deal with Russia would allow the war to be prolonged. Russian strikes have killed at least 12 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says. The deadly strikes came a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow's war in Ukraine. Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Mr Zelenskyy said on Saturday. At least 14 people were wounded in the attack in the early hours of Saturday. "Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Mr Zelenskyy wrote on X. The Russian air strike happened in the early hours of the morning on Saturday. ( Reuters: Stringer ) He said the attacks show Moscow understands "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities," adding that "different signals are needed". Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine in the past 24 hours, the region's Russian-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said on Saturday. There was no immediate comment from Kyiv about those attacks. The latest attacks came a day after United States President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia. The deal is a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine, and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. At least seven people were killed in the strikes in Zaporizhzhia. ( AP Photo: Kateryna Klochko ) Mr Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Mr Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote. Mr Trump's shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine. Following Mr Trump's announcement, Germany said on Saturday it would maintain sanctions against Russia over its war on Ukraine. The Kremlin said Mr Trump conveyed his ideas about how to de-escalate the war in Ukraine to Mr Putin during their phone call on Friday. Mr Putin received the proposals "with understanding", Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Saturday according to the state TASS and RIA Novosti news agencies. He didn't elaborate on what the proposals were or the Russian president's response. Mr Trump has long sought to broker an end to the more than four-and-a-half year conflict, but talks between Russia and Ukraine remain largely deadlocked. Trump deal a 'weak decision', Zelenskyy says In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." 'Poster child' for Putin's propaganda machine Russia is not just abducting Ukrainian kids, it is embarking on a campaign of mass indoctrination, as Denys Kostev experienced firsthand. He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged. "It plays into Russia's hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said. According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Mr Zelenskyy called it "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners". Mr Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC Ari Emanuel said Elon Musk's early AI insights helped inspire his push into the live events business. Emanuel said Musk told him live entertainment could not be "disintermediated" by AI. The Hollywood powerbroker launched Mari, a live events and experiences company, last year. Hollywood powerbroker Ari Emanuel said a conversation he had years ago with Elon Musk about artificial intelligence helped inspire his push into the live events business. Speaking on a recent episode of David Senra's podcast, Emanuel said he first connected with the Tesla CEO after reading about his electric car venture. Emanuel said he called Musk, despite not knowing him, and the two developed what Emanuel described as an "incredible relationship." "I don't agree with him all the time. I do agree with him. I learn a ton. I disagree a ton," Emanuel, the super agent-turned-entertainment-mogul who is the real-life inspiration for Ari Gold in the HBO TV series "Entourage," told Senra. A major takeaway from Musk, Emanuel said, was his early view of where AI was headed. "He was talking about AI in 2007, what it was going to be," said Emanuel. "He said the only thing that can't be disintermediated by AI is live, in the entertainment business," Emanuel told Senra of Musk, adding that he specifically asked Musk about entertainment. That's what Emanuel said gave him the idea behind Mari, the live events and experiences company he launched last year. "We're now building a pretty big business" in the live entertainment space, Emanuel said, adding that his company has acquired the Miami Open and the Madrid Open tennis tournaments, along with the trading card convention, Collect-A-Con. Emanuel — who also leads TKO Group Holdings , the parent company of WWE and UFC — said Mari "will be everything live events on a global basis." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers
events.summary: Researchers say two characters available to typosquatters and phisherfolk can trick Chromium browsers into displaying lookalike URLs as genuine web addresses. Wangling a domain name to look an awful lot like that of a popular website is nothing new. We’ve all encountered phishing sites such as macrosoft[.]com and applle[.]com before in our daily struggles against spam. However, as browsers mature, new characters are always being made available for use. This opens up new opportunities for those whose languages contain characters/homoglyphs that aren’t ASCII-compliant, but it also introduces new ways for attackers to abuse display logic quirks in programs like Chrome and Edge. According to Ian Muscat and Leanne Briffa of Have I Been Squatted, there are still characters available to cyber-imposters that can reliably fool web users into trusting URLs that they certainly should not. The latest glyphs bypassing browser safety checks allow tricksters to run websites from a clearly fake domain name (when displayed in Punycode), although they appear just like the real deal in Unicode. The characters of note, in this case, are ө, which is found in various Cyrillic languages such as Kazakh, Mongolian, and Tatar, and the Latin K with hook, ƙ, used in Hausa and Karai-karai. Both are visually similar to the letters e/o, i, and k, respectively, and allowed the researchers to register 20 lookalike domain names. These included: aррӏө[.]com sрасөх[.]com oƙta[.]com niƙe[.]com Below are the URLs’ Punycode equivalents – how browsers should display them safely: xn--80a6aa68c8d.com xn--80a5aeq0fr0c.com xn--ota-f6a.com xn--nie-g6a.com You can try them out; they’re registered by Have I Been Squatted and are safe to visit. They take you to research demo pages set up by the researchers, and each page explains how exactly they bypass browser protections. Crucially, they all bypass the key security measures deployed by Chromium-based browsers. How the bypasses work Browsers deploy two main defense layers. The first is a set of seven sequential checks run by Chromium’s SafeToDisplayAsUnicode function, which check for a range of common spoofing methods. Vendors began introducing these checks in 2017 after researcher Xudong Zheng registered аррӏе.com – a domain consisting of all-Cyrillic characters. Chromium’s checks, which factor in a hardcoded list of known Cyrillic characters known to be used in place of Latin letters, can be seen as "all or nothing." Built to detect all-Cyrillic strings, the measure only takes action against domain names if every character in the string is on its hardcoded list. If one character is missing, the check is bypassed. Characters such as ө, ї, and ү, are known as “breakers,” as these are not present in the lookalike list, as of Chrome 154 (released to stable channel on September 22). Failing any of the seven display checks tells the browser that the characters are unsafe to display as Unicode and to instead display the Punycode, revealing just how dissimilar they are to the genuine domains they try to imitate. The second measure browsers take is to compare the domain name against a list of popular websites to see if it is trying to imitate one of them. In Chromium, these checks are handled by the GetSimilarTopDomain() function. This step converts a supplied domain name into a "skeleton," stripping its characters of diacritics, such as accents (ó becomes o), and checking the skeleton URL against a hardcoded list of popular websites. Chromium checks against almost 8,500, and if the skeleton matches any of them, then it displays Punycode. However, the Latin K with hook, ƙ, does not have an accent, and is added to the skeleton as a Latin k with an added combining mark, bypassing the security check. In this case, the skeleton is formed as: [o k ‘ t a . c o r n]. (The skeleton maps "m" to "rn"). Likewise, with аррӏө.com, the Cyrillic barred o retains its bar in the skeleton as a combining mark, meaning it does not match the genuine Apple domain. Its skeleton is formed as: [a p p l o - . c o r n]. Browsers are always working to stymie these tools of imposterment. Chrome 148 put an end to attackers being able to use ҏ and ӿ as breakers to imitate their Latin lookalikes, for example. The two main security checks are not the only lines of defense. Chromium also deploys warnings at the time of navigation called Safety Tips. An example domain that would bypass the two main checks is ínstagarm[.]com. The inflection on the beginning character is removed and what’s left is essentially the real Instagram domain with two letters swapped. The Instagarm domain does not match any of the hardcoded sites, nor does it contain any banned characters. In this case, Chrome will display one of two popups, asking the user if they meant to visit the genuine domain, warning that the current direction of travel appears fake. However, there are limits to this extra security layer. The warnings only trigger when an imitation domain is an exact-character match, a one-edit match, or a match with an adjacent swap from the genuine URL. Two or more changes, like with аррӏө[.]com, which has all-Cyrillic characters preceding the ".com," will not trigger these warnings. The warnings will also not trigger with domains consisting of fewer than five characters. Domains such as oƙta.com, which is only one edit from the real Okta, may not trigger defenses because of the one-edit rule and the fact that it is only four characters. Safety Tips also checks the skeleton against the sites users visit regularly, not just the hardcoded list of trusted sites. Frequently visited sites may trigger the same warnings, but for users who do not have a comprehensive visit history, the defense layer may fail. The defenses described here only apply to browsers. Email clients are even less picky with imitation domain strings. Websites like Gmail displayed each of the 20 domains HIBS fed the clients, which were a mix of lookalikes and genuine internationalized domain names (IDNs), as an attacker would want it to, all in Unicode. Outlook Web showed all 20 as Punycode, even the harmless ones, suggesting neither apply the right checks to properly inform users. To quantify the scale of the issue, the researchers looked at ICANN’s list of every .com domain. There are around 167 million of them, approximately 733,000 of which are IDNs, those that contain non-ASCII characters and are stored in Punycode form. The researchers took each of the IDNs and swapped their non-ASCII characters for ASCII equivalents to determine how many matches there were. They found around 162,000 pairs – IDNs that resemble plain ASCII domains. It should be said that this does not mean there are circa 162,000 typosquatted domains, just that many yield lookalikes. Some may be registered by businesses for defensive purposes; others may be owned by the same business that wants to operate multiple websites catering to different languages. events.title: Gen Alpha founders are already pitching VCs. Here's what investors want them to know.
events.summary: Venture capitalists Claire Zau, Jake Jolis, and Sarah Catanzaro gave their advice for Gen Alpha. Lightspeed; Zeno; Amplify Five venture capitalists told Business Insider their tips for Gen Alpha founders. Some older members of Gen Alpha, who are up to age 16, are already pitching to VCs. The VCs discussed AI, social media, and college. There's a new generation of founders on the rise — and they're not old enough to vote. Generation Alpha was born between 2010 and 2024, making the oldest members 16 years old. That's the age Stripe's John Collison cofounded his first company, and when Mike Kittredge set the stage for Yankee Candle. Let's face it: Gen Alpha founders are coming in hot. Many VCs have already been pitched by them; others will be soon. "What I've noticed about Gen Alpha is they seem to have a ton of hustle," said Sarah Catanzaro, a general partner at Amplify. "They tend to have an advantage in markets where execution may be more important than experience." Business Insider asked five venture capitalists to share their advice for Gen Alpha entrepreneurs. They spoke about AI, social media — and that pesky college question. The ChatGPT generation When ChatGPT premiered in 2022, the oldest of Gen Alpha were 12. Gen Alpha has had AI tools since middle school, if not earlier. They've used AI to write their essays and cheat on tests. They've also used it to build new products. Catanzaro thinks critical thinking could take a hit. She's seen it in Gen Z already: they grew up with the internet and could look up answers to their problems rather than thinking them through. "I worry a little bit about that type of cognitive offloading for Gen Alpha," she said. It's too early to know exactly how, or even if, AI will change our thinking patterns. Researchers told Business Insider they observed alarming patterns while studying how humans solve math equations and write essays. On the other hand, Catanzaro said Gen Alpha might be able to wield AI more effectively, precisely because they grew up with it. Zeno partner Jake Jolis agrees: the barriers to entry have never been lower, and Gen Alpha will know how to climb them. "You don't have to raise a trillion dollars to build your own superintelligence," Jolis said. "You can rent it for 20 bucks a month." To college or not to college Before his VC days, Jolis dropped out of Stanford to found his first company. He knows young founders are itching to drop out of college or forgo it altogether. Jolis had built his product while at Stanford and left to pursue it full-time. This, he said, was a good reason for Gen Alpha to skip higher education: if they have a clear plan and some customers. Beyond those specific cases, Jolis said college grads will be happier in the long run. "I would encourage people to think of their life as a whole, more than just this particular startup," he said. There's an anti-college movement ripping through Silicon Valley these days. Palantir has a fellowship for high schoolers; Andreessen Horowitz backed a college alternative . Mo Shaikh, the cofounder of Maximum Frequency Ventures, heard pitches from some Gen Alpha founders at the Alpha School , an AI-focused network of institutions. He came away impressed: "Some of these kids have six-figure businesses already." Still, Shaikh sees value in the college degree, especially from a place like Stanford. College is for "cross-pollination," he said: founders see other worldviews and can then understand them in their customers. Be online — but don't fall for the clout trap How should a 16-year-old get their startup off the ground? Shaikh said get online. Platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and Snapchat are where founders are "looking for signals," Shaikh said. Gen Alpha has grown up with these platforms. It's the generation of brain rot . Kristina Simmons, the founder of Overwater Ventures, has watched the rise of the influencer-turned-founder. She's interested in it: these founders might have insight into their audience that others don't, Simmons said. Still, Simmons had a word of caution. "It's not just having followers," she said. "They'll come." For Claire Zau, a partner at Lightspeed, becoming famous on social media can be a "trap" for Gen Alpha founders. These 15-year-olds look for social media clout, she said, and sometimes disregard the nuts and bolts of building. Zau knows that Gen Alpha grew up on smash successes like MrBeast and Alix Earle . They can help a young founder, she said — but not in the way you might expect. "The lesson there is not necessarily the 'get famous' part," Zau said. "It's that there's so much importance in obsessing over product." Read the original article on Business Insider
