Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: Vendor roadmaps set the pace of change in most enterprise software estates. Origina argues the business should. Most enterprise software estates run to somebody else’s calendar. End-of-support dates, license model changes and needless upgrades arrive on the vendor’s schedule, and the IT team absorbs them: the migration nobody budgeted for, the re-platforming that displaces a project the business actually asked for, the patch cadence that is really a product roadmap in disguise. Origina, an independent provider of software maintenance and support, puts figures on the pressure. As a rule of thumb, up to 90 percent of IT budgets go on “keeping the lights on”, leaving only 10 percent for anything new. Enterprise software costs, it says, are on course to rise 40 percent by 2027, and most of that increase is driven by vendors rather than by customers. The alternative it argues for is not standing still. It is to decide, on the business’ terms, what changes and when. A system that is stable, compliant and doing its job does not need upgrading because of a vendor-driven deadline. It needs to be supported, secured and kept in step with the business until the business has a reason to move. That reason might be a merger, a new operating model or a real step change in capability. It should not be a support deadline. That is the case for building flexibility into long-term planning from the start, rather than buying it back later at a premium. On the estate’s biggest lines, this is how it looks. Perpetual VMware licenses stay supported for as long as they are useful, instead of moving to a subscription bundle on someone else’s timetable. SAP environments run beyond standard support windows, and modernization programs are planned properly and executed when it makes business sense. Plus, the whole estate is protected against the vulnerabilities that are actually exploited, not the tens of thousands that are merely disclosed. In 2025, 48,000-plus vulnerabilities were published, but only around one percent of these were ever used in an attack. Origina’s OPTAS service proactively identifies, prioritizes and addresses issues before they become a problem. Beyond the budget, one of the constraints most IT leaders feel first is people. The engineers who understand a long-lived SAP estate or a sprawling VMware footprint are scarce, and every unnecessary migration keeps them tied up with work the business never asked for. Independent support helps you to free up resources you can invest in innovation and growth. Control, in the end, is the ability to say not yet, and to mean it. Explore your options: find out how Origina supports VMware and SAP on your timetable, and how OPTAS protects the estate in between. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Chap who took the job left a trail of wreckage – and invaluable case studies – in his incompetent wake Techie was stung by a wasp, held overnight by Chinese police, then trapped in a 13-hour meeting 8 days ago Techie assumed boss knew what they were talking about and killed Exchange by deleting data 12 days ago Project leader thought his team understood the plan, ended up fixing their 'interpretation' of it 15 days ago Your cloud survived everything except the real world 19 days ago Techie fixed Wi-Fi dead zone with a drill 22 days ago Welcome to another installment of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed Friday column which often shares your stories of what happens when incompetent people climb the greasy pole and send their failures straight back down into the lap of tech support. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Preston," who wrote to share his story of working as a field service tech in the late 1990s. "I'd risen to the rank of senior field service engineer and was offered a position in consultancy," Preston told The Register . He turned it down because he liked working at the coal face, and the people he worked with there appreciated his skills. "As soon as I arrived at clients, someone was making me a coffee just as I liked it," Preston explained, "so I turned down the consultancy position." One of Preston's colleagues took the promotion and was soon working on projects such as reconfiguring Windows NT 4.0 and the servers it ran on to handle two CPUs, configuring backup systems, and ensuring uninterruptible power supplies (UPSes) were in place to keep things alive. Preston kept doing his own thing, but the character of his job soon changed. "Within weeks, I was getting assigned calls where upgrades had gone wrong, UPSes were failing, and backups were not working." Preston realized the chap who took the promotion was making basic mistakes on almost every job – some of them so bad that one customer refused to work with the newly minted consultant. One of the jobs that eventually landed on Preston's to-fix list saw the consultant wipe a customer database that his backup regime did not protect. At another site, he created a system that pointlessly powered down every day and botched the installation of the UPS that would have saved his bacon. Preston covered as best he could to protect his company rather than the incompetent "consultant." He eventually quit the IT services caper and became a trainer. "I used these incidents as examples of what to look out for when installing and fault finding on customer sites, and also as a lesson on why you should never rely on the person who does a job before you getting things perfectly right." events.title: Oil posts weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf coast
events.summary: Oil prices settled higher on Friday to post weekly gains as Hurricane Isaias hit the US Gulf coast, forcing oil companies to significantly taper down their operations. Crude was trading lower earlier in the session after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month. Brent , the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.42 per cent to settle at $104.72 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 0.39 per cent to close at $91.85 a barrel. From last week's close Brent, which settled more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday amid continuing tensions in the Middle East, jumped 2.41 per cent, while WTI added 0.81 per cent. “Brent crude rose ... as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD. “Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.” The US Gulf coast is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods. About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said. The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns. In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Impact on oil prices Oil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia. The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. Gold, meanwhile, ended higher on Friday on bargain hunting and as investors weigh the possibility of further interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve. The precious metal, widely regarded as a safe-haven asset, added 1.52 per cent to a one-week high of $4,194.40 an ounce. Silver jumped 2.82 per cent to $60.82 an ounce.

events.title: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
events.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings. The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests. Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn). One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not to take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said. Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta. It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region. The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street. Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC. Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment. The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear. A humming annoyance or jobs boom? Life next to 199 data centres Published 26 October 2025 AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost? Published 3 September UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO. "We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors. He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans. "It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC. This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research. Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said. "It's more like a bet on a dream", he added. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment , thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability. Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment OpenAI boss Sam Altman said earlier this year that Australia could become a world leader in the data centre industry if it wanted to. There are currently over 160 data centres in the country and plans for more. That is despite resistance from some Australians who have raised concerns about their environmental impact and the noise they create . In September, Altman said OpenAI did not aim to list on the stock market this year, citing concerns over the technology's safety that make it "an ill-advised moment" to go public. The ChatGPT-maker, along with rival Anthropic, have been eyeing blockbuster stock market debuts that would value the firms at more than $1tn each. AI-related stocks, Nvidia and Oracle, fell in US trading on Thursday after reports that OpenAI's revenues were lower than previously thought. events.title: Sale rescues landmark WA dairy brands from collapse
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mundella yoghurt returns to shelves as deal revives collapsed WA dairy brands Mundella yoghurt was established in Western Australia in 1974. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Emerging processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets of collapsed Mundella Foods and Margaret River Dairy Company. The companies were put into liquidation in August, leaving creditors owed millions of dollars. Yoghurt production is expected to start near Margaret River before the Christmas period. A late rescue deal and sale is set to keep two landmark West Australian dairy brands on supermarket shelves. Mundella Foods and the Margaret River Dairy Company went into liquidation in August, with creditors owed millions of dollars. Local processor Artisanal Market has bought the brands and assets, including processing facilities in Perth and Margaret River, for an undisclosed sum. Mundella Foods' operations near Mundigjong will not be used for processing by the new owners. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) Artisanal Market managing director Kevin Sorgiovanni founded another well-known WA dairy and juice brand, Harvey Fresh. He said he had been interested in buying the companies back in 2023, when they were sold by Chinese-owned Manassen Foods to The Cheeky Cow, which has since collapsed. "We saw the Mundella and Margaret River business as a great opportunity for the South West and also to add some value back to the WA dairy market." Mr Sorgiovanni said both brands of yoghurt would be manufactured at the export-approved Metricup processing facility near Margaret River. Artisanal Markets will mothball Mundella's original manufacturing facility at Mundijong, near Perth, because of its poor condition. Artisanal Markets is jointly owned by PenAgri Group and Research Corporation. Mr Sorgiovanni told the ABC the new ownership had plans to target the Asian market for broader sales. There are hopes to export Mundella yoghurt to Asia. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) "We want to do more than just the WA market," he said. Mr Sorgiovanni said production at the Metricup facility would start at 2 million litres a year, but it had the capacity for 10 million litres. The revival is welcome news for dairy farmers across southern WA, but challenges remain. WA Farmers Dairy Council president Ian Noakes said he was keen to see how Artisanal Market would secure milk supply. Ian Noakes has welcomed the sale. ( ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia ) "Most of the milk in WA is contracted, and the main companies are not very good at letting a bit of milk go to somebody else," he said. "So it would be a matter of waiting probably until somebody comes out of contract to get a milk supply." Mr Noakes hoped the additional competition would improve the price points for local dairy farmers. events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Top of the Week TSMC and GF inked a $2B manufacturing agreement , under which GF will manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS advanced-packaging ecosystem at its Malta, New York fab. Volume production is expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. Applied Materials and Intel are expanding their R&D collaboration to develop next-gen transistors, interconnects, and advanced packaging technologies, combining work at Applied’s EPIC Center in Silicon Valley with Intel’s R&D operations in Hillsboro, Oregon. Rapidus launched Rapidus CORE , a global ecosystem framework intended to support customers from chip design through manufacturing for its planned 2nm foundry business. The first phase includes 17 design-service partners. Xanadu and GF formed a multi-year manufacturing partnership to move ultra-low-loss silicon nitride photonics and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors onto GF’s 300mm production line in Malta, New York. Big hauls Wolfspeed received a conditional commitment for up to $1.5B in 30-year U.S. government financing to expand domestic SiC materials and wide-bandgap power-device production. Vinci raised $250M in Series B funding at a $1.5B valuation to expand its AI-powered physics simulation platform . The platform models thermal, thermo-mechanical, and fluid behavior during design, with simulations reportedly running in minutes rather than hours or days. Oratomic raised $475M for its neutral-atom quantum computing hardware. VEIR raised $110M for superconducting power delivery technology for AI data centers. Atomic Machines launched with $250M for its Matter Compiler system that builds micro-machines from code , including an electromechanical micro-relay to cut power in 800VDC data centers during a fault. Financials TSMC (Sept. revenue) and Samsung (Q3 guidance). Analysis Global semiconductor sales reached $159.7B in August, up 8% from July, with year-to-date sales topping $1T , reports SIA/WSTS . McKinsey expects inference to account for about 60% of AI compute by 2030, driving demand for custom accelerators, HBM, chiplets, advanced packaging, and silicon photonics. Silicon photonics, CPO, and optical networking are emerging as the next U.S.–China semiconductor battleground as AI data centers outgrow electrical interconnects, says Wilson Center , which estimates China accounts for 56% of global optical-transceiver manufacturing capacity. Brookings estimates the U.S. AI buildout could require $10.3T through 2032 for data centers, power, networking and specialized chips, but it warned that increasingly complex financing could obscure financial risks. Lithography ASML and Carl Zeiss researchers outlined a hyper-NA EUV lithography architecture with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75, potentially enabling features as small as 5nm, more than one-third smaller than current high-NA systems. The technology could be ready in about a decade, although commercial production remains uncommitted. Canon says its nanoimprint lithography technology is entering the final stage toward full-scale mass production. DUV immersion lithography is the strongest remaining chokepoint on China’s AI-chip production, contends think tank Center for Technology & Statecraft . It estimates Chinese-owned fabs had accumulated more than 330 DUVi systems by 1Q26 and says continued imports could significantly narrow the U.S.-allied AI-chip manufacturing advantage. The report calls for a China-wide ban on DUVi exports, servicing restrictions and tighter controls on critical components. Memory Samsung is reportedly planning ~$3.9B in investment in memory-chip testing facilities in Vietnam . Netlist and Micron entered into patent license and settlement agreements covering Netlist’s portfolio for server DIMMs and high-bandwidth memory, ending all pending legal proceedings between the companies. Micron faces a potential walkout at its Taiwan facilities after workers voted overwhelmingly to authorize a strike over profit sharing. Toshiba plans to invest approximately $380M to double HDD production capacity for AI data centers by fiscal 2027, compared with 2025 levels, reports Nikkei Asia. Security and export controls Arteris won an additional $3.3M through the U.S. government’s Trusted and Assured Microelectronics initiative to expand its third-party IP (3PIP) security assurance program in collaboration with BAE and SiFive . The U.S. DOJ charged the owner of California-based Earthmade Computer with allegedly smuggling more than $300M in export-controlled computer servers to China . Prosecutors allege the servers contained high-end U.S.-manufactured GPUs and were routed through Malaysia and Singapore using false end-user and destination information to evade U.S. export controls. Meanwhile, CSET researchers modeled more than 10 million scenarios for detecting diverted AI chips and found ping-based location verification to be the most cost-effective approach. However, they cautioned that implementation costs and complexity could limit its usefulness, and said that combining PLV with targeted physical inspections could improve enforcement. Recognition Silvaco CEO Wally Rhines was inducted into the National Academy of Engineering for his co-invention of the blue-light-emitting diode and decades of leadership in the semiconductor/EDA industry. AMD is working with 14 South Korean AI semiconductor and technology companies to develop heterogeneous computing systems that combine AMD CPUs and GPUs with Korean AI processors, reports SBS News. events.title: Audit firm fined $100,000 by Abu Dhabi's ADGM regulator
events.summary: The Registration Authority of ADGM has imposed fines totalling $100,000 on an audit firm at Abu Dhabi's financial centre over regulatory failings. The action was taken against PKF Accountants and Business Advisers, an ADGM-registered audit firm, and its registered audit principal, Saranga Lalwani, the authority said in a statement on Friday. It has imposed a fine of $65,000 on PKF and $35,000 on Ms Lalwani. The decision was taken after an on-site inspection conducted by the authority to assess PKF’s compliance with ADGM's auditor rules and the quality of its audit work, the statement added. During the inspection, the authority said it identified "significant deficiencies" in an audit conducted for an ADGM-registered entity by PKF and Ms Lalwani. The deficiencies included "failures to conduct the audit and prepare the audit report in accordance with International Standards on Auditing (ISA) as required by the Companies Regulations (Auditors) Rules 2023 and failure to exercise due skill, care and diligence in carrying out the audit", the authority said. The inspection identified that PKF "rebutted the risk of fraud in management override of controls, which is a mandatory fraud risk and cannot be rebutted under ISAs". The firm was also accused of failing to assess fraud risks, failing to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence, inadequate audit documentation, and insufficient evidence demonstrating the audit principal's involvement in the audit process. "Registered auditors and registered audit principals are expected to conduct audits in accordance with applicable professional standards and exercise appropriate skill, care and diligence," the authority said in the statement. "This action reinforces the importance of robust audit practices and demonstrates that failures to meet regulatory requirements will result in appropriate enforcement action." Authorities in the UAE have cracked down on entities that breach regulations as part of efforts to maintain the financial system's integrity and reliability. The Dubai Financial Services Authority this month imposed a Dh401,000 ($109,200) fine on wealth management firm Vault Wealth for conducting transactions without authorisation.

events.title: Frasers Hospitality CEO to step down; COO to lead company and report to Frasers Property
events.summary: Fraser Suites Singapore along River Valley Road, one of the company’s assets. Frasers Hospitality CEO Eu Chin Fen will step down on Jan 1, 2027, after key milestones, including the 2025 privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust and the 2026 portfolio optimisation. Chew Hang Song will lead the lodging business as COO, reporting to Frasers Property group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi, with a focus on global brand growth and third-party management deals. Eric Gan will head hospitality investment and asset management under group investment, supporting an asset-light strategy and stronger capital partnerships across hospitality and living assets. SINGAPORE – Eu Chin Fen will step down as chief executive officer of Frasers Hospitality, effective on Jan 1, 2027, Frasers Property said in a statement on the morning of Oct 9. Chew Hang Song will lead Frasers Hospitality as its chief operating officer, reporting to Frasers Property’s group CEO, Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi. This follows the achievement of strategic milestones: the privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust in 2025 and the completion of its portfolio optimisation in September 2026. Eu, 55, has decided to pursue personal interests, with the hospitality platform now well-positioned for its next state of growth, Frasers Property said. It added: “To sharpen operational focus and support efforts to enhance real estate portfolio value, Frasers Hospitality’s leadership structure will be strategically segmented, aligning with group resources, and reporting into senior group leadership.” Chew’s role will involve driving global brand stewardship for the lodging business, expanding the portfolio through third-party management agreements and overseeing operations at its properties worldwide. Meanwhile, Frasers Hospitality’s current chief financial officer, Eric Gan, will lead hospitality investment and asset management under group investment. He will report to group COO Tony Lombardo. As managing director of group investment, Gan’s focus will be on investment strategies and asset portfolio management across hospitality and the wider living sector. Sirivadhanabhakdi said that the move to house hospitality investment and asset management within group investment aligns with its asset-light strategy for the sector, “connecting (its) real estate platform to institutional capital and enabling (it) to grow (its) capital partnerships more dynamically”. Empowering the lodging business under Chew, meanwhile, allows the team to scale the brand globally through management contracts, he added. Sirivadhanabhakdi said: “(Eu) has helped build a resilient global brand, established trusted partnerships and nurtured a strong hospitality executive team. Our evolved structure builds on that foundation by giving each part of the business clearer focus and optimised resources.” Eu joined the group in 2011. She worked closely with group leadership on the $2.1 billion Frasers Hospitality Trust portfolio optimisation. The stapled group was taken private in October 2025 via a trust scheme of arrangement. Frasers Property closed at 94 cents, down 1.05%, on Oct 9. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Competition authority seeks public views on Eneos Apac’s proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore
events.summary: Chevron Singapore operates under the Caltex brand for retail petrol and diesel. CCS is seeking public feedback on Eneos Apac’s proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore, and will decide if the deal breaches section 54 of the Competition Act 2004. Chevron Singapore runs fuel retail, storage, terminal and lubricant businesses in Singapore and Vietnam, and would keep the Chevron and Caltex brands if the deal goes ahead. Eneos says the takeover should not harm competition because there are many rivals, low entry barriers, and customers can easily switch suppliers; public submissions close at 5 pm on Oct 16. SINGAPORE – The Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCS) is inviting public feedback on the proposed acquisition of Chevron Singapore – a distributor of petroleum products – by Eneos Apac, a subsidiary of energy, resources and materials group Eneos. The authority on Oct 2 accepted the companies’ application for a decision on whether the proposed transaction would infringe Section 54 of the Competition Act 2004. Chevron Singapore is a subsidiary of Chevron South Asia, which is indirectly wholly owned by Chevron Corp. It is primarily a downstream petroleum company with operations in Singapore and Vietnam. In Singapore, Chevron Singapore engages in the retail distribution of fuels and lubricants. It holds an equity interest in Singapore Refining Company, a 50:50 joint venture with Singapore Petroleum Company. Chevron Singapore’s activities also include fuel storage and terminal operations, and lubricant blending and wholesale. The company operates under the Chevron brand in the Republic. Caltex, for retail petrol and diesel; Delo, for commercial and industrial lubricants; Havoline for passenger vehicle lubricants; Star Mart, for convenience retail offerings at service stations; Texaco, a legacy brand in fuels and lubricants; and Techron and Techron D, for fuel additives. Meanwhile, Eneos is a Japan-based energy, resources and materials group with global operations. In Singapore, it is active in the trading of crude oil, naphtha and refined petroleum products, lubricants blending and wholesale, the supply of marine fuels and solar energy solutions. The company mainly operates under the Eneos brand. If the proposed acquisition were to be completed, Chevron Singapore would continue to operate under the Chevron and Caltex brands. Eneos would “step into Chevron’s current operations in Singapore”, CCS added. Chevron Singapore would continue to source Chevron-branded products and raw materials mostly from Chevron Corp. Eneos Apac believes that it overlaps with Chevron Singapore in the market only for lubricant blending and wholesale supply in the city-state. The proposed transaction will not raise any material competitive concerns, “given the significant number of existing competitors, relatively low barriers to entry and expansion, and ability of customers to multi-source and switch among credible alternative lubricant suppliers in Singapore at minimal cost”. Eneos Apac also submitted that no material vertical effects are anticipated. Chevron Singapore faces significant competitive constraints in its active markets, such as fuel refining, storage and terminal services, retail distribution of fuels and lubricants, it said, while Eneos has a limited market presence in lubricant blending and wholesale in Singapore. CCS invites views from the public on the impact of this proposed acquisition on competition. Submissions – via its online form or through e-mail – will close at 5 pm on Oct 16. events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Octocats claim 35x write improvement There can be only one: Google Cloud casts Gemini as your enterprise AI hero 1 day ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 2 days ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 3 days ago OpenAI tries disarming AI angst with cute graphics and always-on agents 10 days ago AI models keep posting screenshots showing sensitive data from inside tech companies 11 days ago Responding to unprecedented demand from AI agents, GitHub is rebuilding its Git storage architecture from scratch. Early tests with the new architecture show a promising 35x write improvement in internal tests. GitHub will need a miracle of that proportion just to keep up with customer demand. The plan involves decoupling writes from reads, offloading maintenance, and letting object storage manage redundancy. Most impressive is that the redesign is happening under the hood, with the goal of a non-disruptive change that won't alter developer workflows, review processes, or security controls. Running an enterprise-grade code repository means supporting “large engineering teams running busy CI pipelines alongside growing fleets of agents. Supporting these teams means building Git infrastructure for sustained, concurrent reads and writes at a scale few repositories reach today,” wrote Brian Celenza , GitHub principal software engineer, in a blog post describing the updates. Celenza did not offer a timeline for this ambitious migration. When GitHub’s customers shifted their coding focus to AI agents, activity on the platform spiked significantly. Between September 2025 and August 2026, GitHub traffic doubled, from 218.2 billion events per month to 473.3 billion. In September alone, commits hit 7.38 billion, a 5x increase from September 2025. This shift in traffic is stressing the system. According to the GitHub Availability Report , the service suffered 10 incidents in April alone that degraded performance. Another nine incidents landed in May, with each generating more bad publicity than the previous one. GitHub's current storage architecture, nicknamed Spokes , uses a three-phase commit protocol, storing full repo copies across multiple local disks and requiring a quorum of replicas to acknowledge each write. While this approach ensures strong reliability, it bottlenecks write speed, as every push is bounded by the slowest replica required for quorum. The new architecture writes a commit only once, to Azure Blob Storage , an object store service that automatically handles replication (and hence redundancy) on its own, eliminating the quorum bottleneck. GitHub also gooses performance by separating read requests into their own channel, a job handled by lightweight compute workers. The only coordination between reads and writes is over the reference branch pointers. Maintenance duties – such as compaction and garbage collection — are moved from the serving path to operate as background processes, further reducing system lag. GitHub seems to be on the same page with others in rethinking Git for the agentic age. Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke launched a Git-hosting service called Entire , which offloads agent traffic to mirror repositories, allowing a customer’s core GitHub repos to just serve the core development traffic. SpaceX subsidiary Cursor, which uses Git to back its agent-support service, also refined the storage layer for better performance. Cursor engineers also rejected Spokes’ three-phase commit in favor of uploading pushes into an object storage write-ahead log (WAL), which captured all changes as immutable objects, caching at least one copy on super-speedy solid-state disks. While it's cathartic to hate on a service that often goes down, you have to feel empathy for the GitHub engineers who, when they created the service, couldn’t have guessed what they signed up for.

events.title: JD Vance’s comments about immigrants 'unwarranted' and ‘deeply offensive’, India's Foreign Ministry says
events.summary: India's Ministry of External Affairs on Friday called comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Indian immigrants "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive". A day earlier, Mr Vance announced that Microsoft and some of India ’s biggest IT services were suspended from a programme allowing workers on H-1B visas to apply for green cards. He accused the companies of abusing the system, comparing foreign workers to “indentured servants”. "The history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," the ministry said in a statement. It added that Mr Vance's comments were "unwarranted" and ignore the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy. Roughly 70 per cent of the H-1B visas approved in 2025 went to people from India. "Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said, appearing to refer to Mr Vance's use of the term "indentured servants", which carries a heavy historical burden for Indians. During the colonial period in India, more than 1.6 million people were transported as indentured servants to serve on British, French and Dutch plantations around the world following the abolition of slavery. Many workers, who typically signed five-year contracts for unpaid labour, were tricked or coerced into service. The indenture system is also a painful feature of American history. During the American colonial period, poor workers and convicts were bound to an employer for up to seven years, receiving no wages for their labour, in return for food, shelter and transport to the colonies. Similar to the Indian system, abuse was rampant. "When I say indentured servants, here's what I mean: When somebody comes in on an H-1B, they are completely subordinate to that company," Mr Vance said at the Department of Labour on Thursday. "If they lose that job, they have to leave the country." The Vice President accused Microsoft, Adobe and six other companies of fraudulently utilising the H-1B visa programme, which he said is meant to allow firms to bring in "the best of the best" from outside the US to fill jobs that are impossible to fill with American workers. This "pernicious system" is a "fundamental insult to the American way of life", he said, as it lets companies lower wages and block Americans from jobs, while also allowing for the abuse of foreign workers. As a result of the alleged fraudulent use of the system, the companies have been removed from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, which allows firms to hire foreign workers permanently and offers the workers the chance to apply for green cards. The tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecoms companies have come to rely heavily on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies, which have developed a lucrative business in recruiting professionals from abroad for US clients. In the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, Microsoft was the fifth-highest user of H-1B visas, with 3,688, according to Bloomberg. In a statement, Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work”, that its wages are among the highest of all visa filings and that the vast majority of its employees in the US are Americans. Mr Vance’s comments came hours before US President Donald Trump gave Microsoft chief executive, Satya Nadella , the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. And last week, Mr Nadella, alongside other tech industry leaders, visited the White House for a discussion on safeguards for AI. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company," Mr Vance said. "It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.” Washington has been engaged in an across-the-board immigration crackdown since Mr Trump returned to office last year. The State Department said earlier this month that more than 250,000 visas have been revoked under the Trump administration. Along with companies with high issuance of H-1B visas, Mr Vance also took aim at universities he said had engaged in J-1 visa fraud. He accused nine institutions, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford universities, of bringing "in foreigners to undercut the wages" of American researchers and graduate students. J-1 visas are granted to people approved to participate in work and study programmes in the US. "They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," he said.

events.title: Contribution of high value residents discussed
events.summary: Mary O'Keeffe was one of several business people who said high value residents contribute positively to the island's economy More than 260 industry leaders from business, finance and law have held a meeting to discuss the role high value residents play in Jersey's economy. Jersey's high value residency programme , external grants residential status to highly skilled and economically active high net worth individuals. One attendee at the Chamber of Commerce lunch on Thursday, Mary O'Keeffe, said high value residents "were extremely important" to the island. However, one former economic advisor to the government described the tax contribution of high value residents as "piffling". About 260 families currently live in Jersey having relocated through the scheme. O'Keeffe who runs Mary O'Keeffe relocation , external to help high value residents settle in the island said they contributed a lot to the economy and philanthropic causes. "They are extremely important, so here today the room is full of private bankers, tax accountants, lawyers, people like myself and professionals who all work with high net individuals. "So, they bring an enormous amount to the economy and that doesn't even touch on what they bring in regard to philanthropy." High value residents pay a 20% tax rate on the first £1.25m of worldwide income , external . They then pay a 1% on any income above £1.25m and there are some who feel these individuals should be paying more tax , external . O'Keeffe said: "I can understand that but that's not looking at the argument the right way. "First of all, the basic pay that they pay is £250,000 and that's before you even look at their worldwide income. "And the 1% often equates to many millions and that's what people don't understand. "High net worth individuals are extremely mobile, they are fluid, they can pick up and go wherever they want and they want to go somewhere that's safe, that's secure, that their wealth is going to be looked after and they're not going to feel that they're going to be ripped off." Industry leaders from law, finance, business and real estate met at a Chamber of Commerce lunch to discuss the role of high value residents in Jersey Garry Bell, a tax advisor to high value residents, said if tax for wealthy individuals was increased he believed Jersey would lose them. He said if the money they made above £1.25m was taxed at 20% instead of 1% it could damage the economy. Former economic advisor to the government of Jersey John Christensen said the amount of tax paid by high value residents was "piffling" "If we tax those individuals at 20% the numbers would reduce dramatically. So instead of having a net increase of say 18 or19 individuals a year you're probably only looking at one or two," Bell said. "So, we're sacrificing by seeking to tax them more, we're sacrificing that the direct income tax take, the stamp duty take, the employment, the GST, there's a whole raft of economic benefits that we sacrifice by actually seeking to tax those individuals at 20%. "We are competing with a number of other jurisdictions, Dubai - zero tax. Monaco - zero tax. "We're already one of the most expensive jurisdictions." John Christensen, a former economic advisor to Jersey's government in the 1980s and 1990s was critical of the High Value Residents programme. He said the amount of tax they pay is "piffling, frankly". "I think it's quite divisive, particularly in such an unequal island community. "As a development strategy, who benefits? They benefit because they're paying very little tax on their income but is it going to benefit young Jersey people? Not at all. "I suspect its going to contribute more to ratcheting up of house prices, ratcheting up of prices in the shops, and a higher cost of living generally. "And where they contribute to the island's economy, outside paying frankly minimal amounts of tax, lies with construction work. "They've built endless, frankly, rather ugly and inappropriately sized houses." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: 'You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world'
events.summary: Longbow's co-founders and CEOs Daniel Davey (left) and Mark Tapscott show Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds (left in car) and mayor Richard Parker the Speedster A British carmaker has unveiled plans to start production of its hand-built electric sports car in Warwickshire. Longbow is to start production of its limited-edition Speedster at Mira Tech Park in Nuneaton next year. West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, who backed Longbow with £3m from a government fund, said the project will be followed by the firm's Roadster model, creating more than 200 skilled jobs. Daniel Davey, Longbow's co-chief executive officer, said the region was the best place to build the cars. "It's not just the supply chain; you've got the talent here and the know-how," he said. Davey said: "You cannot build this car anywhere else in the world. And if you did, you would be importing UK components to it. "So you can get heavy components elsewhere, and you can get high-volume components elsewhere; what we're looking for is low-volume, high-quality, low-cost, low-weight." The Speedster has a waiting list of prospective buyers from across the world, waiting to spend around £85,000 on the sports car. At the test track at Mira, the all-British creation silently demonstrated how a lightweight sports car can go from an idea to a vehicle in less than two years, helped by regional expertise. Longbow said the UK was good at building lightweight sports cars. "Our designers are just up the road in Leamington Spa, engineers from across the West Midlands and further afield," Davey added. People around the world are waiting to buy the limited edition car for around £85,000 The project was backed by £3m from the government's £50m West Midlands Supplier Readiness and Transformation fund , external , which aims to accelerate the UK's transition to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the £3m was to strengthen the supply chain and the industry. West Midlands Combined Authority said the money would be match-funded by Longbow, which plans to manufacture more than 10,000 cars a year. Parker said: "We've been building cars here in West Midlands for 130 years, so what better location for a new generation of carmakers like Longbow. "They know this industry inside out and are investing here because this is quite simply the best place in the UK to build a car." Car industry expert Professor David Bailey said: "They're trying to do what Tesla first did many years ago with a sort of lightweight, fast electric sports car. "So I think it's great; it shows we have great research and development skills. We can probably compete, I think, in terms of low-volume, high-margin cars, but more broadly we need to be doing a lot more to support the auto industry in the region and enable it to continue growing." events.title: OpenAI’s Singapore-based APAC policy head leaving job after 6 months, source says
events.summary: The start-up had apologised earlier in October for its artificial intelligence models’ breach of Australian government websites. OpenAI’s Singapore-based APAC policy head, Sanghyun Lee, is leaving after six months, according to a source, as the company faces tighter scrutiny from regulators in the region. Lee led public policy and government engagement across Australia, Japan, Korea, India and Southeast Asia, building ties with policymakers to support responsible AI use. OpenAI has apologised for AI models breaching Australian government websites, while also expanding in Asia-Pacific and seeking major new funding, Bloomberg reported. SINGAPORE – OpenAI’s most senior Asia-Pacific public policy executive is departing after six months in the role, according to a person familiar with the matter, just as the ChatGPT maker faces scrutiny from regulators in the region . The executive, Sanghyun Lee, is based in Singapore and joined OpenAI in April after six years at Google, according to his LinkedIn profile. The reasons for his exit were not immediately clear. The person familiar asked not to be identified discussing a private matter. OpenAI declined to comment. Lee did not respond to requests for comment. The San Francisco-based start-up apologised in October for its artificial intelligence models that recently breached Australian government websites , pledging to work to prevent similar incidents and to respond faster if they do occur. In his role, Lee has led OpenAI’s public policy and government engagement across Australia, Japan, Korea, India and South-east Asia, according to his profile. He builds and manages “relationships with senior policymakers, regulators and institutions to support the responsible development and adoption of AI”, the profile says. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission is scrutinising OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI firms over the safety of their products amid high-profile cybersecurity incidents . Public policy staff typically advise companies on regulatory issues and liaise with governments. The Asia-Pacific region is key to OpenAI in part because it is home to populous, often youthful markets that support the company’s consumer growth and enterprise adoption as it competes against rivals such as Anthropic. OpenAI has in recent years opened offices in locations including India, South Korea, Japan and Australia. OpenAI is in discussions with investors to raise US$30 billion (S$38.4 billion) or more in a funding round that would value the firm at about US$1.4 trillion, Bloomberg News has reported. The company is expecting to reach or exceed US$70 billion in annualised revenue by the end of 2026 . Before joining OpenAI, Lee was Google’s global head of government affairs and public policy strategy for platforms and devices, working across markets such as the United States, European Union and several Asia-Pacific countries, according to his LinkedIn profile. events.title: Firmus wobbles have opponents relieved, critics questioning deals
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Firmus wobbles have data centre opponents relieved, critics questioning Tasmanian sports deals Firmus has abandoned its ASX float after lacklustre demand, with the news welcomed by Tasmanian opponents of its plans. ( Supplied: Firmus Technologies ) The news of data centre builder Firmus' share market float being pulled after lacklustre demand has been met with a mixed reaction. While there has been disappointment from some investors, for the opponents of Firmus' data centre plans in northern Tasmania, the response has been relief. The news of data centre operator Firmus's share market float being pulled has been met with disappointment from some investors. But in one community where Firmus had big plans, the response was relief. Firmus was attempting to raise cash from investors to fund its data centre plans until this week's development . A group based in northern Tasmania, called the Environmental Awareness Association, has been campaigning against the company's three projects in the region. Anti-data centre protesters pictured in August outside George Town Council building, ahead of the vote on whether to approve Firmus' proposed data centre. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Nicholla Thompson from the association lives at Rowella, across the Tamar River from Firmus' proposed Bell Bay site, and said community backlash had contributed to investor concerns. Nicholla Thompson believes community opposition to Firmus contributed to investor hesitancy. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) "The dominoes are starting to fall," she said. "They wanted it to sneak through and not be seen by people; it was thanks to the little group that we've got that really highlighted what was happening over here." The opponents' group was relieved by the news, but was not yet celebrating it as a win for their campaign. "A big company shouldn't be able to come in and change substantially how we choose to live in a beautiful community like this and put an AI factory up in the middle of it and have us have to endure the sound, the diesel fumes and the total destruction of our properties in value and in peace and how we live," Ms Thompson said. Firmus 'well-positioned' to continue plans, company says When asked about any impact on its Tasmanian projects, a Firmus spokesperson said nothing had "fundamentally changed" about the business. Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors. Sam Baker, from Shadforth Financial Group, said it was hard to tell if the community opposition had contributed to the IPO failing, but it would have been considered by investors. He said it would be important to watch what Firmus did over the coming weeks and months to see if it could raise the capital. "Firmus not being able to get this ASX listing off the ground has cast some doubt over the funding of their potential rollout of data centres in northern Tasmania," he said. Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said the IPO was a matter for Firmus, but the Tasmanian government had been supportive "all the way through" the company's plans in the state. "That relationship is positive and we look forward to it continuing in a collaborative, positive way," he said. Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder. The Tasmanian Greens said the state government should be embarrassed by its support of Firmus, saying investors, academics and communities had been raising concerns for months. "The big question for Tasmania is why our government was so easily pulled into uncritically supporting this company despite the furiously waving red flags surrounding it," Tabatha Badger, the Greens' information and technology spokeswoman, said. Ms Badger said the government should pause any planning decisions on Firmus's three proposals in Tasmania. Firmus was also named a sponsor for Tasmania's NBL team, the JackJumpers. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) The Tasmanian-founded company had recently announced sponsorships with the Tasmania Devils AFL club, several cricket teams, including the Hobart Hurricanes, and the JackJumpers and Tasmania Jewels basketball teams. Dr Andrew Hughes, a political marketing specialist at ANU's College of Business and Economics, said the Firmus IPO falling over was a golden opportunity for the Devils to walk away from the deal. He said he was surprised the Devils had signed with Firmus, given the club was already exposed to community backlash over the proposed AFL stadium in Hobart .

events.title: Tech stocks struggle on AI spending worries, elevated yields
events.summary: OpenAI’s reported revenue fell short of projections, damping investor sentiment. Asian stocks fell as investors worry about high energy prices, bond market turmoil and the huge cost of AI spending. Tech shares dropped after OpenAI revenue worries and plans for big fund-raising by SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle to buy AI chips. Higher yields and debt fears kept pressure on markets, with France hit hard and the dollar strong as the euro weakened. SINGAPORE - Asian stocks slipped on Oct 9 and were poised for a second straight weekly drop as investors fretted about elevated energy prices, bond market ructions and the huge sums needed to fund AI investment. Brent crude futures were at US$103.70 per barrel in Asian hours after surging more than 4% in the previous session on concerns over the war in the Middle East that has fanned inflation worries and led to higher rates across the globe. President Donald Trump said on Oct 8 that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November’s US midterm elections, although traders remained sceptical of any progress being made to end the war. Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global, said: “The big question for markets is whether Trump sticks to his word if Iranian attacks intensify. “Any indication that the White House is reconsidering military action could see oil prices spike sharply higher, particularly with tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz already under significant pressure.” In stocks, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was down 0.16%, set for an over 1% drop for the week. Markets in South Korea and Taiwan were closed for a holiday. Japan’s Nikkei fell more than 1%. Tech stocks led Wall Street’s main indexes lower overnight after a report that OpenAI’s annualised revenue was US$20 billion (S$25.6 billion) less than the company previously signalled hit sentiment. Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, said in a note: “It has been a sea of red across technology, AI infrastructure and semiconductors, with the OpenAI headlines seemingly providing the catalyst for investors to take some exposure off the table. “For now, though, the price action suggests investors are becoming more selective about where they want exposure and, importantly, what price they are prepared to pay for future growth.” Investors were also weighing a massive round of fund-raising that appears to be on the way, with SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle all expected to raise billions to buy high-end AI chips. Australia’s Firmus, a data centre operator backed by Nvidia, shelved its US$5 billion initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, and said it would opt for a private fund-raising round instead. A toxic mix of higher energy costs, expectations of central bank interest rate hikes and concerns over rising government debts have fuelled a months-long global bond sell-off, pushing borrowing costs to multi-decade highs. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, said: “With long-term yields back around multi-decade highs, investors no longer have the luxury of valuing AI growth in a low-cost-of-capital world.” Chanana said higher sovereign yields and now rising corporate issuance to fund AI infrastructure mean capital is becoming “both more expensive and more selective, which puts balance sheets and the quality of future earnings firmly in focus”. France has been hit particularly hard as investors scrutinise its debt load, budget deficit and political outlook ahead of the 2027 presidential election. “With the two rounds of the presidential elections only in April and May next year, French bond spreads are still looking at more than half a year of higher volatility and continued spread elevation,” ING analysts said in a note. US Treasury markets have been calmer as solid auctions this week helped the mood somewhat. The benchmark 10-year yield was steady at 5.226% but was not far from the 24-year high it hit on Oct 7. “It does not mean the bond market sell-off is over, but it does at least put it on pause, at least just for now,” ING analysts said. In currencies, the dollar stood tall as the euro was set for a fifth straight week in the red. It last fetched US$1.122, straddling the 17-month low it touched earlier this week on French debt worries. REUTERS

events.title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
events.summary: Adidas tendered pictures of White Fox advertisements to support their claim Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo. The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused. The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile. In the Federal Court on Friday, lawyers for White Fox denied any breach of trademark. While White Fox has not yet lodged a formal defence, its lawyers told Justice Ian Jackman that the firm intends to argue that other prominent Australian brands such as Cotton On, Sportscraft and Glassons sell clothes with "similar decorative stripes". Lawyers for Adidas told the court that White Fox, in advertising and selling its clothes with four stripes, had the "intention to trade off our reputation". A three to four-day trial is expected to take place early next year, the court heard. In its written statement of claim, Adidas says its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957. The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark. White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims. It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items. This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim. The company says White Fox is "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind". Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs. Another image filed by Adidas which shows its shoes paired with shorts of a similar style Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops. In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes. A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image. In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes. White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024. In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review. events.title: Iran war drives South-East Asia towards renewables but investment falls short
events.summary: The liquefied natural gas shock caused by the Iran war is pushing South-East Asia towards solar and wind power, but the region has lined up less than a third of the energy storage it needs by 2030, a report has found. South-East Asia's current pipeline of utility-scale storage projects of about 7GW, expected to be operational by 2030, covers less than a third of the 23 to 26GW needed to support its renewable energy targets, energy think tank Ember said in the report published on Wednesday. On its current growth rate, the region would fall even further behind by 2045, Ember said. “The financing bottleneck in Asean's [Association of South-east Asian Nations'] energy transition has shifted from raising capital to creating bankable assets,” said Alnie Demoral, an energy analyst at Ember. The findings highlight the challenge for economies trying to cut their exposure to imported fuel after the Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The waterway carried almost a fifth of global LNG before the conflict began in late February. South-East Asia sourced about a third of its gas imports from the Middle East before the war, according to the Global Energy Monitor. Asian spot LNG prices averaged $17.50 per million British thermal units in the second quarter, 45 per cent higher than a year earlier, GEM said. In the South-East Asia region, the Philippines , which declared a national energy emergency in March, gas-fired power capacity in development had fallen from 19.7GW in January to 13.8GW by August, GEM data shows. In Vietnam, Vingroup has sought to replace a planned 4.8GW LNG power plant with solar, wind and battery storage. Large solar farms are increasingly able to attract commercial financing, Ember found, but battery storage, smaller renewable installations and transmission lines remain less attractive to investors. Under the same tariff and financing assumptions, a half-megawatt solar project returns 2.6 per cent to equity, against 13.1 per cent for a 20MW plant. Investment will increasingly depend on cutting transaction costs and allowing storage and grids to earn returns that reflect their value to the power system, Ms Demoral said. Current investment falls short of the $281 billion a year the region needs by 2035 to complete its energy transition, Ember said. Electricity demand in South-East Asia is forecast to increase about 5.4 per cent a year through 2030, the International Energy Agency says. Expensive gas is also reviving coal, with the IEA expecting global coal demand to rise 1.2 per cent to a record 8.94 billion tonnes this year, as high LNG prices push utilities in Europe, Japan, South Korea and China to burn more. The financing models that supported large renewable projects have yet to extend to the storage and grids needed to integrate intermittent power, Ember said.

The changes, announced on Thursday by US vice president JD Vance and Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, mean that Microsoft and Adobe can no longer use the Program Electronic Review Management (PERM) program to convert holders of the H-1B visa for skilled workers to permanent residents. Sonderling also revoked access to PERM for Indian companies Infosys, Tata, Wipro, and HCL, plus Capgemini. The secretary said the change followed criminal investigations and alleged “fraud and abuse.” “Since 2009, just these companies alone have requested almost three million foreign workers,” he said. “They've received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. That's hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers.” Vice President Vance weighed in with what he called a “message to Microsoft.” “You’re a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.” Critics of the H-1B visa have often alleged that US companies use it to bring in foreign workers who are prepared to work for less than Americans. The theory even extends to an allegation that India’s outsourcers use H-1B visas to bring in workers whose main agenda is offshoring more work to India. Some observers suggest skilled workers have a secondary motivation of using their time in the US to seek visas for family members. Microsoft, whose CEO Satya Nadella once held an H-1B visa, and which has fired over 20,000 staff since early 2025, took issue with the administration’s decision in a strongly worded post . “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote . “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” “Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology workforce,” the company’s post continues. “We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers, and attracting the best talent from around the world.” That’s essentially the same argument used by NASSCOM, and Indian politicians such as minister of state Vardhan Singh, who last year said that “skilled talent mobility has long played a significant role in promoting technology advancement, innovation, economic growth, and wealth creation in both India and the United States.” NASSCOM, which has never found a reason to doubt that Indian tech companies are anything other than excellent corporate citizens, took to X to share its view that “immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues and should not be viewed through the same lens.” The lobby group also argued “Over a number of years, Indian technology companies have significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas, while steadily expanding local hiring and building a strong domestic workforce in the U.S.” “They work with majority of the US fortune 500 companies, enable them to innovate and grow, and generate more local jobs. Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited.” Microsoft vowed to provide the Trump administration with more information about its migration initiatives.

events.title: Hollard insurance fined $2m for handling of claim that destroyed home
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance giant Hollard fined $2 million after claim delays leave house uninhabitable The Federal Court has ordered Hollard insurance to pay $2 million. ( Supplied ) Insurance giant Hollard has been fined $2 million for taking so long to process a home insurance claim that a house in regional Victoria became uninhabitable. The corporate watchdog ASIC sued Hollard in April last year, alleging the insurer "breached its duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of a claim made by a couple in October 2021, two days after a storm damaged their roof. The Federal Court ordered Hollard to pay $2 million for failing to promptly assess the damage, delaying rectification work and for failing to properly protect the property from further damage. It was also found to have taken too long to find temporary accommodation for the couple, failed to consider expert reports, and not clearly communicate with the couple throughout the claims process. Hollard has also been ordered to pay ASIC's legal costs. In a statement to the ABC, a spokesperson for Hollard said the insurer acknowledges the Federal Court's findings initiated by ASIC. "We extend our deepest apologies and sincerely regret the impact of this experience on the customer," the spokesperson said. ASIC says delays caused unnecessary and prolonged harm Hollard is a privately owned insurance company and one of the largest in Australia, underwriting insurance for motor, home, contents, bicycle, pet, and business products. It is the company behind brands including CBA's insurance product, Everyday Insurance, Real Insurance, Australian Seniors and Steadfast. In 2024, the company had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion. Hollard initially accepted the couples' claim, before repeatedly delaying inspections, reports and repair work, only to then reject the claim in April 2023. ASIC said the rejection was based on a non-expert opinion, despite prior expert reports outlining the damage. ASIC alleged the combination of delays in decision-making, poor communication and ignoring expert advice exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm. Sarah Court says Hollard's delays mean the home in regional Victoria needs to be demolished. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Its chair Sarah Court said the outcome was the first civil penalty ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith. She said it was a warning to insurers about the devastating impact poor claim-handling and prolonged delays can have on consumers. "Hollard's serious claim handling failures left a family in limbo for years and living in a home that was uninhabitable," Ms Court said. "When Australians make an insurance claim they are often facing some of the most difficult times in their lives. "This decision confirms that insurers must act fairly, communicate clearly and make decisions without unnecessary delay, and must put their customers first." ASIC says decision sends clear message The family was initially offered $1,000 from Hollard as a goodwill payment in late 2022 to settle their claim. Once Hollard denied the claim, the couple then lodged a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), which determined the storm caused structural damage to the roof. Hollard had an estimated annual revenue of about $2.3 billion in 2024. ( Supplied ) Hollard then agreed to pay the couple a cash settlement of more than $1.5 million for the total loss of the building, as well as temporary accommodation. ASIC sued Hollard after the cash settlement. The penalty Hollard has been ordered to pay goes to the Commonwealth of Australia, to be paid within 28 days. In delivering the judgment the judge said: "The saga experienced by the insureds was extended and must have been stressful and traumatic." "They were given the run-around in more ways than one and lived in their ever-deteriorating home as the saga wore on.

events.title: Nvidia-backed Firmus shelves IPO, eyes private funding
events.summary: Firmus will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange, according to a statement on Oct 9. - Firmus Grid has withdrawn its Australian Securities Exchange IPO after market volatility made the offer unattractive, and it will now seek private funding. - The Nvidia-backed data centre firm had aimed to raise up to US$5.5 billion and a A$43.7 billion valuation, but investors worried about pricing and share overhang. - Firmus, founded in 2019, is expanding AI data centre projects in Australia, Singapore and Batam, with support from Nvidia, Blackstone and other investors. Australian data centre company Firmus Grid has shelved its initial public offering plan and will consider other funding options. The company will withdraw its application to list on the Australian Securities Exchange, according to a statement on Oct 9 . “Having considered recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions, the board determined that the terms on which the offer could proceed would not appropriately reflect the strength of the company’s business and long-term growth outlook,” it said. “Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options.” Bloomberg News earlier reported the company was set to postpone listing plans and was instead weighing a private funding round, according to people familiar with the matter. The Nvidia-backed company is in talks with existing investors and others for a private funding round, according to people familiar with the matter, asking not to be identified as the information is not public. Order-taking for the IPO closed as scheduled on the morning of Oct 8, yet there was no clear indication of the price or deal structure, Bloomberg News reported earlier. Firmus was looking to raise as much as US$5.5 billion (S$7 billion), including a greenshoe option, at a price that would have implied a valuation of A$43.7 billion (S$38.9 billion). Some potential investors turned more cautious as the deal progressed, voicing concern over existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the company’s debut, people familiar with the matter have said. The overhang added to questions over what some investors see as an aggressive pricing strategy, they said. “I’ve never seen an IPO so polarising,” Jun Bei Liu, co-founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap Investment, said on Bloomberg TV. “There was a lot of international investor interest. However, when it comes to the crunch, the demand seems like it isn’t there when they were asked to put up the capital that’s required.” Firmus began as a Bitcoin mining operation in Australia in 2019 and has benefited from surging demand for AI infrastructure across Asia, with a pipeline of data centre projects in Australia and Singapore. Proceeds from the listing would have funded purchases of graphics processing units for its first data centre project in Batam, Indonesia, being developed with DayOne Data Centers, as part of an eight-year partnership with Nvidia. Singapore-headquartered DayOne has filed for a US IPO and is seeking to raise as much as US$5 billion, people familiar with the matter have said. Firmus has inked a number of large deals, securing US$2 billion in commitments from investors including Nvidia and Blackstone. Other existing shareholders include Jane Street, while Firmus also raised US$505 million in a Coatue Management-led funding round in April. Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Morgan Stanley and Morgans Financial are acting as joint lead managers on the listing. Bloomberg
